Chapter 6

Chapter Notes

See the end of the chapter for notes

“So,” Lena folded her arms over her chest. She was still clad in an elegant black coat, the wide pipes of her black satin pants just barely being kept from touching the floor by the considerable height of her dark pumps. “She’s giving you iPods now too, huh?”

The Other Lena shot her a sharp smirk.

“What? Jealous?”

Lena looked down, a smile on her face. She nodded to herself before looking back up, not a shimmer of glee in her eyes. The Other Lena could almost admire it. At least it allowed her to see what she looked like when she smiled to mask her anger. Pretty damn powerful, if she said so herself.

“Very funny,” Lena said softly. “But let’s cut the bullshit.”

She took a step closer to the glass wall, eyes narrowing as they zeroed in on the Other Lena.

“You might be rotting away here, but I have an actual company to run. I can’t spare the time entertaining your little jokes.”

Other Lena’s smile dimmed just the slightest bit, which Lena seemed to take great pleasure in. A pleasure that Other Lena wouldn’t allow her to hold on to for too long.

“Are you here to yell at me again?” Other Lena sighed. “Not that I mind, it’s up to you really, but we both know it takes such a toll on you, and in the end, we both know you won’t get the resolution you’re hoping for.”

Lena took a step closer to the glass window, a scowl on her face.

“Won’t I?”

Other Lena closed her book with a sigh and stood up.

“Let me guess,” she said, walking towards the window. “You’re here to tell me I should stay away from Supergirl. Seeing as you’re talking to the party who is literally physically incapable of escaping any conversations pushed on her – exhibit A,” she nodded at Lena, “I’m going to assume you’ve already tried reasoning with Supergirl and things didn’t work out.”

Lena’s jaw clenched and Other Lena couldn’t suppress a smug smile.

“So now you’re here to once again berate me for, well I don’t know, talking to your precious Supergirl? Initiating contact? Enlighten me.”

“I am ordering you to break off your contact with her,” Lena said sharply. “You need to stay away from her.”

“She’s the one who keeps coming by my cell,” Other Lena reminded her.

“Because you keep encouraging her!”

“What? And you don’t like that she’s so fond of me? That she just can’t stay away?”

“You have some nerve – ”

“Was I right before, Lena?” Other Lena asked, ignoring her counterpart. “Are you just jealous?”

Lena scoffed. “That’s idiotic.”

“Is it?” Other Lena walked up to the glass separating the two of them. She could see the quiet disdain in Lena’s eyes as she stared at her döppelgänger – just barely resisting a shudder.

Lena’s eyes narrowed. “It is.”

“I don’t believe you.”

“I don’t care what you believe,” Lena cut in. “Stay the fuck away from her.”

“You should try telling her that.”

“Don’t get cute,” Lena warned. “Right now you’re in a comfortable cell, given enough freedom and space to waste your time here however you see fit. I can change that.”

“Ah, yes. All the freedom to spend my time however I want, right?” Other Lena asked. “Look around, Lena. There is absolutely nothing to do here. Nothing to engage my mind. I might just as well wither away in here.”

“Well,” Lena smiled, “be my fucking guest.”

Other Lena shook her head and smiled.

“You’d like that, wouldn’t you? Easier to think about me dead than having to think about me here, all alone with my thoughts.”

Lena’s smile froze on her face.

“Yes,” Other Lena whispered. “You do know what it’s like, right? When there is nothing else to distract us anymore? When it’s just us and our thoughts? You do know how ugly that can get.”

Lena clenched her jaw, her face expertly uninterested in Other Lena’s words, but Other Lena saw the way Lena’s knuckles were turning white, clenching around the handle of her purse as if it could physically keep her from remembering those awful moments in which she’d been all alone with her thoughts.

“You deserve it,” Lena finally said. “You deserve this – this punishment.”

“Do I?”

“Yes,” Lena whispered. “You deserve to rot here. I can think of no better way for you to make up for what you’ve done.”

“And what about what’s been done to me?” Other Lena hissed. “At least I have a reason to do what I do. I’m trying to correct the wrongs that have taken place in my world. What is it that you do, huh?”

Lena scoffed and turned around, but Other Lena wouldn’t let her go. She dug her claws in deeper.

“You think I haven’t heard about what you did?” she asked almost greedily. “You think I don’t know that you attacked the Kryptonian with Kryptonite?”

Lena stiffened, her back ramrod straight like she’d been frozen in time.

“Yes,” Other Lena whispered. “You did exactly as I did – ”

“To get Myriad!” Lena finally spat, turning around with an expression so furious, it would make anyone cower in fear. But not the Other Lena. She smiled with such satisfaction that it made Lena’s blood boil. “I needed that instrument to help people. To change the world for the better!”

“Turn and twist it however you want, darling. You and I both know we did the exact same thing.”

“That is – ”

“Did you like it?” Other Lena asked. “Did you like hurting her like that? Feeling so powerful, knowing you’d brought a god to her knees?”

“She’s no god,” Lena said through clenched teeth.

“No,” Other Lena agreed. “Hurting her like that proved she wasn’t, didn’t it? Didn’t it feel good, realizing you’d brought the most powerful being to her knees? Knowing you had the power to decide whether she lived or died?”

“No,” Lena whispered. “No.”

“You don’t have to lie to me, Lena,” Other Lena smiled. “We are the same, after all.”

Lena looked up, finally locking eyes with her doppelgänger.

“No,” she said. “We’re not.”

“No?”

“No.”

“How do you figure? We both used Kryptonite against her for our own reasons. We both wanted to make the world better, no?”

“No,” Lena said coldly. “We are not the same. Because I would never, ever do anything like it again. Because I regret what I’ve done. Because If I could go back in time and undo it, I would. And that where you and I are different,” she whispered. “Because while I try to find a way to live with myself every day, knowing what I’ve done, you’re just biding your time. Because you can’t fucking wait until you get the chance to hurt her again.”

She straightened up again.

“But I won’t let you,” Lena said simply. “I will stop you.”

“Will you now?” Other Lena asked. “Why?”

“I – What?” Confusion clouded Lena’s features. “What do you mean why? You need me to tell you why killing is amoral? To explain to you the emotional toll it would take on her family, her friends, the people of National City if she were to… if you were to kill her? Or would you prefer cold numbers and fact on how many people would statistically die without Supergirl there to save them?”

“No,” Other Lena sighed, exhausted by the conversation. “I mean, why? Why does it need to be you to stop me?”

“I… I don’t understand – ”

“They’re not going to thank you, Lena.”

Lena fell quiet. She looked oddly surprised for someone who should theoretically be able to predict exactly what her clone would say, Other Lena mused. “It won’t erase what you’ve done. Not in reality and not in their eyes. You know this.”

It sounded almost sympathetic.

“That’s – it doesn’t matter,” Lena whispered, more to herself than to her doppelgänger. “It’s not – it’s not about that. It’s not,” she stressed when Other Lena didn’t look convinced.

“If you say so.”

“I do,” Lena said harshly, taking an instinctive, angry step closer to the glass. “It does not matter. You’re me. You’re my copy. That means you’re my responsibility.”

“Thought you said you weren’t anything alike.”

“Psychologically speaking,” Lena bit. “I won’t fool myself denying our biological identicality.”

“You would need to squint pretty hard,” Other Lena mumbled.

“But that doesn’t make us equal. You’re vile and pathetic. A complete waste of oxygen.”

She took a step closer to the glass, the vein on her head pulsing like it was about to burst. The Other Lena could recognize it all too well. Still, she held fast and raised her chin defiantly.

“If it were up to me, we’d just destroy you. I don’t even care how. Because while everyone should be spending their time trying to rescue people on this planet, they’re wasting time, effort, and resources on helping to relocate you. A murderer. A monster,” she spat.

The Other Lena raised an eyebrow.

“So do it,” she whispered. “Grab that gun that’s most definitely hidden away in that purse of yours,” she nodded at the bag, “and shoot me. It won’t be hard, I’m defenseless after all.”

She held up her hands and turned her head to emphasize how empty the cell was, save for the books stacked up under her bed.

“I highly doubt that,” Lena smiled mirthlessly. “I’m sure you have all sorts of nasty tricks up your sleeve.”

“Why don’t you come find out?” Other Lena smirked.

“But it’s not about that,” Lena ignored her. “And don’t for a second think I wouldn’t. But I know that as soon as I do, I’ll have so much bullshit to deal with that I can’t even spare to think of right now, and believe me, darling. You’re not worth the headache.”

Other Lena clutched her chest theatrically. “You wound me."

Lena laughed soundlessly, nodding her head to herself.

“Taunting me won’t work,” she finally whispered. “You want me on your side here. I might not be allowed to kill you, but that doesn’t mean I can’t do anything else. I could turn you into an interdimensional guinea pig if I wanted. I could make you suffer, all in the name of science. And I could get away with it.”

“I don’t think you could.”

“No?”

“No,” Other Lena shrugged. “I don’t.”

“Please,” Lena smiled as if her counterpart had just made a joke instead of having her threats of torture rescinded. “Do tell.”

Other Lena shrugged again, noticing with glee that Lena’s smile tightened on her face. It was almost fun to be able to tell when Lena was really fantasizing about strangling her. Almost comedic to observe her own thoughts reflected back at her through a different, unharmed version of herself.

“It’s quite simple, really,” Other Lena smiled, tilting her head. “I don’t think our local Superhero would like that very much.”

Lena’s satisfied smile turned into an ugly scowl, and Other Lena just barely kept from laughing at the crude anger on the other woman’s face.

“Just because I don’t want you to kill her doesn’t mean she has to like me,” Lena said. “I’m still her boss here. She gets no say in what happens to you. That’s all me. So don’t for a second think she has the ability to override my authority on – ”

“Oh, I wasn’t insinuating that,” Other Lena said, brushing some dust off her blue pants.

Lena narrowed her eyes. “Then what were you insinuating?”

Other Lena smiled broadly. “That you won’t upset her like that. Not when your relationship is in shambles – and that’s putting it nicely.”

“And what do you know of my relationship with Kara?”

Other Lena shrugged, a small, innocent smile playing around her lips.

“Not much. The Kryptonite thing was a big one.”

Lena didn’t look impressed.

“Although,” Other Lena leaned in conspiratorially. “The guards around here are very loose-lipped. It seems like you two were close. Really close.”

“Stop it.”

“And then it all turned sour. Why’s that, hmm?”

“I’m not joking.”

Other Lena rolled her eyes, but leaned back against the wall, letting Lena relax for just a moment before she did actually have an aneurism. Lena’s phone buzzed and she fished it out of her bag with an annoyed sigh. Her eyes scanned the screen, a frown appearing on her face as she quickly typed out a response.

“She’s starting to like me, you know?”

“Is that so?”

“Mmm. She must be feeling pretty lonely. I can’t get her to leave me alone,” Other Lena teased. “She’s here all day every day. Maybe she just needs a friend.”

“And you’re that friend? The woman who repeatedly tried to kill her?”

Other Lena batted her eyes innocently. “There are worse ways to start a friendship.”

“Cute,” Lena deadpanned. “Tell her to leave. Tell her to stay away.”

“Yes,” Other Lena folded her hands on her knee, “the problem with that, Lena, is that I don’t particularly want to do that. And you can glare at me as much as you like,” she smirked, “but we both know there is nothing you can do. You’re at a stalemate, darling. You can rant and threaten me as much as you’d like,” she tilted her head with a smile. “You’ve got no more moves left. Whatever you do, you’ll always lose.”

Any trace of a smile had left Lena’s face. Her fists were clenched by her side, trembling with rage. And Other Lena knew she’d won. It was so damn easy to hurt herself. And if she had the energy to, she would’ve had to analyze just why it felt so good to make her mirror image hurt. To watch her suffer in blind hatred and disgust.

“You must hate me so,” the Other Lena murmured almost thoughtfully.

“Words cannot describe – ”

“No,” Other Lena sighed almost tiredly, cutting Lena off, “not because I’m you and I killed and I’m a monster,” she rolled her eyes, bored. “But because I’m close to her. I’m getting close to her. Because she cares about me.”

“She cares about everyone,” Lena folded her arms over her chest. “I’ve seen her get caught up in her own moral dilemmas over the worst of people on this planet. You’re not special.”

“Aren’t I?” Other Lena tilted her head. “It’s not killing you even a little bit, knowing she’s reaching out to me? Desperate, I would even argue, to get me to change?”

Lena’s mouth was a hard, red line, and Other Lena enjoyed it so. She leaned in, studying Lena’s face.

“Do you want to know what I think?”

“Not even a little bit.”

Other Lena bit back a smile and shook her head.

“I’ll tell you anyway,” she said sweetly. “And you’ll stay and listen, because you know that I’m the only person in the whole universe who understands you. Who gets you, perfectly. You can’t resist talking to someone as brilliant as yourself.”

“You sound like Lex,” Lena said bitterly. “I’m not that self-absorbed.”

“No,” Other Lena agreed. “But it’s not about that. It’s about the need to be understood. The need to be heard and listened to by someone who understands you. And psychologists don’t really cut it for us now, do they? They don’t understand that our minds are racing at a speed they can’t even conceive of. They have no understanding of just how deep our issues are buried, what traumas we’ve had to endure and survive to get to where we are today. They couldn’t possibly comprehend how we deal with that trauma every single day of our lives, from the moment we wake up the minute we go to sleep – and that we do it all while finding the secrets this world holds for us. Tirelessly.”

She leaned back again, exhaled slightly, as she felt a tiny crack in her lip with her tongue. She clacked it and looked at Lena.

“We have learned more about this world in the few years we have been in it, than any mortal ever has or will. That makes us special, Lena. It doesn’t mean that therapists and other people are stupid. It just means they can’t understand us. It means you need me to explain yourself to you. To analyze your mind. Your thoughts.”

“I… I don’t – ”

“Come on, now, Lena,” Other Lena said. “I already know what you’re going to do. So instead of wasting both our time, just do what you and I both know you are going to do. Listen.”

Lena stiffened, frozen in her minimalist, stylish outfit in front of Other Lena’s cell. Other Lena’s lips curled up in a smile and she cast her eyes down for just a second. It wouldn’t be fitting to flaunt her obvious win in Lena’s face. But God, did it feel good.

“I think that your issue with me goes to the root of your relationship with Supergirl,” Other Lena said. “I think you’re projecting.”

Lena didn’t say anything. She looked so still, one might even wonder if she’d heard Other Lena at all, but she knew. She knew Lena was listening.

“I think you’re scared,” she whispered. “Because you were furious with Supergirl. Justifiably so. That’s important. Because it made her feel guilty. Guilty enough to traverse the universe to make it right. Guilty enough to bear the brunt of your anger.”

Lena let out a small sound from the back of her throat, and Other Lena knew she was on the right track.

“And knowing us, we wanted to relish in that power, didn’t we? After having been denied the accountability and guilt of those who wronged us, it must’ve felt exhilarating to watch a goddess beg us on her knees for forgiveness. To watch her grovel.”

“I told you,” Lena whispered. “She’s not a goddess.”

“But not far from it either,” Other Lena said. “Awkward bumbling aside, we’re talking about one of the most powerful beings in the galaxy. And she was at your feet, begging you for forgiveness.”

Lena shook her head, closing her eyes as her eyebrows knitted together in agony over the memory.

“Stop.”

“So you didn’t back off,” Other Lena whispered. “No, that power – you wanted to keep it. So you pushed. We always do. You pushed and you pushed at her limits, and you must’ve gotten such a rush out of seeing how far you could make her bend for you – just how much she renegotiated her own morals to give you the benefit of the doubt. To make you the one exception to all her rules.”

“Please stop.”

Lena held no more power in that room. Even if she wasn’t the one behind bars, rotting away in a cell in a prison outfit, she might just as well be. She could no more decide on leaving as Other Lena did. She was captured in a web of misery and self-loathing, and Other Lena just couldn’t resist pulling on every string, wrapping her in it entirely.

“You pushed and you pushed,” she pressed, “and I don’t know when, but at one point or another, you must’ve noticed the change. You must’ve realized – oh you must’ve felt so paralyzed – realizing you took it too far. That you might’ve pushed too hard. That you reached even the limits of poor Supergirl’s ability to stick up for you. When was it, huh? When was it, Lena, that you finally saw that you pushed too far? When did she stop apologizing for your behavior? Tell me.”

Lena trembled, blinking tears she probably didn’t know she’d shed. Her mouth opened and she stammered weakly, trying to voice her thoughts.

“Tell me,” Other Lena pressed again.

“She… she told me she’d stop me,” Lena whispered, dazed, her eyes glassy and far away. “Just like she would any other villain.”

Other Lena hummed.

“You thought the bad she’d done would outweigh the tiny misfortunes you caused her, didn’t you? You thought you could push and push – but now you’re not so sure anymore. Now you’re not so sure she’d save you over someone else. She might’ve, at one time. But no,” Other Lena shook her head. “After all you’ve done, you worry she’d choose someone else, the city, the world, over you. Not like before, when you knew she’d let the city burn if it meant saving you. Isn’t that right, Lena?”

“I… I don’t know.”

“Oh, but you do. But if there’s one thing we know best, it’s how to be stubborn. You’re rolling around in that resentment towards her, knowing you’ve fucked up everything – knowing you’re on your own, this time by your own doing. You’ve managed to turn the most forgiving woman against you, and now you don’t know how to handle yourself anymore,” Other Lena said. “There’s no going back, so you just keep pushing.”

“I’m not a villain,” Lena managed to croak out. “Just because she can’t see that I’m trying… Trying to help people. Trying to stop my brother from doing harm…”

“But there’s the problem,” Other Lena said gently. “Once upon a time, she might’ve taken your word for it, but she won’t anymore. She doesn’t trust you anymore. And that’s what kills you, isn’t it? To know that she may think you to be beyond help? To know that if something were to go wrong, she would think you were the one to blame. The one person who always believed in you.”

“She wouldn’t,” Lena whispered, tears shining in her eyes as she stubbornly refused to let them fall. “She wouldn’t.”

“Oh, Lena,” Other Lena tilted her head. “We both know you’re lying.”

Lena let out a dry sob and covered her mouth with her hand, shaking her head as she closed her eyes – almost as if she was willing herself to forget. To wake up in her bed, free of this nightmare. Free of all of it.

“And that is what bothers you so much, isn’t it?” Other Lena said softly. “It kills you to see her extend her hand to me. It kills you to see her try so hard with me – knowing you got that same exact chance, and refused it. I believe,” she whispered, “that you’re scared that if it came down to you or me, she’d believe that I’m the one still worth saving. That you’re the one she deems lost. And I think it’s torturing you.”

Lena turned around and stifled a sob in her fist. Other Lena sank back on her bed, leaning against the wall. She stared at Lena’s shaking body, just outside her cell.

She thought she’d feel more joy, seeing her condescending, holier-than-thou counterpart crumble. Spirits crushed and dreams evaporated. But instead, she felt nothing. She felt empty and – strangely – even almost a hint of pity for the woman in front of her.

“It’s not her approval you need, Lena.”

Lena was still shaking and didn’t give any sign she’d heard her.

“She would’ve disappointed you eventually,” Other Lena murmured. “They always do. Believe me when I say, you found out the easy way.”

Her hand absentmindedly rubbed her chest, right over where the green rock had replaced her beating heart. She could feel it pulsing inside of her, poisoning her as the rods and wires dug into the veins and muscle around it in a constant flare of agony. She’d learned how to ignore the pain – but could never repress it completely. It was always there. A reminder of Supergirl’s cruelty twisting inside of her with every beat of what had once been her heart.

“It’s better you find out now, when you can still prepare yourself. Not when you’re falling out a helicopter and know she won’t come and save you.”

Lena stiffened.

“I’ll make it right for us,” Other Lena promised softly, unsure of whether she was talking to Lena, or reminding herself. “I’ll make her pay.”

“No.”

Lena’s voice was so cutting, so harsh after the sounds of her quiet, muffled sobs in the room, that it tore Other Lena out of her reverie.

“I’m sorry?”

“I said no.”

Lena turned around. Wet streaks ran over her pink cheeks, her eyes red-rimmed and glistening, her lashes clumped together in wet little strands – and yet she glared at Other Lena with a fit of fiery anger that overpowered her piteous look.

“You can’t hurt her,” Lena said simply. “I told you. I won’t let you.”

“Lena,” Other Lena warned, “I just told you – ”

“I don’t care if you’re right,” Lena interrupted her. “I don’t even particularly care whether you’re wrong. I told you no. You can’t hurt her.”

Other Lena stood up.

“She won’t thank you for saving her, Lena,” she said coldly.

“I don’t need her to.”

“Liar.”

“I haven’t forgiven her,” Lena whispered. “And you’re right. I may have pushed too far for her to forgive me either. But that doesn’t make me you.”

Other Lena glared at her.

“That doesn’t make me want to destroy her. That doesn’t make me want to fuck over the world just to see her burn.” She shook her head, and for just a second, all the anger left her body. “It just makes me numb,” she whispered.

Other Lena recoiled. A hint of a sad, bitter smile spread over Lena’s lips.

“And I bet that even after everything you’ve done – everything you think you’ve succeeded in – it’s only made you numb too.”

A silence so heavy it felt like it was crushing the air around them fell over the hallway. Other Lena almost buckled under it. Her eyes were fixed on Lena’s, mouth open in quiet disbelief. She balled her fists by her side, shaking with rage, or… she couldn’t even name the typhoon of emotions swirling around inside of her anymore. It was pain and anger and… hurt, all wrapped into one.

“No,” she managed to say. “No.”

Lena didn’t reply. Her smile had disappeared, and she just looked empty. Tired. The dark circles under her eyes only served to intensify the lost, dazedness that had slowly consumed her over the course of their conversation.

She looked at Other Lena with something akin to pity, and it made Other Lena irrationally more frustrated. After a beat, Lena shook her head and took a deep breath, ignoring all of Other Lena’s bottled-up feelings about to explode. She nodded to herself and picked up her purse.

“No,” Other Lena said again, standing so close to the glass she could see her own reflection twice. Once in the glass, and once standing before her like a far-off spirit, grieving some long-lost love.

“I am not numb,” Other Lena whispered. “You’re projecting!”

Lena smiled softly, eyes sad as they locked with her doppelgänger’s.

“Now who’s lying,” she whispered.

It stunned Other Lena so suddenly, her mouth fell shut on its own. For once, she didn’t quite know what to say anymore, brows knitting together in confusion.

“Goodbye, Lena,” Lena murmured. “Take care of yourself.”

Other Lena didn’t say anything. Not as she heard the heels clacking away from her cell through the hallway, and not when she heard the door open and close until her hallway was silent again. At one point, she sank back down on her bed, her mirror image staring hollowly back at her.

She was alone again.

 

 

“Lena!”

Kara rushed in with the usual bustle and enthusiasm that she was sure Other Lena had gotten used to by now. Red cheeks, arms full of books, and a broad smile that – since it had convinced Cat Grant not to fire her – she hoped would manage to win over Other Lena as well.

“Supergirl,” Other Lena said easily. “Gracing my humble presence once again.”

“Oh,” Kara let out a short, self-conscious laugh. “Sorry, I can’t really give you a heads-up. My schedule’s kind of crazy. But I do have good news!”

Other Lena’s eyebrow went up, so suave and self-confident in a way that shook Kara to her very core every time she saw it. In the five years since she’d met Lena, she had never, ever gotten used to it.

“Yeah,” she shook her head. “I convinced the D.E.O. – ”

“Your sister,” Other Lena clarified.

“ – and my sister,” Kara conceded, “to install a TV here! In the hallway! In front of your cell!”

“Wait, what?” Other Lena asked, and Kara felt slightly proud for having caught the woman by surprise.

“Yes!” she could barely contain her excitement, bouncing excitedly on her feet. “It’s a small one,” she had to admit, “and you’ll have to ask the guards to turn it on and off, and there might be a lot of restrictions on which channels you’re allowed to have access to – ”

“Wow, I’m really getting the deal of a lifetime here.”

“But you’ll be able to have some entertainment that isn’t completely dependent on me visiting you with books,” Kara smiled. “You won’t have to ration your own entertainment anymore. You’ll have other things to do if you’d like.”

Other Lena hummed thoughtfully.

“Does this mean you won’t come visit me as often anymore?” she asked slyly.

Kara’s eyes widened.

“Oh no!” she exclaimed. “I mean, unless you want that? In theory, I can come by as much as I do now! I was just worried, you know, what with my job and my Supergirl activities, that if I wouldn’t be able to visit, you’d just be stuck here with nothing to read and nothing to do, and it just made me feel terrible, so I just thought – ”

“Supergirl,” Other Lena cut off her rambling with one hand.

Kara quickly shut up.

“It was a good idea,” she smiled. “Thank you.”

“You’re welcome,” Kara said, a little out of breath. “It should be installed sometime this week.”

“My hero,” Other Lena teased, and Kara ducked her head, biting her lip to keep from smiling.

“So,” Other Lena smiled. “Did you bring me anything else? Or just good news?”

“Oh!” Kara’s face lit up. “Yeah, I brought you a couple of things!”

Kara didn’t miss the young, excited sparkle in Other Lena’s eyes. She had to bite her tongue to keep from smiling, because she knew that if she commented on it, she wouldn’t see it again for days.

“So you said no classics,” Kara said, “and no post-colonial children’s books…”

“Right,” Other Lena said slowly.

“So I got you…”

Kara pulled a dark book with a curious cover out of her bag.

“A dark, very non-classical, modern children’s book! Two, even!”

She walked to the little hatch on the side of Lena’s cell, trying not to skip in excitement. Lena stood up in one fluid move too, both of them having found that their truce started right at that little hatch. It was the place of gifts and peace offerings. Kara felt no fear opening the lock and extending her hand into Lena’s space, just as Lena never made any move to reach for the buttons of her prison suit and unleash her weapon underneath.

It was no one’s land, and it was safe.

“Neil Gaiman?” Other Lena read.

“Yes. Coraline and Stardust,” Kara said happily. “I have a feeling you’re going to like the first one.”

“Oh yeah?” Lena raised an eyebrow. And something about standing so close to her – Kara’s hands still carrying the weight of the books, while Lena’s fingers were holding on their sides – made it feel so much more intimate.

Kara hummed, staring straight into Other Lena’s green eyes, wholly unafraid. “I think you’ll find the villain very relatable?”

“Oh?” Other Lena’s eyes scanned the cover. “Who’s the villain?”

“A sociopathic, demonic mother.”

It was followed by just a second of silence, in which Lena just blinked at her – and then she burst out laughing. It surprised both of them equally, Kara thought. It seemed like Other Lena hadn’t laughed so openly in ages. Such spontaneous, irrational laughter about something so dumb, that it shocked them both. It was a full-body laugh that made Other Lena’s eyes crinkle and the corners of her mouth curl up enough to uncover a row of perfect teeth – and that Kara couldn’t help but laugh along to.

“Too soon?”

Other Lena shook her head, slowly coming down from her high.

“No,” she smiled, shaking her head. “I promise. Oh my God.”

Kara chuckled.

“So you’ve got some experience with my mother then?”

“Oh yeah,” Kara shook her head. “She’s a handful.”

“That’s a kind of way of putting it,” Other Lena deadpanned.

“Yeah, well, she tried to have me killed repeatedly, but we’ve also worked together to save Lena’s life. I’d say our relationship is complicated at best.”

Other Lena frowned, confused. “You and my mother worked together to save your Lena?”

“Yeah, I wouldn’t say it was the most pleasant of team-ups? She stabbed me in the back a couple of times, I had to have her arrested – but we got the job done, and that’s what counts.”

Other Lena just stared at Kara.

“What?” Kara asked self-consciously.

“You just… you continue to surprise me.”

“I do?”

“Yes.”

“Is that… a good thing?”

Other Lena’s eyes bore into Kara’s, neither of them acknowledging that their hands were touching once again.

“I don’t know yet,” she whispered. “I hope to find that out soon.”

 

 

Days changed and rolled into fresh, new weeks with new CatCo editions to be published, but Kara barely noticed. She was vaguely aware of Andrea stressing out in the bullpen, tossing out articles here and there, and forcing the technology department to dedicate entire sections of the magazine to her Obsidian tech. Kara didn’t care. She wrote articles that fit within Andrea’s narrow view of what the magazine was supposed to focus on, and she collaborated with Nia and William when she had to.

But it wasn’t her main goal anymore. She found herself unwilling to work late anymore, stuck in a place she didn’t like anymore. She checked into the D.E.O. often, asking Alex about the progress on the portal to get Other Lena home, but it was always the same answer. With Mxy still missing, it was damn near impossible to get Other Lena home safe.

And Kara would always personally update Other Lena on the matter, who seemed entirely indifferent to the whole process. The only thing she really wanted to know was what books Kara had brought along with her, and whether she had time for a chat.

And Kara always would. If not for a minute before she had to patrol the city, then for as long as possible, to talk about anything safe, like what Lena thought of the books. What she had teased the guards about that day.

Kara would always come back.

 

 

“Uno?”

“Uno.”

Other Lena sighed, closing her book with a regretful, longing glance in her eyes.

“You wanted to bring us a game to play together and you brought Uno.”

“That’s correct.”

“And you didn’t brink poker because…?”

“Oh, because I have a terrible poker face. I lose every time.”

“When I tell you that I am shocked to my very core, Supergirl.”

“Don’t be mean! Also, it’s not like you have anything to bet against me,” Kara shrugged. “And Alex has told me that poker with no stakes is totally boring.”

“Awtch. Now who’s being mean?”

Kara bit down a smile, dividing the cards.

“It’ll be a bit awkward playing with a glass wall between us…”

“Oh you can open the door, I don’t mind,” Other Lena said playfully. Kara threw her a look and Other Lena smiled. “Very intimidating, Supergirl. Fine, fine, we’ll manage.”

Other Lena watched as Kara meticulously shook the cards, giving them each seven cards before dividing the biggest pile of cards into two stacks. She walked to the hatch on the side handing Lena her seven playing cards, and the extra stack of cards.

“Thank you,” Other Lena smiled.

“You’re welcome,” Kara said, trying not to notice Other Lena’s hands against hers.

She did, though. They were warm, her skin a little dry from the lack of fresh air inside the D.E.O. cells, but still soft. Still Lena.

Kara sat down cross-legged in front of Lena’s cell, picking up her own cards with a little frown. For a moment, the hallway was quiet again, filled with nothing but the rustling of cards.

“So,” Other Lena said conversationally, folding her cards out like a fan. “NSYNC, huh?”

Kara’s eyes widened, and she looked up at Other Lena like a deer caught in headlights.

“What?” she stammered. “How?”

Other Lena picked up the iPod and waved it in front of Kara’s face.

“No,” Kara groaned. “I forgot that was even on there!”

“Oh I’m sure.”

“Please ignore that.”

“I mean it’s cute. A little too fifteen-year-old/ 2000's American for me but – ”

“Oh my Rao, give it back.”

“No, now I don’t want to.”

“Give it back! I’ll put some other music on there, please!”

“No,” Other Lena smiled petulantly, “I want to listen to NSYNC and Britney now.”

“Lena, please.”

“No, I’m serious,” Lena insisted, “I like it.”

“Oh dear Rao, I told you I hadn’t updated it in forever!”

“Clearly,” Other Lena mused. “There’s a lot of music on here that hasn’t seen the light of day since people realized low-cut jeans weren’t the sexy, stylistic fashion phenomenon they thought it was.”

“Oh my God,” Kara groaned, and Lena laughed. A warm, young laugh. Carefree and spontaneous again – it made Kara so inexplicably happy, she didn’t even mind that it was at her expense.  

“Fine,” Kara clutched her chest dramatically, “insult the best music ever made. See if I do you a solid ever again.”

“Best music ever – how long have you been on this planet? There is more to discover than just Justin Timberlake and every cheesy boyband from the 2000s, you do know that right?”

“Okay, I’ve been to several different planets and I have heard more music than anyone else on earth! Except maybe J’onn. So yes, I feel like I’ve balanced all the options, and have concluded that JT and Britney are simply the best in all the universe.”

Other Lena groaned, rolling her eyes and Kara laughed.

“You’re just like my sister, she does the exact same thing when I say that.”

“Well for once, your sister might have a point,” Other Lena glared.

“Uhu,” Kara hummed. “I’ll tell her.”

“Don’t you dare.”

“It’s your turn to play, Lena.”

“I mean it.”

“Uhu.”

Other Lena sighed and picked up her cards again. She frowned, eyes flitting from one card to another.

“Right,” she said slowly. “So how does one play Uno again?”

 

 

Before she left that day, Kara remembered the final item in her bag.

“Lena?” she asked, rumbling around in her bag.

Other Lena hummed, looking up from the book she’d opened when Kara started packing her stuff up for the evening, ready to go home.

“I got you something else.”

Other Lena instinctively sat up straighter, trying to take a better look at the little plastic box in Kara’s hands. It didn’t look like much, Kara knew, but she had a feeling Lena would like it.

“What is it?” Other Lena asked curiously, once Kara had handed it to her through the hatch.

“Oh,” she blushed. “It’s kind of silly.”

“Oh yeah?”

Other Lena frowned, her nails following the line where the box could seemingly be folded open. She tried to pull it open, years of neglect having made the plastic stubborn and almost unyielding. It opened little by little, and Kara got nervous at the sight of it.

“I found it among some old stuff of mine. It’s a car game, you see? So you can play on the road? You’ve got the tiny box, but if you open it, it forms a tiny board. I know it looks silly but – ”

The box clattered open, two small bags containing small, white, and black pieces fell on Other Lena’s bed. Other Lena stared a little disoriented from the pieces on her bed to the checkered little box.

“You gave me a chessboard?” she whispered.

To be fair, ‘chessboard’ seemed like an entirely inaccurate, overachieving term for what that thing really was, but Kara wasn’t about to say that. Not when Other Lena had fallen completely quiet, in utter and total surprise for the first time since they’d met. Speechless, clutching the box, that had now unfolded into a tiny chessboard, in her trembling hands.

“Yeah,” Kara said awkwardly. “It’s magnetic, you see? You have the tiny pieces and you can move them around, you know, even when the car’s moving. I’m not a good enough player to play against you, but I thought, you know, maybe you could play yourself? Lena once told me she does that from time to time, so I figured you might like that too?”

She brought her shoulders in and rubbed her arms in discomfort.

“I know it’s silly,” Kara blushed. “I don’t have the real deal. I just… I saw it, and I couldn’t resist bringing it here. I know you have your own handcrafted sets and all, and I know you’d much rather play with real pieces. It’s stupid. I – look, if you want, I can try and score a real chessboard but – ”

“No,” Other Lena whispered, her fingers gliding over the admittedly ugly beige and black tiles of the box. “No. This is perfect.”

She looked up, seeming genuinely confused by Kara and her every action.

“It’s not,” Kara was turning red at that point. “It’s old and tiny – and one of the rooks got lost on our trip to San Francisco, so if you find a tiny, round magnet? That’s the rook.”

Lena smiled, and it looked so fragile and so confused that Kara didn’t know what to do with herself.

“It’s just really dumb,” Kara concluded lamely.

But Lena wouldn’t have any of it. Her fingers spread over the little board like it was magical, the pieces gaining in value just from being held by her expert fingers.

“Thank you,” she said earnestly.

Kara smiled, a little unsure of herself.

“Well, I had to give you something for your win just now,” she whispered.

Other Lena let out a short laugh.

“Yes,” she said slowly. “For someone who claims to have played this game over and over again with her sister, you’re really bad at it.”

Kara ducked her head and laughed, allowing herself to feel the bizarre silliness of the situation for just one short moment. Allowing herself to forget that this was the woman who hurt her – and that instead, she was just Lena, and she was just Kara. For a moment, Kara could just forget and smile at Other Lena.

“You won’t be so lucky next time,” Kara promised.

Other Lena laughed and nodded to herself. She arched her eyebrow and smirked.

“Bring it on, Supergirl.”

 

 

Kara walked back into the D.E.O. on a bright Saturday, a happy smile on her face. She greeted the guards – even the ones that Lex had hired, the ones she knew were just waiting on their chance to arrest her and throw her into a cell with all the other aliens. Today, she wouldn’t even allow them to get her down.

It was a good day. The sun was out, Andrea had approved her article – albeit it while she was on a distracted high from a sales boom of her platinum Obsidian lenses, but Kara counted it as a win. She’d gone to the fancy, little French patisserie on 3rd Avenue and treated herself to a cruller, and a box of macarons for Lena. It was way too expensive, and probably not even half as good as they looked – but Rao, did they look pretty. So cute and colorful in their little box with the golden ribbon. Kara just couldn’t leave them behind. She wanted Other Lena to have something pretty in her cell, something pretty to enjoy. So she’d brought it along.

She was so happy and so focused on getting to Other Lena’s cell, already imagining the way her eyes would sparkle when she got the little box in her hands, that she had completely lost touch with her surroundings. She walked with only one goal in mind, and in doing so, didn’t even notice when someone was heading straight for her, nose buried in a thick file, a frustrated frown on her face - until it was too late.

Papers went flying, and Kara heard a familiar shout when she abruptly collided with the other woman. Kara blindly reached around to steady the woman and was already stuttering a thousand different apologies, when her eyes locked with the woman whose arms she was holding.

“Lena?”

“Supergirl!”

“Oh!”

Kara quickly let go, leaving Lena to wobble on her feet – unsteady in her trusted high heels like Kara had never seen before.

“Gosh, I’m so sorry! Are you okay?”

“I’m fine,” Lena said curtly. “It wasn’t your fault. I wasn’t looking where I was going.”

“Oh, me neither!” Kara rushed to say. “It’s definitely on me too.”

“Let’s just call this a tie,” Lena said tiredly, and Kara quickly shut up.

Lena sighed as she looked around at the flurry of papers on the floor, a sheet or two still softly swaying downwards, waiting to mix in with the rest.

“I’ll help!” Kara said quickly, falling to her knees, rushing to collect all the documents.

“You really don’t have to.”

“It’s okay, I got it!”

Kara went as fast as she could, gathering everything she could find like she was on the clock.

“Kara, you – oh.”

Lena blinked in confusion as Kara gently pushed the neat stack of papers back into her hands.

“Here you go,” she said shyly. “Sorry about, ehm, everything.”

“It’s fine,” Lena said slowly. “Thank you.”

“Any time.”

Kara caught a glimpse of a sheet full of scribbled formulas and numbers.

“That for the portal?” Kara asked conversationally.

“What? Oh,” Lena shook her head. “Yes. It’s just some notes from my research last night. I’m going to see what Brainy thinks.”

Kara nodded. “So no new progress?”

“Not really,” Lena sighed, and Kara thought she looked tired. “But we’ll keep trying.”

And then, to Kara’s utter and complete surprise, Lena shot her a small, tired smile. Kara couldn’t be sure whether it was a slip-up due to extreme sleep deprivation, or if the frustration of her work had finally pushed Lena over the edge of insanity, but Kara was dumbfounded at the sight of it.

“I, eh, yeah,” Kara whispered, all at once completely unable to make sense of anything around her anymore. “Sure.”

Lena nodded, pulling the documents close to her chest. Her eyes fell on Kara’s tote-bag, bulking with everything she’d collected for Other Lena again.

“You going by to bring her more books?” Lena asked, surprisingly neutral.

“Yeah,” Kara said slowly – cautiously.

“Here.”

Lena dug in her own purse and fished out an edition of the academic editorial journal of Biochemistry.

“I finished it this morning,” Lena said somewhat kindly. “I’m sure she’ll appreciate it. It has some interesting – and some laughable – ideas about the future study of alien elements on earth. It’s a good read.”

“Thank you,” Kara said slowly. “That’s… really nice of you.”

Lena shrugged, put her files back into her purse.

“It’s just a magazine, Supergirl,” she said, smile gone, voice back to the neutral detachment from before.

“Okay,” Kara straightened up too, refusing to let herself feel bad about Lena’s change in moods again. “Thank you anyway.”

Lena nodded.

“Supergirl.”

“Bye.”

Lena turned, her heels clicking on the floor again, waiting to turn left towards her own personal lab. Just before she could disappear, however, an idea sprung up in Kara’s mind.

“Lena?” she called out.

Lena froze. She hesitated for just a second, contemplating her options before she shook her head and turned around. Kara could see her breathing out slowly, trying to find her patience again.

“Yes, Kara?”

“Ehm, what hair dye do you use?”

Lena blinked at her. “Excuse me?”

Kara blushed. “Your hair. Ehm, sorry. You maybe didn’t want me to know about that. It’s just… Other Lena’s roots are showing? I wanted to give her something to touch up her roots, but I didn’t know the exact shade. I’m sorry, forget I said anything. I didn’t mean to – ”

“I’ll get you a box,” Lena cut her off, holding up her hand. “Just… don’t tell her I gave it to you. She’ll be insufferable,” Lena muttered.

“Oh.” A smile spread over Kara’s face. “Thank you!”

Lena nodded. She half-turned away, ready to walk off, but she paused. Her eyes seemed to do a double-take, taking in the blush on Kara’s cheeks and her bright smile – a smile she probably hadn’t seen directed at her in a very long time.

“She told you I dye my hair?” she asked, almost curiously.

“Oh, not directly? I saw. The light made it obvious.”

Lena nodded. Before she could turn and walk away though, Kara stopped her.

“I like it,” she whispered softly.

“My hair?”

Kara smiled shyly. “It suits you, the color. It’s warm. Pretty.”

“And you think that suits me?” Lena hadn’t meant to sound so bitter, but the pitying scrunch in Kara’s eyebrows was enough to make her curse her sarcastic self-loathing. She hated seeing that pity in her eyes.

“It does,” Kara said seriously. “Anyone who takes even a second to get to know you would see, Lena. You’re not cold. At least – you aren’t on the inside. You’re soft,” she whispered with a smile. “Soft, warm, and kind. So yes,” she said simply. “It suits you.”

Kara shot her one final, soft smile, before leaving as quickly as she had appeared, leaving a stunned, confused Lena behind. Kara didn’t even see how Lena reached up and touched the end of a strand of hair, absentmindedly feeling the softness against her fingers as Kara practically pranced away in the directions of the cells.

Lena suppressed a tiny smile, before she shook her head, straightened her spine, and headed for her lab.

Chapter 7

Chapter Notes

See the end of the chapter for notes

“Kara!”

Kara almost skidded to a stop when she heard Alex’s voice coming from the main hall of the D.E.O. She turned around in a haze, instantly finding an impatient-looking Alex. 

“Oh hey, Alex! I was just on my way to drop off some books for – ”

“Lena, yes,” Alex said irritably. “I’d guessed as much.”

Kara closed her mouth, her shoulders dropping as Alex folded her arms across her chest in that all-too-familiar ‘God-I’m-so-disappointed-in-your-bad-ideas-but-I-won’t-comment-on-it-just-yet’ way of hers. 

“Is now not a good time?” she asked hesitantly.

Alex sighed, shaking her head like it was taking everything inside of her not to say anything.

“We’ve got some news down in the lab,” she said curtly. “I thought you might want to see.”

“Oh. What about?”

“You’ll see,” Alex turned around. “Follow me.”

“Well can it wait?” Kara raised the pile of books in her hands for Alex to see. “I have some things that I – ”

“It can’t. You’ll have to have your chat with Lena later.”

While the sentence itself was entirely innocent, something about the tone just stung. Kara had no illusions about what Alex thought of her repeat visits to Other Lena’s cell, but at the very least she could pretend that Kara was intelligent enough to make her own decisions. She didn’t need Alex to hover over her to remind her of what terrible mistakes she was making. She didn’t need Alex’s demeaning words to know that her approach was unorthodox, to say the least. But it was something, and despite all of Alex’s study and all her years of experience at the D.E.O., she had yet to come up with an alternative to approach Other Lena, so Kara didn’t appreciate Alex’s attitude in the slightest.

With a drag in her step, she resigned herself to her fate and followed Alex downstairs to the grey, but well-lit lab hiding underneath the D.E.O. complex. Alex scanned her ID card by the door, and after the screen lit up green, they both entered the hall. Alex briskly strode over to where Kara had followed her many times before to analyze alien life forms that had attacked her, or to wind up on a table herself to be saved from whatever worrisome state she had managed to put herself in. 

Alex walked straight ahead while Kara took her time, glancing around the room with slight disinterest until a figure in the corner of the room caught her eye.

“Lena?”

Lena, clad in her white lab coat and a stylish black skirt and checkered blouse looked up in mild surprise.

“Supergirl.” She turned to Alex, a questioning look in her eyes.

“She was here,” Alex grunted by way of explaining, picking up a file and impatiently flipping to the right page. “Figured it was best to bring her up to speed.”

Lena didn’t seem to agree wholeheartedly, but she wisely shut up and gave a single nod.

“Explain what?” Kara asked, taking a cautious step deeper inside the room. “What’s going on?”

Lena looked at Alex, who didn’t look from her file. Lena sighed irritably, like she hadn’t planned on being the one to let Kara in on the news. She clenched her jaw, but eventually looked up and turned to Kara.

“Don’t get too excited,” she warned.

“Okay?” Kara’s heart started picking up in speed. “What is it?”

“Well,” Lena said, “nothing’s certain yet, but after working on this for months and going over our options…” She glanced at Alex, who finally looked up.

Alex sighed and looked at her sister.

“We may have found a way to get… the clone out of this world.”

“We think we know how to get rid of her.”

Alex kept talking, words and analyses and explanations flowing out of her mouth and into the room, but Kara could barely register them. Because as soon as Alex had started talking, it felt like the air had been knocked from her lungs. Kara’s knees felt shaky, her entire world buzzing around her like it could simply collapse onto itself. 

“ – and so in calibrating that, we could theoretically reach the fifth dimension, and construct her parkour to this world from her own. Then it would simply be a matter of retracing her steps, and forcing her back into her world,” Alex said.

Kara could feel herself nodding. Could hear her own voice agreeing with Alex’s words, but it sounded hollow in her own ears. Far away. A familiar hum coming from a stranger. 

Other Lena was going to leave. She was going home, back to her own dimension. 

She would leave.

The thought hit Kara harder than she ever thought it would. Sure, she’d vaguely been aware of the idea that Other Lena couldn’t stay in that cell forever. It was inhumane. She didn’t belong in this dimension. All of that was all perfectly rational, and all perfectly rationally stored in a dark corner in the back of Kara’s head. But to actually face the idea that Other Lena would go… that she would leave. Forever. It hurt more than Kara could bear. It squeezed her heart in its iron grip of fear she had come to associate with people leaving so much over the years.

Her parents. Lucy, leaving for Metropolis, leaving her without a best friend once more. Mon-El, ripping himself out of her life and her tender understanding of love so harshly. James and Winn, her oldest friends. Or, at least, the first friends she had built her superhero dream with. Gone to pursue different life goals she could never bring herself to keep them from exploring, no matter how much it hurt. Kenny, gone. Astra, gone. Jeremiah, gone. Lena… 

A cold panic started to set over her. She didn’t know how she would do it again. She didn’t know if she could do it again. The thought of losing someone else – despite her best efforts to remind herself that she still had so many people in her life, terrified her. Her mind stubbornly stuck with Other Lena. It forced her to accept the reality that she wouldn’t get to see her again. Not really. Not ever.

Kara let out a shuddering breath, though neither Alex nor Lena seemed to notice, too engrossed in their own scientific and technical explanations on how they planned to pull yet another person from Kara’s life. And Kara knew that wasn’t fair. Not to them, who had worked so hard to find a solution to an almost unsolvable ethical and scientific dilemma, or to Other Lena, who had been stuck in a dimension that wasn’t her own for too long now. What if her body rejected being in a different dimension for too long? What if Mxy had made a mistake in opening the door between their dimensions?

There were no answers yet, but one very obvious one. Other Lena would have to go at one time or another. And while Kara had conveniently managed to ban that thought to the back of her head, Alex and Lena had just forced it back to the surface, unaware of the storm of feelings it had erupted within Kara. There was a solution within reach. A one-way trip for Other Lena out of Kara’s life and into a world so cold and unyielding to her very existence.

“So what do you think?”

Kara snapped out of her own thoughts, blue eyes zooming in on Alex’s face.

“Huh?” she blinked at Alex who sighed.

“The plan, Kara,” Alex said. “Thoughts? Comments?”

“Oh, a question, actually.”

Alex hummed.

“What’s the timeline on this?” Kara asked, trying not to sound too desperate. “Like, your plan sounds incredible,” she quickly reassured a confused-looking Alex and Lena, “but it also sounds very… theoretical?”

Alex and Lena exchanged a look.

“So, ehm, my question would just be… how long would it take? You know, for ehm, all of this to become reality?”

Lena sighed and folded her arms across her chest. She frowned, her lips pouting just the slightest bit as if Kara’s question had personally affronted her.

“Well that’s the thing,” she said reluctantly. “We don’t quite know yet.”

A flutter of hope grew in Kara’s chest.

“Oh?” Kara asked hoarsely.

“We’ve got a plan,” Alex interrupted. “That’s more than we had a few days ago. The only thing is – ”

“ – the only thing is, we have to design a fifth-dimensional portal,” Lena cut in. “And not to spoil anyone’s mood here, but we very much only have access to our dimension’s technology.”

Kara would’ve sighed in relief if it wouldn’t have instantly made her look suspicious. But that meant she had more time. Just a little more time to… prolong the inevitable? Change the Other Lena? Make her see some kind of truth that Kara herself couldn’t even figure out? She didn’t know. She didn’t understand anything beyond the unreasonable nagging voice in her head that pleaded with her to get Other Lena to stay just a little longer. Just so they could spend a little more time together before she’d be gone forever, and Kara would be alone again.

Alone, with no Lena to talk to. The idea almost forced her to revisit her own theory that she needed Lena in her life. Lena in any shape or form she could get. Whether it was her friend who currently ignored her entire existence or a shadow that only looked like her, and was often set on Kara’s demise. But it was something. It was Lena. A different Lena than the one she had come to know over the years, but still… Lena. Her friend.

She forced the painful lump in her throat down and raised her chin, trying to regain some semblance of control over the situation.

“So how do you think you’ll create the portal?” she asked, a tiny unnoticeable crack in her voice that she quickly covered up by scraping her voice. “If you don’t have the required tech, I mean.”

“Well,” Lena stated softly, “we have some options. We have some… contacts we can visit.”

“Some unsavory contacts,” Alex mumbled.

“Yes, well, it’s better than nothing, isn’t it?”

Alex held up her hand in quiet defeat and Lena sighed, shaking her head.

“I’ve already analyzed the chemical components and structures of the portal through which she entered our world,” Lena said. “I’ve managed to take some samples and I think that we could also try to artificially recreate the portal, but that would of course carry an innumerable number of risks, not to mention that it derails any kind of short-term timeline. It could take ages.”

Kara tried not to look too overjoyed at that, squeezing her fists tightly by her sides, and clenching her jaw to keep from smiling.

Just a little longer, she whispered to herself. Just a little more time with Other Lena. 

“But that’s not even our only issue,” Lena sighed.

Kara shook her head. “What?” she frowned. “It’s not? What’s the other problem?”

“The ethical one,” Alex answered for Kara. “Luthor is a tyrant. She’s working with Reign to terrorize an entire city and eradicate all alien lifeforms from National City. We can’t just send her back and subject the people of National City to her crimes again. It would be like returning a bow-wrapped war criminal.”

Lena’s eyebrows went up at Alex’s analogy, but she didn’t disagree. Instead, she slowly looked up and let her eyes fall on Kara.

“But?” Kara asked hesitantly. 

“But,” Alex sighed, “we can’t just go to National City and tell them how to deal with Luthor. Those people – to a certain extent – believe in her. If we take over the city, tell them how to rule…”

“We can’t be playing inter-dimensional colonialists, is what Alex is trying to say.” 

“Oh.”

“Yes. So that begs the question,” Alex said, rubbing her temple. “What the hell do we do with her after we’ve opened the portal?”

Kara’s heart sank a little. 

Other Lena had undoubtedly committed more atrocities than Kara would be able to count. She wasn’t sure she even wanted to know all the specific cases in which Other Lena had purposefully hurt other people – Kara included. But the Other Lena Kara had been talking to for weeks now… the Other Lena facing her, playing card games with her, sharing donuts and gossip stories about the guards at the D.E.O… Kara couldn’t reconcile the two entities, the Other Lena who had tried to kill her, and the one who had laughed so hard when Kara had pouted about not having a poker face after losing four games in a row. 

How was she supposed to let Other Lena be sent back, knowing that everything bad that had happened to her was a direct consequence of Kara’s own wish? How was it fair that Other Lena had to suffer from and react to circumstances she could never have been prepared for? 

Kara absentmindedly hunched her shoulders closer together but stopped when the groaning sound of the books buckling under the pressure of her biceps pulled her out of her trance. She quickly relaxed her arms and checked on her books, fingers thumbing down the spines of each and every one of them. Luckily, apart from some strained lines across some of the spines and a suspicious crook in the cover of one of the other books, Kara couldn’t detect any issues. 

The books were fine. Other Lena would still get to read them. 

A tired, slightly relieved breath left Kara’s lips. She’d still get to read them. There was still time. Other Lena wasn’t gone yet. They weren’t anywhere close to finding a solution for Other Lena, ethical or technical. Kara still had some time left to share with Other Lena – and she would make the best of it. She would. She’d get Other Lena as many more books as time would allow her to, and it would mean something. 

It had to.

“Either way,” Alex sighed, running a hand through her hair, “we’ve got our starting point. We have something concise to work with. The moral argument can come later.” 

Her arms dropped by her side, and for the first time that day, she seemed to actually look at Kara. Not just over her. Her eyes fell to the books in Kara’s hands and something softened in her eyes.

“We’re not making any decisions without you,” Alex said softly, misinterpreting the confusion in Kara’s eyes. “Once we find a way to get her out of here and out of this cell, we’ll try and work with our team in that world to figure out what to do with her. Okay?”

“Okay,” Kara heard herself say. “Sounds good.”

“We just wanted to bring you up to speed,” Lena said, with a distinctly surprising kind note in her voice.

“I know,” Kara said quickly. She gazed down at her books. “Thanks.”

She didn’t see her sister exchange a look with Lena, but she could almost feel the hesitance in the air. It wasn’t until she noticed Lena’s black heels on the white tiles before her that Kara looked up. 

“May I?” Lena asked, not unkindly, holding out her hand to take one of Kara’s books. But Kara wasn’t prepared and instinctively pulled the books closer to her chest, a move obviously not gone unnoticed by Lena. But just the tiniest fraction of hurt in Lena’s eyes, followed by that familiar feigned indifference was enough for Kara to immediately feel guilty.

In a flash, she tried to make it right, before Lena could raise her chin and ignore Kara again, pretending her actions hadn’t cut deep. Before Lena could object – or even move a muscle – Kara pushed the books forward, into her unsuspecting arms.

“Here,” she said hastily. “Please, go ahead.”

The move made Lena wobble on her heels for just a second before she regained her composure and could control her grip on the books she’d been given.

“I – okay,” Lena said, slightly bemused by Kara’s probably erratic-looking actions. 

She’d be embarrassed if her heart wasn’t beating on overtime, strangled by the pressure of the situation around her, so afraid of pushing Lena just an inch too far, and fracturing the frail peace they’d somehow managed to build in the few minutes since Kara had entered the lab. 

Lena awkwardly moved the books from one arm to the other to better manage to single one out. She tilted her head and inwardly read the title of the first book, her lips moving soundlessly with the words as she did.

“The Girl Who Loved Tom Gordon,” she read. Then she looked up. “Stephen King,” she asked with a bemused – but not entirely mocking – smile around her lips. “Really?”

Kara blushed.

“I think I may have overdone it a bit with the philosophy stuff. I thought she might like a good thriller or two.”

The smile spread around Lena’s lips, almost reaching to the point where her dimple would form too – but not quite yet.

Lena hummed. She looked back up at Kara, whose breath hitched so suddenly, she was afraid Lena had heard.

“I’m sure she will,” Lena said. “This one.”

Kara was startled when Lena’s hand came down on one of the books in her arms, before pushing it back into Kara’s own hands. Kara just barely registered what book Lena was talking about, too surprised and engrossed by Lena’s actions.

Lena's fingers rapped on the cover and she hummed. “She’ll like this one.”

Kara took a second glance at the book Lena had handed back to her.

“Never Let Me Go?” Kara asked. “You know it?”

“I’ve read it,” Lena said simply. “I think she’ll like it. You picked well.”

Kara didn’t quite know what to say to that. She just nodded, overwhelmed by the nerves that ran through her system with every confusing, new interaction with Lena. She liked that Lena thought she had picked the right book. She liked that Lena seemed to imply that Kara could still, after everything, pick out the things and books that she knew would appeal to Lena. That she still knew Lena, strange as their new dynamic might be. She still understood Lena on different levels.

Kara tried her best to raise her chin and look Lena in the eye. She shot her a shy smile, though she was almost certain it was a shaky one at best. Kara was trembling, trying not to look away. Lena didn’t give up and held Kara’s stare.

“You know,” she said lightly, “might be best to give her something lighter to read after that?”

Kara froze, for a fraction of a second worried about the choices she’d made, but there was a twinkle of a smile in Lena’s eyes that allowed her to reconsider.

“Oh,” she laughed nervously. “Yeah. Maybe. I, ehm, sorry,” she extended her hand to take the books back from Lena. “May I?”

“Sure.” 

Lena moved the books back into a neat pile, one hand carrying the weight of the books, while the other held the pile from the top. Her hand brushed Kara’s palm as she carefully transferred the stack of books Kara had so kindly selected for her Other Half. Kara pretended the warmth of that hand didn’t almost make her drop all those books at once – pretended she didn’t feel Alex’s suspicious eyes on her, just waiting for a nervous reaction she could (wrongly) interpret. Anything she messed up now would be an excuse for Alex to barge into her apartment later and demand answers to questions Kara didn’t have any answers to. 

“Thanks,” Kara whispered. “I just meant that I picked out some other books too. Some that are a little less…”

“Riddled with despair?” Lena added helpfully.

Kara managed to crack a tiny smile.

“Yeah. Just a little. Here.”

She moved one of the books up and showed the cover to Lena. 

“I liked this one. Miss Grant had me read it to make sure we could publish a review on it. She wanted us to be more involved with reviews of contemporary shows and books and stuff, instead of just fashion.”

Kara smiled thinking back to how Miss Grant had basically thrown some titles her way and had dismissively told her to read them all and report back whether or not they were worth dedicating a precious half of a page to. The speed with which she had read three young adult novels in one day had surprised even herself. Not that they had ended up reporting on any of them, of course. 

“Paper Towns. Chick-lit, huh?” Lena teased.

Kara shrugged and shot her a toothy smile. “I think she might like it.”

“Really?” Lena tilted her head. “Why’s that?”

“I don’t know,” Kara whispered, studying the cover in her hands once more like she hadn’t gone back and forth in the store about a thousand times contemplating whether she should bring it with her or not. “Something just tells me she’d like it.”

She didn’t know whether it was the flighty vibe of one of the main female characters, driven by dissatisfaction with her perfect life, or the found family Kara herself could always appreciate in young-adult-novels, but Kara just thought Other Lena would like it. She wanted her to like it, to enjoy something nonsensically airy and happy. She hoped it would make her feel lighter and freer too. 

When she looked back up at Lena, she was met with pure puzzlement in those wondrous eyes.

“What?” she asked self-consciously. “You think she’ll hate it?”

Lena hesitated and Kara felt her heart sink just a little.

“No,” Lena said eventually. “I don’t know.”

Her face grew a little steelier, a little smoother than before, like the warmth and kindness that had relieved between the two of them for just those few surprising minutes was slowly but suddenly dissipating from the room. Lena’s spine straightened, and a casual look of disinterest flashed in her eyes, making Kara herself want to pull back too.

Lena shrugged and took a step back, clearing her throat and looking back towards her worktable, like she’d suddenly remembered all the work she still had left to do. The work that would lead to the Other Lena disappearing from Kara’s life.

Suddenly, the conversation wasn’t so fun anymore, and a weight settled on Kara’s chest. It felt like the world was drained of a bit of its brightness. Not too much to change the world, but enough for Kara alone to notice. Her life outside the lab didn’t seem that exciting anymore, and the thought of seeing Other Lena, just to say goodbye after just giving her something to pass her time until she could go home, didn’t seem worth it to her anymore.

She felt a little sick. 

Lena must’ve noticed the change of emotions on her face because a hint of guilt sparked in her eyes.

“I…”

“I know,” Kara said, flashing a polite smile, straightening up herself too. “I’ll let you get back to work.”

Lena seemed surprised by both of their actions.

“Right,” she nodded. “Thank you.”

“You too,” Kara whispered, and turned around. She walked over to Alex’s desk and put the books down. Alex looked up, confused.

“Could you bring these by her cell later?” Kara asked, trying to keep her voice from trembling.

Alex seemed to want to protest, but something on Kara’s face kept her from it, and instead, she just looked worried.

“Yeah,” she said softly. “If you want. Are you okay?”

“Fine, fine,” Kara said quickly. “Just remembered some assignment Andrea gave Nia and me. I should get to the office and get on that.”

“What assignment?”

“Oh, nothing too complicated. She wants us to write some soft profiles on the new candidates for mayor this term. We already compiled the interviews, but we haven’t actually written anything. If I don’t help Nia finish it, she’ll be stuck at work all night.”

Alex nodded slowly. “Okay? Do you need me to get dinner for you, or…?”

“No, no, you’re sweet,” Kara rushed to say. “I’ll be fine. I’ll just get some work done and go to bed early. I’ll talk to you later, promise.”

“Okay.” Alex didn’t sound convinced, but she seemed to feel that Kara couldn’t or wouldn’t stick around. Alex was good like that. Rough on the outside, but surprisingly empathetic on the inside. She understood people and their complicated emotions a lot more than people gave her credit for. Kara always loved her for that, but on that day, she loved her a little more for it.

“Call me when you get a chance?”

Kara smiled furtively at Alex. 

“I’ll try. Oh, and, ehm, thanks for keeping me up to speed on… all of this,” she gestured around the room. “I really do appreciate it.”

“Always.”

Kara shot her a final smile before she headed for the door. Her eyes were dry, but her heart was beating madly in her chest. Just bordering on the edge of painful, loud enough to reverberate through her skull.”

“Kara?”

Kara looked over her shoulder, bringing the books close to her chest when she heard Lena. Lena looked nervous, eyebrows furrowed like she couldn’t believe what she’d done. Like she’d regretted calling Kara over. 

Kara looked at her questioningly. She tilted her head and tried to find Lena’s eyes.

“Yeah?”

Lena hesitated and Kara waited. The entire interaction felt so familiar and tiring, Kara suddenly felt exhausted. She wished Lena would just get to a place where she knew exactly what she wanted, or didn’t want, from Kara, instead of this endless limbo in which neither of them knew exactly what to say to the other.

Kara was tired.

“I – ” Lena shook her head before she could lock eyes with Kara again. “I’m sure she’ll like that book,” she said, calmer than before. “You seem to know what she likes.”

Then – 

“You know her better than we do.”

 

 

Other Lena turned the page of her novel, taking a sip of her lukewarm lemon tea. An unavoidable consequence to her reading sprees. She could get so engrossed in the words on a page, she forgot about her hot beverages entirely until she had to inevitably stretch or move, and her eye would catch on the forgotten mug on the pile of books serving as a bedside table. She didn’t mind it too much.

She absentmindedly swerved her spoon in her cup and took another sip. The taste still lingered, and Other Lena sighed contently. For all its shortcomings, this room did really provide the most peaceful atmosphere she’d known in the last five years. Maybe longer. It even beat the tiny forgotten nook in the Trinity Library where she could hide and find solace from the loud students and insufferable professors to quietly work on her papers. This place, hidden in the depths of the D.E.O. with no other people to bother her, provided the first reprieve from the loudness and misery that had plagued her life for so long.

The only person who did come by, besides the silent guards who brought her food and drinks and who would never let Other Lena’s teasing taunts get them to speak up, was Supergirl.

Kara.

She came by bumbling, stuttering, and tripping over her own feet in her haste to get to Other Lena with flaming cheeks and a bag full of secondhand books to give her. Those rare visits – which had become increasingly less rare over the last few weeks – were, though Other Lena hated to admit it, becoming the highlight of her week.

She could never predict when Kara was coming by, though she could sometimes tell by the way the guards looked when they brought her her food. Slightly tired and grumpy from having to deal with Alex Danvers and Supergirl within the same space, which was, apparently, never a quiet affair. Supergirl’s presence usually meant extra enthusiasm, less focus on administrative work and more attention to the research of ongoing crimes in the city, and lately, visits to Other Lena’s cell. The guards would shove her food inside the hatch and spend less time than usual in the hallway like they knew Kara’s presence would make up for it. The normal routine.

Today had been no such day. The guards had taken their normal amount of time bringing her food and drinks by, being kind enough to open the hot lid on her meals that would have to be cut open by a pair of scissors that were not allowed in Other Lena’s cell. They had cut it open, shoved it through the hatch along with a cup of lemon tea and a bottle of water. No anomalies that would indicate Kara would stop by that day. Other Lena hadn’t thought anything of it.

So when the door did open again after lunch, Other Lena looked up, surprised. She thought that maybe Kara had come by the D.E.O. unannounced. It could be the reason why the guards hadn’t been more short with her when they brought her meals by. Perhaps they hadn’t known about Supergirl coming.

Other Lena looked up from her book as the person who walked in came closer to her cell. She raised her chin, a smirk already on her face, witty comment ready on her tongue – when she was brusquely let down by the figure rounding the corner to appear before her.

“Lex,” Other Lena said bitterly, almost baring her teeth at the sight of him. “What the fuck are you doing here?”

Lex tutted. “Such harsh language, Lena. And so undeserved! I came by with a peace offering.” He held up an expensive-looking cream box with a pink satin ribbon tied around its sides. “I hear it’s the only way one gets your attention these days.”

Other Lena let the jab slide, watching how Lex’s eyes took in every squared millimeter of her face, eager to take in every minor feeling crossing her face so he could manipulate it and use it against her.

She wouldn’t let him.

With trained impassiveness, she leaned back against the legs of her bed. Instead of cursing herself for not taking a seat on the bed before he came in – allowing her to glare at him from a more appropriate height at least – she channeled everything that had made her her, in her own world. The power and intelligence she knew she could and did exude in every single one of her interactions. She allowed herself to stay down and take him in, not budging. Not giving Lex an inch. 

She stayed on the floor, staring him down just as he did her, a silent battle that neither of them were willing to concede. Other Lena waited.

Suddenly, without breaking his stare, Lex smiled. It disturbed Other Lena enough to let a whisp of disgust flash over her features – and Lex’s smile grew. As if it had confirmed his victory, Lex stood up a little straighter, chuckling to himself in a way that made Other Lena want to tear that smug smile off his face. 

“I see you’ve been entertaining herself.”

He nodded to the back of Other Lena’s room, but she didn’t break her stare and refused to turn around. She already knew what she’d see. The piles of books that had once been stashed under the bed, but had slowly started creeping up against the walls and in the corner in beautiful mosaics of colorful covers and titles, all stacked in puzzles that could only have stayed up in their rickety towers through Other Lena’s engineering skills. She loved it. If she turned her back to the window, she could almost pretend she was in a library of her own making, with every brick in her wall being a single book, carefully selected especially for her. Somehow, that made it more special. A library, not just one she owned, but one designed for her. With everything she loved and was associated with by people who knew her, all collected in that tiny cell in the dull government building she was slowly starting to call her home. 

“I pass my time,” Other Lena said coolly.

Lex hummed disdainfully. It caused a ball of sudden hatred to rush up inside of her. The idea that he could criticize the one place, the one thing that had taken so much effort and perseverance – only out of the love of another person for her… 

Other Lena had known luxury in life, both in her childhood and in her adult life, barely noticing the riches and the glamor that she was just naturally surrounded by. It didn’t faze her anymore, it had never brought her an inkling of happiness. But this cell, decorated by one person’s kindness, was more than Other Lena had ever gotten. It was better than any other library in the world, better than the money that could buy her private hours of strolling and reading in the Trinity Library and the Bodleian Library. It was a testimony of her own ability to spark enough love in someone else – well, her counterpart’s ability, more correctly – to want to create something so personal to her. It was a place made up of her own interests and passions, ranging from the various scientific journals scattered in organized messes around the cell, or the dozens of thrillers Kara had gotten her hooked on. 

This was her place. And he didn’t just get to look down on it. It wasn’t the cell or the books that weren’t supposed to be there, that were gross anomalies within that world; it was him. He wasn’t supposed to be there. He was the one whose stench of power and awfulness permeated a hallway that was supposed to be light. Gentle. He was the problem. And Other Lena hated him for ruining the atmosphere with every breath he took in her presence. 

“Is that… a miniature chess game?” Lex said disbelievingly, accompanied by a husk of a laugh.

Other Lena glanced down at the game Kara had given her. The magnetic car chess game. She had to have looked at the game for almost an hour, not daring to touch or even breathe in its direction, just studying the tiny scratches along the box, the discolorations in the tiles that made the game seem so lived. A testimony of the hours of fun, or maybe bored, mild entertainment the game had known in the Danvers family car on long car rides. Other Lena wondered about each scratch on the magnetic pawns, and could almost see how Kara would’ve beaten an unfocused, uninterested Alex on a sweltering summer day on an endless road trip, a glint of excitement in those blue eyes as she beat the King with a little too much enthusiasm, and knocked it to the floor of the car. All those little scenarios stayed with her so much, it almost felt like intruding, when she touched the pieces instead. When she moved them. It felt like the most personal gift anyone could’ve ever given her.
