Chapter 8

Chapter Notes

See the end of the chapter for notes

Lena took a cautious step closer to Other Lena’s cell. A step closer to Kara, who felt like the air had been knocked straight from her lungs.

“What are you doing here?” Kara managed to say, her voice not nearly as casual and steady as she would’ve liked.

“I wanted to stop by and give… the other me this.”

She pulled two rolled-up magazines tied together with a black hair tie from her purse and awkwardly held them up in front of her. Kara could only catch some faint shapes and colors and couldn’t determine what magazine Lena had picked out for her.

“I didn’t mean to interrupt,” she said, though her weary tone and the way her eyes shifted from Other Lena to Kara seemed to indicate that she wasn’t too keen on leaving knowing she had interrupted. “I thought I heard… arguing.”

“It’s fine,” Kara said. “I was just about to leave anyway.”

“But…” Lena’s eyes found Other Lena’s and narrowed. “What happened?”

“Oh you missed the event of the season,” Other Lena said dryly. “Supergirl here dropped F-bombs by the dozen. Parents all over National City must be clutching their pearls by now.”

Kara clenched her jaw but refused to comment. She refused to let Other Lena win this round. She just picked up her bag from the floor, but when she turned on her heel, she faced Lena, who was looking at her with big, alarmed eyes.

“Kara,” she asked slowly, “what happened?”

“Shall I just tell her?” Other Lena said lazily.

“I didn’t ask you,” Lena snapped her head in her Doppelgänger’s direction. Other Lena didn’t seem surprised by Lena’s outburst. She rolled her eyes and sighed, leaning back against the wall and folding her arms in front of her chest like a teenager who’s getting berated by a pestering teacher for the umpteenth time.

“Kara?” Lena asked.

“Supergirl?” Other Lena mocked.

“It was nothing.”

“It didn’t sound like nothing.”

“And what do you care?” Kara snapped.

The look of pure shock – not even hurt, just a wave of disbelief at Kara’s words on Lena’s face – was enough to make Kara feel sick to her stomach with guilt. It hit Kara that in all the time she’d been fighting with Lena, she’d never been so mean to her. It wasn’t an argument, it wasn’t a raised voice to make a point or to accuse Lena of something – no. It was just plain rudeness. Fishing for a pressure point that would hurt Lena for no good reason at all. In all the time Kara had known Lena, she hadn’t done that before. Not on purpose. Not once. Not verbally like that. And she definitely hadn’t deserved it. Not then. Kara would argue that maybe not ever. Lena had been yelled at and belittled too many times in her life, and for Kara to realize that she was just the next person in a long list of names to do so… it killed her just a little inside.

“I’m – I’m sorry,” she stammered.

“It’s fine,” Lena straightened up, erasing any signs of shock or discomfort from her face like Kara had never raised her voice – or had merely been discussing something trivial instead of tearing Lena down. It made Kara want to scream.

“It’s not,” Kara whispered. “I’m sorry.”

Lena looked at least a little surprised at that and gave an almost imperceptible nod in return.

“Am I now allowed to ask you what happened?” she asked, a hint of caution in her voice.

Kara locked eyes with the Other Lena in the cell facing her. She raised a daring eyebrow that Kara had to turn away from. She had too much power over Kara, and she was so very aware of it. Kara felt uncomfortably watched with any second she spent under both Lena and Other Lena’s eyes as if they could predict her actions before she could just from looking at her. It made her feel vulnerable in a way she never wanted to feel again.

“It’s nothing,” she whispered. “You were right.”

Lena frowned in confusion but patiently waited for Kara to continue.

“You were right,” Kara echoed again. “Coming here was a waste of time. I should’ve listened to you the first time you told me not to come here.”

This time Lena either couldn’t or didn’t attempt to hide her surprise. The shock was etched in her face in the sharp lines of her face, the raised eyebrows, and the worried eyes.

“Really?”

She almost seemed disappointed. The worry lines on her forehead deepened and Kara couldn’t stand to look at either version of her right now. She smiled unconvincingly and tightened her hold on the strap of her purse.

“Really,” she said. “So I think it’s better if I just – ”

“Why?” Lena interrupted.

“Why what?”

“Why was it a bad idea to come here?” Lena asked softly.

“Are you kidding?” Kara let out a humorless chuckle, but neither Lena responded to it. Lena only looked more worried, and Kara hated that she couldn’t predict anything about her anymore.

“No,” Lena said simply. “I’m not. I’d like to know. I’ve been trying to stop you from coming here for months now, and you’ve always refused. Now all of a sudden after one heated visit you think all of this was a waste of time? That doesn’t sound like you. I’d like to know what happened.”

Kara scoffed. “So first you bite my head off when you hear that I’m coming to visit Other Lena, making constant threats and underlining just how stupid I am for even believing I could stand a chance here – and now you want to know why I’m giving up here?”

Lena didn’t say anything. She just stared at Kara with those permanently sad eyes that made Kara feel so utterly weak. So defeated.

“You told me I was delusional for thinking I could change her. You told me to my face that I wouldn’t be able to change a thing and that she’d be the death of me. You told me I was reckless – suicidal – for coming back here. Wasn’t that the gist of what you were saying?”

Lena didn’t reply but Other Lena chuckled.

“That’s about accurate,” she muttered. Kara ignored her. She just stared Lena down like she was still brave enough to do so.

“Aren’t you happy that you were finally proven right? All my visits, all my time here – it was all futile. I was fooling myself thinking I had somehow booked some progress here. Apparently,” she shook her head and had to bite her lip to swallow another empty laugh, “apparently it was all for nothing. She hasn’t changed her mind, just like you said. I’m still a target, again, just like you said. So congratulations, Lena,” Kara shrugged to mask the pain that was sinking into every part of her body, making it so much harder to get all her words out without crying. “You were right. I was delusional. I didn’t change shit.”

Lena’s lips opened like she wanted to say something, but a moment of hesitation was enough for her to remain silent. Her eyes flew over Kara’s face with immense sadness before settling on that of her counterpart with a consideringly harder look.

“I see,” she said. “Kara – ”

“It’s fine,” Kara said, though this time, she did direct her attention to Other Lena, who sat up a little straighter, her eyes a little sharper.

“We’re on the same page now, right?”

“I believe so, Supergirl.”

Kara nodded. She wanted to turn on her heel and leave, but just before she could, a thought popped into her head and she stayed. Other Lena perked up, seemingly coming alive with every new millimeter of space she took up in Kara’s head. Like she needed it to sustain herself. Like she was a mythical figure that only existed if people were obsessively thinking about her. If she was, Kara thought harshly, she would be bursting with life from Kara’s mind alone. It occurred to her that she willingly gave Other Lena the space in her mind to occupy – to invade. She allowed Other Lena free reign when it came to her mind. She gave her all the information she could want about her life, let her make a home for herself in Kara’s brain until it had grown into a blood-thirsty parasite, breaking through the layers in Kara’s mind until there was nothing left anymore.

But Other Lena wasn’t the only one who had been observing her interlocutor. Kara had been listening to Other Lena just the same. And Kara knew her. She knew her, that was absolutely clear. And Kara realized very quickly just what she had to say. She ignored Lena, looking between the two of them like it was a game of tennis. Kara could hear her heartbeat pick up when Kara seemed to grow colder like she was scared Kara would burst out against her again. She wouldn’t.

“I do want to say,” Kara turned to Other Lena softly, almost like it was an afterthought. “I’m not afraid.”

Other Lena’s eyebrows went up in mild confusion while Lena looked considerably more confused and a whole lot more worried.

“Is that so?” Other Lena asked lazily. “And why’s that?”

“Because despite all your horrid words and all your empty threats, you won’t kill me,” Kara smiled tiredly. “You won’t. You can’t. You just don’t want to admit that.”

“I’d take that back, Supergirl,” Other Lena warned, leaning forward in her seat like a predator waiting to pounce. “Wouldn’t want to get too big for your boots again.”

Kara shook her head.

“You can continue to be as rude as you want,” she said softly. “It’s okay. I may be delusional about our friendship, but I’m not wrong about you. You’re not evil. You wouldn’t be able to live with yourself if you killed me.”

“You believe what you believe,” Other Lena finally said, her voice a low, threatening whisper. “But I will get out of here one day. And I won’t wait. I won’t hesitate. I will hurt you with all I have. And I will get out of this trip exactly what I needed.”

Other Lena stared at her with anticipation, but Kara suddenly felt so very tired by the whole ordeal. So she simply nodded, staring sadly at her vague, haggard reflection in the glass staring back at her. She looked so tired, Kara mused. So very tired. When she looked up again, she met Other Lena’s expectant eyes. Her shoulders were raised high, her fists were balled as if she was ready to fight Kara right then and there. Like Kara would catch her in a surprise attack. After all the time they’d spent together, Other Lena still believed Kara would catch her unguarded and would attack. Would hurt her. The idea made Kara want to laugh at the ridiculousness of it all, then sob for an hour after because of the hopelessness of it all.

“Okay, Lena,” Kara instead said tiredly. “Okay.”

Other Lena looked surprised but didn’t quite know what to say when Kara just slowly picked her stuff up off the floor, gathering her belongings – the magazine Other Lena didn’t much care for and the stack of cards she’d brought to play poker but had never gotten to use – as if it physically pained her to do so.

Other Lena’s eyes tracked her every movement, her eyebrows knitting together in a sad, angry burst of confusion, but Kara just ignored it. She was so tired. She shoved her stuff into her bag and stood up, walking away. She passed Lena who seemed to want to say something so bad, but still couldn’t bring herself to talk to Kara like she actually knew her. Kara didn’t want to wait until she had crafted the perfect calculated response to everything that Kara had done that night, so Kara merely shot her a tired smile as she passed her.

“Good night, Lena,” she muttered. “See you around.”

Without a final glance at the woman she had started to call her friend in her head, Kara clutched her belongings tightly in her hands and walked out of the hallway, leaving two Lena’s with lingering gazes behind.

Lena threw one last scathing look Other Lena’s way, before turning on her heel and stumbling to follow Kara out the door.

“Kara!” Lena called out. “Please, wait up!”

Kara was already halfway up the stairs, heading to the D.E.O. entrance hall. She could’ve flown right through the building to get out, but Alex always got dizzy when she sped up around her and a complaint had been issued. So now she was just walking as fast she could without the room spinning around her. Lena’s heels clicked loudly on the tiles as she rushed to catch up to Kara, her breaths short and hurried as she tried to match Kara’s pace.

“Please!”

This time, Kara couldn’t pretend she hadn’t heard her. Lena was practically begging her to stop, and Kara would be cruel for using her powers to get away quickly. Lena didn’t deserve that. So Kara stopped. She waited. Her lips moved soundlessly as she started counting the cracks in the concrete wall. Waiting. Bored. A dull task she took note of to tell Alex later. Maybe they could get someone to fix it. Kara could think of mundane things like fixing up an old building as if nothing had happened before. As if visiting Other Lena had just been one task on a long to-do list she could tick off. Like she could move on so easily. Like nothing bothered her. Like she could be cool and collected – like she could move on as if nothing had happened. Like she hadn’t felt like the room had collapsed around her when Other Lena had torn her down. Like she was the invulnerable superhero who couldn’t be brought down by anything, no other force on earth.

Kara had to swallow a lump in her throat as a mean, little voice in her head seemed to snicker at how blatantly obvious that lie was. It seemed to gleefully wonder how long Kara could keep up that pretense.

Lena luckily caught up with her before Kara could drift off too much in that horrible spiral of thought. Kara could hear Lena panting as she crossed the final stretch to get to her. she sighed, but eventually did turn around. Her inability to actually refuse Lena when she sounded so desperate – so out of breath – did not work in her favor.

“What, Lena?” she asked tiredly.

“Please,” Lena looked scared. Like she hadn’t figured out what she wanted to say when she got to Kara and was terrified of Kara rushing off before she could find her words. It hurt. For the hundredth time that month, Kara wondered how they’d ever gotten to this place. This limbo of mistrust and confusion. This awful, awkward state of detachment.

“What do you want?”

There was a surprising gentleness in Kara’s voice this time. The soft sound contradicted the harshness of her words and was enough to make Lena falter.

“I…” she stumbled, her lower lip trembling. Kara could see her throat bob, her eyes flying over the stairwell like she was looking for an escape. Kara watched as her eyes lingered on the steps away from Kara, back into the D.E.O. Into the world that wasn’t complicated and engulfed by this horrendous loneliness that came with watching someone she used to be so close to and could now not be further away from. Kara definitely recognized the feeling. But against all odds, Lena looked back at Kara. Her eyes a little clearer, her lips drawn in a trembling, more combative determination. Kara could almost see her shaking on her feet before her.

“Do you maybe want to get a drink?”

Of all the questions Lena could ask Kara, that was one she absolutely didn’t see coming. Kara could only blink while Lena shuffled on her feet, pulling on her fingers like she wanted to both immediately retract her words and vanish into thin air. But at the same time, the anxious sparkle of hope seemed to want Kara to agree with everything she had, and Kara couldn’t refuse. Not when she could hear Lena’s heartbeat picking up, fluttering erratically like she was mentally preparing for Kara to blow her off. Steeling herself for the inevitable rejection that she was so used to.

“Sure,” Kara faked a smile. “Lead the way.”

 

 

Kara didn’t think she’d ever been in such a nice coffee house with so many nice people, sitting at a cute little table decked out with flowery plates and teacups with hearts, stuck in a conversation where both parties wanted nothing more than to come up with an excuse to leave.

The building was old, with large windows looking out on the busy shopping street by the water, filled with happy people. Mostly happy people. Waitresses with stressed smiles and flowery aprons had taken their orders, apologizing profusely for the long wait because of the lunch rush. (They’d probably recognized Lena, and were sweating bullets just thinking about what one bad review from her would do for a small, independent business like theirs.) Truth be told, both her and Lena had been surprised when they’d apologized, so caught up in their own thoughts, trying to come up with something to say that time had escaped them completely.

Lena was touching her steaming cup of mint tea with two fingers, tracing its rim or nervously tapping one of her nails rhythmically against the ceramic. Kara herself was observing it all somberly, ignoring her half-empty cup of hot chocolate, the sweet taste having barely registered in her mouth.

Kara twirled the copper-colored spoon around in her cup, the sound of the spoon hitting the glass eerily loud at the quiet table, even with the bustling liveliness of the crowded teahouse around them. The sound sent shivers down Lena’s spine and she had to break out of her reverie to bring her own cup to her lips, taking a hesitant, careful sip of her tea before she brought it back down again.

“Too hot?” Kara asked quietly.

Lena looked up at her briefly, before nodding slightly as a reply. Kara shut up after that. She didn’t know what she had to say. Or what Lena was expecting her to say. She wondered what she could say that wouldn’t sound obnoxiously out of place in their conversation?

She folded her lap and looked around the room. There were different tables of families with small kids and tired-looking parents ensuring their kids wouldn’t spill their drinks all over themselves. Groups of teenage friends, shoving their phones around and laughing loudly over things Kara couldn’t see. Couples holding hands over the table, gazing into each other’s eyes while they ignored the room around them, only breaking apart when stressed waitresses brought over trays full of hot drinks. Kara watched as the waitresses hopped from table to table, balancing trays and moving around people hurrying to snatch up a rare empty table, crossing the room like they were performing a complicated modern ballet with a grace Kara knew she’d never be able to match in a million years.

“Kara?”

Kara broke out of her spell and looked back at Lena. It was like the world she’d been observing before muted itself. It was now only white noise in the background, Lena’s face and voice sharp on the forefront of her world. Sitting this close to one another again made it all too easy for Kara to count the different shades of green and blue in Lena’s eyes, and seeing how the worried lines in her forehead creased whenever Kara’s eyes darted away – like she was afraid Kara herself would soon too.

“Are you okay?” Lena asked.

“Why wouldn’t I be?” Kara leaned forward and twirled her spoon in her cup again. The chocolate was getting colder, lumping on the bottom of her cup while her milk cooled down.

It was too hot of a drink for a day like this, but Lena had ordered for her, and she still knew Kara’s favorite order by heart. After ordering, there was a moment of hesitance and doubt in her eyes. She'd thrown threw Kara a scared look, stammering that if she was wrong about the order, Kara would for sure be allowed to change it and that she in no doubt meant to speak for Kara – so Kara had just smiled and had lied that it was perfect.

Lena still remembered her favorite drink and that was enough for Kara.

“I… I know you were disappointed,” Lena said slowly, “with everything that happened today.”

She waited, but Kara didn’t reply.

“I know you expected more from her after all the time you two spent together. I’m sorry she disappointed you.”

“She didn’t,” Kara interrupted her. “She’d been honest from the start. It’s not her fault I just ignored it all in favor of spending more time with her.”

Or that she was enamored enough by Other Lena to forget all about it, despite everyone around her begging her to understand just how blind she was being.

“Oh.”

It seemed as if Lena didn’t quite know what to say to that either. She just fiddled with the tiny napkin she’d scrunched up in her hands. Kara watched as the brown paper slowly got torn apart as Lena pulled at small patches of paper, the flakes collecting on the table like breadcrumbs.

The sun shone through the window again, unencumbered by the clouds that drifted in and out of sight. It was a sunny day, and all of National City had taken notice. It was one of those Autumn days that didn’t feel like an Autumn Day. Like the seasons had messed up and had exchanged schedules, leading to bright Autumn days, and what Kara could only predict as rainy Summers. But she didn’t have to worry about that yet. The feel of a late Spring Day had livened up the city that had been groaning under cold winds and rainy weather for the past couple of weeks. This, the sun and the warmth that had people rush to walk around in skirts and dresses for as long as they could still enjoy them before having to change into sweaters and thick winter coats, allowed the city to rejuvenate. Ice cream vendors were boosting their final big sales and children bounced on their feet through the streets, enjoying cool drinks after school with their backpacks still on their backs with jackets carelessly pushed into their front pockets. Not a care in the world.

Kara would give anything to be out in the city with her friends too. To have a drink in one of the city’s many parks and enjoy the last warm summery evening in a long time, to relish in the energy that the sun so freely gave to her. But instead, she was here. In the coffee house with Lena sitting in front of her, looking horribly uncomfortable and out of place as she rubbed the sleeves of her elegant blazer until they looked slightly crumpled. Lena didn’t seem to notice.

“So, erm,” Lena scraped her throat, gathering all her courage to look up and face Kara directly. “What now? What happens now? What… what will you do when you see her next?”

“I’m sorry?”

“The Other Me.”

Kara remained confused.

“I’m not following.”

“I – well, I know that she hurt you. And she must’ve scared you when she went so far in your last talk… but once you get the chance to process all of it… Well,” Lena fiddled with her thumbs. “I guess I was just wondering what you were going to do when you saw her.  I get that she’s disappointed you today, but she’s made progress since you first saw her, right?” She swallowed, like talking only made her more nervous, the words painfully stuck in her throat. “I mean, you’ve clearly had a big impact on her already. She’s already much more amenable than before you two met, right?”

Kara was getting more confused by the second, but Lena continued, unaware of the alarm bells going off in Kara’s head.

“I kind of wanted to strategize with you,” she said quickly, as if she didn’t want Kara to mull those words over for too long, lest she realized how distanced and business-like they sounded. “Your approach worked the first time. I guess I was just wondering if you’d change up it this time around? Like, what will you do differently? Have you thought about what you’re going to say? What do you think your options with her are now?”

Lena stopped then, her attentive, calm eyes fixed on Kara’s face as she patiently waited for her to mull over her questions and provide the detailed, rational answer that would put all her worries to rest. Kara felt a sense of horror wash over her at the realization that Lena was actually waiting for Kara to formulate a plan in the apparently already fixed course of action that would inevitably bring Kara and Other Lena back together in the same room.

“What…” Kara paused. She took a deep breath before she could even bring herself to put her thoughts back in order. “Lena, what makes you think that I want to go back after all of this?”

Lena’s slight smile froze on her lips, the only sign she had heard Kara at all. It took a few seconds before Kara’s words actually seemed to hit home, her eyebrows slowly knitting together in confusion while her eyes got that familiar lost look in them – a look that made Kara’s guilt instantly drop to her stomach.

“You…” this time it was Lena’s time to pause, her eyes wide and puzzled, like even with all her knowledge about the universe and its specific scientific composition, Kara’s simple words were too enigmatic to understand. “You’re not going back?”

Kara swallowed and looked down at her mug. The chocolate milk looked like a dark sludge, entirely unappealing after the long time it had sat in the open. With the tiniest movement, she shook her head, too much of a coward to look up at Lena while doing so.

“But why?” Lena asked, a desperate edge in her voice. “Why won’t you go back?”

“Why? Lena – you’ve been ordering me not to visit her for months now! You can answer that yourself!”

“But – ”

“I’ve tried!” Kara burst out. “I’ve tried to be her friend! I wanted to be her friend – I… I thought I was! But I haven’t changed anything! She is just as angry as she was the day she climbed through this portal, and I have just fooled myself into thinking she likes me just as much as I like her. This isn’t a friendship, Lena. It failed.”

“But your tactic – ”

“What tactic?” Lena’s eyes widened a little. “There was no plan, Lena. There were no ulterior motives! I was desperate for a friend, I…” Kara ran a hand through her hair trying not to burst. “I know she isn’t you. I realize that. But I was desperate to find someone I could talk to and I convinced myself that she could be that person!”

Kara had to swallow when the frustration suddenly morphed into grief that felt like a punch to her stomach.

“Look,” she tried again, her voice lower and her words softer. “You were right before. She doesn’t want someone to change her. Least of all her sworn enemy. But I needed a friend,” Kara shook her head and managed to hold Lena’s eyes. She could swear she saw a light quiver of Lena’s lower lip and it made her feel absolutely awful. “I missed you. It just seemed too perfect. I got a do-over, Lena,” Kara said softly. “With someone who looked like you and sounded like you… I got to try again. Even when I knew I was talking to someone completely different, I felt better than I had in ages. I got my friend back and I could learn how to do better. How to be a better friend. It was dumb and completely misguided, but I needed it. I couldn’t be alone anymore. I didn’t want to be.”

Kara couldn’t read Lena’s face anymore. She couldn’t tell whether the shimmer in her eyes was due to hurt or anger, or a perfect combination of the two. Lena’s lips were pursed together, her clasped hands trembling like she was about to burst. It made Kara incredibly sad. Her inability to read Lena just another sign of their relationship deteriorating into nothing. No, Kara thought, worse than nothing. A vague familiarity expressed only in polite smiles and small talk, nothing like the warmest, most intense relationship Kara had ever had. It would be baffling if someone had told her a year ago what her friendship with Lena would dwindle down to. This horrid corpse of an affair built on shoving down feelings and playing pretend. It was the worst kind of feeling, and Kara didn’t know what to do with it.

“It wasn’t a tactic,” she continued quietly. “It was selfish. I needed her. I couldn’t stay away. She’s been honest about her goals since the very beginning. I guess… I guess I was just more amenable to… ignoring certain parts of our conversations if it allowed me to still talk to her. I think I could take the threats and the hatred if I could get just some semblance of a friendship out of it.”

Her lips quirked up in a self-deprecating smile.

“And I did. There was so much good that I could filter out the bad, I think. It’s pathetic. I guess I just never wanted to actually think about it.”

“Kara – ”

“It’s okay, Lena. You got what you wanted, right?” It took everything in her to shoot Lena a sad smile. “I’ll stay away from her. You guys can work together to send her back, and I’ll pretend none of this ever happened. Then – ”

“Don’t give up on her.”

Lena said it so quickly and with so much force that it made Kara’s head snap up in surprise. Lena’s eyes were shining with a sort of distraught determined spark that locked Kara in place.

“Lena,” Kara warned, but Lena plain ignored her. Her hand was flat on the tabletop like she was physically holding back from leaping over the table and forcefully making Kara see it her way.

“Please,” she said instead. “Look, Kara, I know you have every right to stay away from her. I know that I have asked a lot from you before, and I know it is unfair to ask this, but I’m asking.”

“Lena, please.”

“We were friends once,” Lena implored.

Kara sank back against the wall. She shook her head.

“Don’t. That’s… that’s unfair and you know it.”

“Of course I do,” Lena said. “But I’m asking you anyway. If we were friends before… if it truly meant something to you then I need you to show me.”

She licked her lips as she caught her breath, clenching her jaws as if it could keep her face straight. It couldn’t. Her lower lip quivered and her eyes got wider and sadder with every word she spoke.

“I need you to try,” Lena said simply. “I need you to go back and try.”

Kara pursed her lips and balled her fists under the table in frustration, but she couldn’t do much more than that. Not when Lena was throwing her a look that was enough to make her heart shatter and her brain turn to mush. It was unfair – on all accounts. It was emotional blackmail, and they were both so perfectly aware of it too. And they also both knew that Kara would give in so very easily. But Kara would stubbornly refuse to admit that for as long as possible. So if shooting Lena her dirtiest look was the best she could do right there, she would. It didn’t deter Lena. The dichotomous softness in her determination would be hard for anyone to refuse, least of all Kara.

“Why?” Kara finally asked, crossing her arms over her chest. “Why is this suddenly so important to you? You’ve advocated for arresting her and locking her up more fervently than anyone else in the D.E.O. You told me she was irredeemable. You hated me for going. You tried to threaten me into not going!”

Lena at least had the decency to look ashamed.

“So why now?” Kara persisted. “What’s the point, Lena?”

“Because maybe I wanted you to succeed, Kara! Maybe the point is that she has to change!” Lena’s voice became more shrill, almost panicked. “You have to be able to change her! She has to be able to be different than the mess she is now, and if you can’t help her do that then…”

Lena stopped herself, but Kara could hear the skin of Lena’s hand breaking under the sharp pressure of one of her nails digging into it with too much force.

“Then what?” Kara asked, kinder, calmer this time, in an effort to let Lena release at least a little bit of tension. “Why would it be so bad to leave her alone for these final few weeks she’ll spend here? What difference does it make?”

“All the difference,” Lena whispered hollowly. “It makes all the difference.”

Kara’s brow furrowed.

“Lena,” she hesitated, “I’m not sure I understand – ”

“Has it ever occurred to you that she terrifies me?” Lena cut her off.

Her eyes burned into Kara’s like they willed her to comprehend the swirl of feelings bursting under her skin. But Kara couldn’t follow. She felt herself growing smaller under Lena’s demanding eyes, trapped in a situation where she couldn’t give Lena the one thing she so desperately needed, crushing Lena’s hopes like the whole situation bored her to death.

“She scares you?” Kara asked softly.

“To death.”

Lena’s lower lip wobbled like she was just barely keeping it together, and Kara wished for a time where she could just reach out and cover Lena’s hand with hers and promise her that things would be okay. A time where she could simply stand up, move around the table and pull Lena into her arms before she could even break. But that time was long gone, and Kara hadn’t hugged Lena in months. So instead, she kept her hand on her lap, covering it with her own as if she had to physically keep it from crawling its way over the table towards Lena.

“Why?” she asked. “Are you scared she’s going after you? She’s been pretty securely enclosed, Alex made sure of it. But if you’re worried…”

She trailed off when Lena looked like she was about to cry. She looked away, bringing her knuckles to her lips like she had to stifle a scream. Through her muffled lips, Kara could just make out Lena’s sudden distressed sob that mixed in with a little laugh just bordering on the edge of hysteria. The sound made goosebumps break out on Kara’s arms, and she started to feel hopeless as her confusion grew and she understood less and less of the situation Lena had brought Kara into.

“Lena, please,” Kara leaned in with worried eyes. “I want to help you, but I just don’t understand what’s wrong. Please tell me,” she added softly. She put her hand on the table, her fingers twitching to reach out. “You know I only want to help. That hasn’t changed.”

Lena finally managed to look at Kara, her eyes starry with unshed tears that made Kara’s heart sink. She searched Kara’s own eyes like she couldn’t quite distinguish sincerity from betrayal, and Kara knew that that one was on her. Before all it had changed, Lena had never looked at her like that. Like Kara could so easily pull back and break her heart.

Finally, something in Kara’s face seemed honest and heartfelt enough for Lena to relax just the tiniest bit, her throat bobbing as she forced down another sob, and nodded. Kara felt her heart spill over with relief.

“Whenever you’re ready,” she said, trying to sound calmer than her ridiculously jumpy heart made her seem. “Take your time.”

Lena nodded again and Kara shot her a tentative, reassuring smile. Lena couldn’t quite smile back, but Kara could see that her eyes were calmer now, her heartbeat just a tad slower than before as Lena forced herself to take deeper, even breaths.

“Okay,” she whispered. “I… I don’t know where to start.”

“Wherever you want,” Kara encouraged her softly. “Whatever pops into your head.”

“I don’t know if it’ll make sense.”

“Then we’ll just figure it out together.”

Kara had a feeling Lena wanted to smile at that, but her lips only quivered in a way that made her look closer to crying than smiling.

A beam of light fell in through the window and illuminated a patch of Kara’s skin. Kara unconsciously leaned into the sunlight, her cells quietly cheering at the boost of unfiltered energy entering her body. It made her feel more alert, more sure of herself. Lena looked at her like it was the first time she really saw her. Like the sunlight made Kara look more ethereal and otherworldly than ever before. Like maybe Kara’s more self-assured presence was comforting. Lena nodded.

“I just…” Lena clenched her fists on the table until her fingers were white and thin as bones. “She’s… she’s me. She’s the future me. Or, what could’ve been me.” She let out a shuddering breath. “She’s what I could still be.”

Kara immediately felt a wave of protest rise inside her, but she forced it down. She knew that this was Lena slowly unraveling the feelings that had been eating away at her for weeks now, and she couldn’t just disturb that process. She had to let Lena find her own words before Kara would cut her off, and Lena would refuse to open up again.  

“Kara?” Lena asked with a voice so fragile and shaky it made Kara’s heart shatter. “What does it mean if she could’ve been my future? If she could be so cold, so beyond help – what does that say about me?”

Her voice was almost childishly pleading – like Kara was the one grown-up who could reassure her that the monsters under her bed were just shadows and that there was nothing out there in the world for her to fear. But Lena’s biggest fear was only a couple of blocks away from where they were sitting, just two floors under the ground, waiting.

“I don’t know how… how I can be that person,” Lena whispered. “I don’t understand the decisions I’ve made in my life that led up to this monster that’s already inside me. I don’t… I don’t want that to be me, Kara! I don’t – I can’t become her.”

“You won’t!” Kara couldn’t help but interject. “You won’t.”

“But what if I do?” Lena insisted. “What if she is in my future? What if I am destined to become delusional like my brother and mother before me? If it really is a family trait,” her eyes became blurry, “if it really is in my blood? If that’s my future and I change into her, I… Will you give up on me too? Will I be beyond help too? Unfixable and evil?”

“Lena, you are not evil!” Kara interrupted with a harshness that only came from the surplus of emotions that Lena’s words had erupted inside of her. “You never have been and you never will be! You’re a good person. It hurts knowing that even after all our missions together and all the years we’ve spent together, you would still believe that.”

Lena covered her eyes with her hand and Kara felt her whole body deflate. She knew exactly why Lena had never been able to put the thoughts aside. The years of trauma could very well keep those feelings of doubt and fear extremely alive. But Kara also knew that it was her actions that pushed Lena back over the edge and into the whirlpool of conflicting feelings, self-doubt, and self-depreciation once more. There was no one Kara could blame for that but herself.

“Lena, her actions, her… her being here, it says absolutely nothing about you! Nothing!”

Lena rolled her eyes with a disbelieving scoff, and Kara felt the frustration ignite her desire to push harder, to make Lena see it her way.

“You’re two very different people! It’s not just what happened to her that changed her, Lena. It’s her entire outlook on life that did. Whether or not she’s capable of change says nothing about you at all!”

“She could’ve so easily been me, Kara! All it took was one accident!” Her voice broke and Kara flinched.

“It wasn’t one accident, Lena,” she tried softly. “It was years of torture and abuse combined with a perfect storm of terrible circumstances. As someone who’s spent a lot of time with her, I can tell that you are two completely different people! You just… you can’t compare it,” Kara whispered empathetically, her eyebrows knitting together with worry. “It’s not possible.”

“She’s still me, Kara,” Lena shook her head tiredly. “You can’t just magic that away for me. She’s still me. The worst version of me.”

Her approach wasn’t working. Kara felt her heart sink with each new, defeated sound coming from Lena. She watched as Lena seemed to collapse in herself, fingers digging into the sleeves of her blazer like she had to keep herself knitted together with her digits or she would break at the seam.

“And you would equate yourself to the worst possible version of you?”

Lena looked absolutely miserable as she struggled to brush her hair back over her head, her fingers tangling in her dark locks.

“I mean, shouldn’t I?” she asked. “Weren’t you the one who pointed out what path I was on? The path that would lead to you treating me like a villain?”

Kara felt like she’d been slapped, and the dumbstruck wide-eyed expression on her face gave Lena all the answers she needed. She let out a sad laugh.

“See?” she asked. “The worst version of me is not that far away from the woman I am now. So why shouldn’t I equate myself to her?”

The question was almost rhetorical. She was both begging Kara for an answer, yet convinced Kara didn’t have one. She didn’t expect Kara to fight any further. She expected Kara to look resigned – to sigh and to tell Lena to simply try and forget about it.

Luckily, Kara had always been told by a very frustrated Alex that she was nothing if not stubborn. She wouldn’t give up so easily. A flash of a memory popped up in her head, and Kara suddenly knew exactly what she had to say. She also knew exactly that she did not want to use it as an argument with Lena. In fact, she almost instantly tried to push the memory back, tried to ban it from her mind like it could erase the event that sparked the memory altogether. But she couldn’t. And for the first time, Kara realized that there might be just one tiny good thing to come out of it. Even if she already felt sick at the idea of having to bring it up. Of having to face it again.

Her own, red-veined face seemed to stare right back at her with a grin as if Kara had brought her back to life with a mere thought. Her dark shadow seemed to loom over the pretty, bustling café like it threatened Kara and everyone else in the café with just the uptick of the corners of her mouth. Kara balled her fist as a shiver ran down her spine. She felt the hairs in the back of her neck stand up and clenched her teeth. Lena didn’t seem to notice, eyes far away as she looked out on the busy street through the window of the café, where crowds of people were rushing in and out of stores, trying to get home on time, while others rushed into their little café to get that one shot of coffee that could get them through the next half of their busy workday. Lena looked out the window longingly, her chin resting on the back of her hand, her eyes taking in every single person out there, and Kara wondered whether she wished she could trade lives with anyone there.

“Before you got to National City,” Kara suddenly said, her voice steady and calm, even as her heart raced and thumped against her ribcage. “Did you ever read anything in the news about… about Supergirl?”

It felt too hard to say her own name. It felt easier to distance it, to name Supergirl as the guilty party, like she could set herself apart from the events that could still break her down into pieces when she thought about it for too long – when it would show up in her dreams, hurting the people she loved until she screamed herself awake and her voice was nothing more but a raw, bloody whisp in her throat.

Lena frowned. Kara could see the bemusement on her face as Kara seemed to change subjects entirely. Lena seemed to actually ask herself whether Kara had nothing left to defend her position with and was just trying to make conversation until they had both finished their drinks and could actually leave.

“I… sure,” Lena said, leaning back in her chair, looking a little more tired than before, though Kara was glad the confusion was at least enough to drown out the glassy tears in her eyes. “It was big news. The first time she showed up in her suit, the Daily Planet waited outside my apartment building to get a quote.”

“Oh,” Kara cringed, “I’m sorry.”

Lena waved her apology away with a dismissive annoyed expression.

“It’s fine. That’s how I found out about… you,” she concluded softly. “After that I kept up with the news, yes. I wanted to know what kind of superhero you were. I wondered whether you’d show up in Metropolis too.” She tilted her head sideways with a small smile that hid more of what she was feeling. “Kind of wondered whether you’d come to arrest me too.”

“I wouldn’t!” Kara said.

“You never did,” Lena agreed softly. “But it took me a while before I realized that. Every time the wind hit the balcony door I’d freeze.” Her laugh tinkled softly, but Kara’s throat felt too dry to chime in. “But you never did, and I realized that running into me was probably not on your mind at all.” She shrugged. “After that, I was a little more at ease with the whole idea of you in National City, I think. When you and your cousin didn’t come by to harass me or anything. After that I could observe you on the news like I was just… anybody else. Watching the new superhero in the cute skirt fly through the sky.” She smiled a genuine, warm smile for the first time that day. “It felt exhilarating to watch your adventures on the news each day. How you saved the city, time and time again, looking younger and cuter… more excited than your cousin ever did.”

Kara blushed and nodded. As much as she wanted to go in on that conversation of Lena fearing Kara’s intervention in her life so early on in her superheroing career, she had much bigger issues to talk about. She tucked her hair behind her ears and nodded again like she had to brace herself for going any further with their talk. When she looked up, Lena was looking at her with inquisitive eyes. Like she couldn’t quite figure out Kara’s angle – the reason for changing topics so suddenly.

“You saw me on the news,” Kara echoed, her throat suddenly bone-dry and the room a size too small around her. “For a while.”

“Yes,” Lena said, a hint of confusion creeping into her eyes. “It was kind of hard to miss. You were on every screen in Metropolis.”

“Right,” Kara said, her own words reverberating in her ears. “Right.”

She looked down. Her hands were trembling, so she put them on her lap so she wouldn’t accidentally nick the table with her strength.

“Then you know,” she whispered, so quiet she seemed to have almost hoped Lena wouldn’t catch it. “You must’ve seen…”

Rao, this was so hard. Kara felt like a coward, her cheeks red with shame as her dark counterpart seemed to watch her intently with that disgustingly greedy grin of hers, waiting for Kara to lose.

“Lena, there was a time when I was at my lowest in the city,” Kara said, heart beating so fast she could hear it, but looking Lena in the eye all the same. “It wasn’t exactly a secret. Cat went live with the news.”

Kara could see the spark of recognition in Lena's eyes and watched as it mixed in with pity the longer she looked at Kara. Kara couldn’t take it and looked at the table, to the spot where her chocolate milk had spilled over and had stained the light wood.

“It’s… I don’t talk about it much. The news covered most of it, I think.”

“I… I saw.”

Kara nodded. She tried not to show the embarrassment and the hurt that those memories always brought about. She clenched and unclenched a fist, but it still felt like opening her heart for all to see and judge, and it made her want to crawl away from Lena. From everyone. Just like it had that day when she woke up on the table in front of Alex.

“They said you were poisoned.”

Lena’s voice was light, almost as kind as Kelly’s usually was when she wanted to help people. “They said that that’s why you acted… out.”

That was too kind of a verb to use for that situation and they both knew it.

“I was,” Kara said. “But the poison didn’t make me evil. It didn’t turn a switch to make me change from one conviction to another. It… it made me act on feelings I already had. It amplified all my emotions, my strongest feelings, desires, and frustrations… It could have only gone down that way. It just kept growing and growing until I did horrific things. Until my own family couldn’t even recognize me.” Kara swallowed. “Even though everything I did, everything I said… it was all me.”

Her fingers brushed up and down the fabric of her soft-ribbed pants. The velvety texture made these one of her favorite pieces in her closet. While Miss Grant would have no doubt dubbed it as horrendous to stare at for longer than two seconds, Kara cherished it. She thought the feel of them would ground her, would make her feel more like herself, more like Kara Danvers again, when discussing a past she so desperately didn’t want to associate with anymore.

“They were my wildest, craziest impulses, all freed from my rational restraint. It’s… it’s hard to explain.” Lena hung on her every word. “It’s like… everything you’ve ever thought… everything you’ve ever considered – not even considered! Everything that’s ever crossed your mind but never acted on because the consequences, both moral and legal would be too insane to even dare consider… It all comes out. Whether you want to or not, you become your darkest thoughts.”

Kara looked up at Lena.

“Can you imagine that?” she asked softly. “Your darkest impulses, the ones you wouldn’t tell anyone about… Could you imagine liberating yourself from the codes we live by to just act on it? To take whatever you want, no matter how terrible? To act on the darkest thoughts you’ve ever had?”

Lena’s eyes drifted down to Kara’s lips for just a second before they snapped back up, a hazy glance replaced with a sudden alertness. A blush blossomed on her cheeks all the way down to her neck and chest, and Kara could hear Lena’s heart rate speed up. Whatever Lena had flashed through Lena’s mind, Kara realized with a small, sad smile, she got the picture.

“That’s terrible,” Lena managed to choke out. “I just – I don’t know what I would do.”

“Neither did I,” Kara said somberly. “But that day I found out just how much resentment and frustration I had built up over the years. I hit on the friend who I knew was in a complicated relationship. I threw my boss, a woman I love and admire so much, off a building because she’d been mean to me that day.”

Kara shivered when she remembered the fear in Cat’s eyes. The way she’d changed from the most powerful woman in the city to this frail woman begging for her life with her eyes, and just how powerful Kara had felt when those hands had dug into her skin, begging to hold on and…

“And I – I…”

Kara’s breath hitched in her throat. She was caught by surprise by the tears suddenly rushing to her eyes, just barely able to be kept at bay.

“I hurt Alex,” her voice was no more than a whimper. “I hurt Alex because I was annoyed by how much of my life she controlled.” She shook her head and shot Lena a shaky smile. “Controlled. That’s how I saw it that night. Alex has always, always had my back through everything. And that one voice in the back of my mind reminding me that I sometimes disliked just how she cared about me… it caused me to lash out against her. I hurt her, Lena.”

Lena seemed to want to round their table just as much as Kara had before. Her fingers contracted on the table. Her worried, compassionate eyes took in every one of Kara’s words with so much love that it was hard to remember just how little there was left of their friendship.

Kara took a breath and tried to school her breathing. She blinked her tears away, trying to push the memory of Alex’s terrified eyes and tear-stricken face from her mind. Her doppelgänger’s grin in the back of her mind only grew.

“I was the most evil version of myself that day,” Kara continued softly after only a beat of silence. “I didn’t care about any of the emotional distress my actions would cause and I enjoyed hurting the people I loved so much, it still scares me today.”

Lena nodded like she understood, eyes so soft and empathetic Kara almost believed her.

“So is she me?”

The question broke Lena’s spell. She blinked. The worry and the compassion slowly gave way to just plain befuddlement.

“What?”

“The Red Kryptonite version of me,” Kara said slowly. “She’s me. The worst version of me, with all my darkest impulses amplified and exploited. So again the question: is that me?”

Lena understood and she shook her head with a tired sigh.

“Of course she’s not,” she said softly. “You are not your worst impulses. Anyone can see just how much you care for Alex and Cat and…”

And all of us, she seemed to have wanted to say. But Lena didn’t seem too sure that she still belonged in the us category. Like she wasn’t at the top of Kara’s every list and would always remain there.

“Lena, all this proves is that different circumstances have different outcomes. Under the influence of a manufactured drug, I was a monster. After years of rejection, abandonment, and torture, a new, different version of you was brought into being. That in no way means we are destined to become those versions of ourselves.”

“I understand the analogy,” she said with a weak smile. “But it’s not the same. You’re a good person whose darkest thoughts were just put to the extreme for everyone to see. I hardly think it’s comparable to this very real manifestation of my future.”

“Your conditional future,” Kara reminded her. “Lena, can’t you see? The fact that you’re so scared to turn into her can only mean that you never will in your life! I was so scared after what happened with the Red Kryptonite that I was scared to face everyone in my life, but you know what?”

Lena raised an unenthusiastic eyebrow.

“I did. I worked on gaining my trust back, and I grew. I know I can never turn into her again because I learned and I know better! I can recognize the signs of my own destructive thoughts, and I can put that aside! If I ever came into contact with something that could make me lash out at the people I loved, I would recognize the signs, just as you are now.”

“Kara – ”

“You’re reaching out to me,” Kara continued softly. “Because the Other Lena scares you into questioning your life choices. I’m not here to tell you whether they’re right or wrong either, Lena,” she said before the amicable conversation they’d been having could turn into one of their bitter arguments that could make the world so much darker. “I’m saying that I trust you. That I believe in you. I have no fears about you turning into someone you’re not, Lena. All I ever worried about was the grief and disappointment that might wait on the end of the road you’re walking with Lex. Nevertheless,” she caught Lena’s eyes softly. “You’re the smartest person I know. You’re a good person. I know you’re very capable of assessing the risks and benefits of the choices on your path. You won’t turn into her, Lena.”

Kara shot Lena a sweet smile.

“I believe the Lena Luthor I know could never turn into the woman who attacked me, no matter how scared or hurt you might be. You are not her, and you never will be. You’re your own person, Lena. I trust you.”  

In the stunned silence that followed, the one where Lena could only stare at Kara with big, wet eyes and an open mouth, it occurred to Kara just how long she’d been talking, and just how much she had shared. She started blushing and quickly took a sip of her chocolate milk and immediately grimaced at the cold, flavorless taste of her drink. She was inclined to order another, but she hadn’t quite figured out whether she’d spooked Lena enough for Lena to want to dash from the café, or whether she was embarrassed enough to leave Lena sitting on that chair as she flew out the window herself.

“For what it’s worth though,” Kara shrugged, shooting Lena a small smile, “I don’t think she’s evil. Not even after what happened today.”

That seemed to spark something in Lena, and she stared deep into Kara’s eyes again. Something burned in hers, something that seemed to be searching for the truth in Kara, willing her to be right.

“She threatened to kill you again,” Lena said, almost with a tinge of worry, like she was concerned Kara might have actually forgotten.

“She’s lashing out,” Kara shrugged. “I think she’s just scared. I’m not this evil person she’d made me out to be and that makes it harder for her to hold onto the feelings of hatred and revenge that have probably motivated her to go on all these years. I took that away. She might be scared, trying to find something new to keep her from falling apart. After all,” Kara smiled sadly, “I think she might not have a lot left. But anger can only sustain you for so long, right?”

Lena looked stunned. She blinked at Kara before her look turned more inwardly contemplative, and she took an absent sip from her tea.

“You know,” she said after a beat. “I think you have the weirdest perception of people out of everyone I’ve ever met.”

Kara pouted.

“Is that bad?” she asked.

Lena smiled, looking down at her empty teacup.

“I don’t know,” she murmured. “I used to think it was a god-sent. I figured your innocent acceptance of everyone in the world allowed you to befriend me, National City’s most hated inhabitant.”

She let out a husky laugh, but it sounded hollow and terribly lonely in a way that Kara hadn’t heard from Lena in a long time. Not since Lena had understood that Kara loved being around her just as much as she did, and needed her just as badly. Kara could still remember how it looked like the sun had lit up in Lena’s blue-green eyes, the second she realized that Kara had canceled her plans to go watch a long-anticipated movie with James and Winn in favor of getting drinks with Lena, who had shown up at her door after a terrible day at work. The way she had instinctively scrambled to apologize when Kara mentioned she had plans with the guys already in her apartment but had barely kept her mouth from falling open when Kara had sent the guys on their way just to pull Lena into her apartment instead and had allowed her to vent all evening. If Kara could remember only one moment from their budding friendship, it would be the smile that had spread over Lena’s face with so much warmth, surprise, and childlike excitement that very day, and the way Lena never seemed to have any doubts in later days and weeks to call Kara up unexpectantly to set up something for them to do. The way she never forgot that she was a highlight of Kara’s day, something she relished in with proud smiles and sparkling eyes. How she always realized, smugly, almost, that second to Alex Danvers, she was Kara Danvers’s favorite person in the whole world, a title she took with pride and incredible joy. The proud smirks on her face when she would show up to Kara’s work or apartment unannounced and could see Kara’s face light up because she was just so happy to see her.

Kara hated that she’d taken that away from Lena.

“Now… now I think I need it again. Your view of people.”

Kara was broken out of her daydreams at Lena’s words. She waited patiently for Lena to continue, leaning in just a little to take in every word. Lena took a deep breath, steadying herself.

“Kara,” she said, a lot calmer and more authoritative than before. “I… I still need you to try. What I asked before… I want – ”

She sighed, eyebrows scrunching up in frustration at her inability to find the right words.

“Kara, can you… can you keep trying?” Her voice was so soft as she looked up at Kara through her eyelashes. “If – if what you say is true. If she really is just one version of me formed by an array of different factors and circumstances then… then I think it would just help to know that… even if the worst comes to pass? Someone would still… try for me. You know?”

“Lena.”

The pity was so obvious in her voice that Kara could predict Lena’s flinch before it even happened.

“Please, Kara,” Lena seemed to draw into herself before Kara’s eyes. “I can’t…” she paused. Looked at Kara. “It would just… mean a lot to me. If you didn’t… give up just yet. Please. I just need to know that there’s a way back.”

The last ‘please’ was hoarse, like Lena felt embarrassed just having to ask Kara for help. It had been so long since Lena had asked Kara for anything – for a coffee, some advice, or some superhero protection – that Kara agreed before she realized the words had left her mouth. But the double meaning that Kara had caught in her words – the desperation not just for Other Lena, but for herself in the narrowing corner of the room she had locked herself in, with Lex holding the only key, she was scared. So Kara agreed without a second thought.

They both looked equally surprised too. Not that Kara was surprised she was going to continue to talk to Other Lena – she already knew she would, even if she didn’t want to admit it to anyone on the planet and beyond. Despite the constant threats and the hateful remarks that got shot her way, Kara could still see the human side of Other Lena peeking through at every turn. It happened when she played a winning card and her eyes would light up with glee before she would shoot a confident smirk Kara’s way with a sly; “Your turn.” It happened when she would talk about one of the books Kara had given her, forming essay-worthy opinions that would make an English scholar weep. It happened when Kara stood just outside her the doors leading to the hallway with Lena’s cell, and she heard Lena quietly singing along to one of the songs on Kara’s iPod she’d deemed ‘terrible’ and ‘outdated.’ Kara grew to love Lena’s off-key rendition of Breathe (2 AM) more than any other version in the world. (Besides maybe Alex’s version when she had sung it to her on that couch that one time after Kara had come home inconsolable after a break-up. But Lena’s version was a close second.

So Kara wasn’t surprised that when she agreed with Lena, the words seemed to make sense. It was one of those decisions that felt indisputably right like there was no other decision to make. Other Lena, as terrible as she could be, wasn’t someone Kara could throw away and ignore. She couldn’t move on without even trying to set things right. Even if Other Lena fought her all the way until her transportation to her own world, Kara would continue to try. She didn’t care how many books, movies, and one-sided conversations it took.

She wasn’t so much surprised by her own agreement, as much as she was by the fact that she did it just to make Lena feel better. It surprised her how Lena’s pleading words affected her. The fear that Kara wouldn’t come to her rescue. That Kara would just let Lena destroy herself without batting an eye.

“Lena?” she asked.

“Yes?”

“You do know that I wouldn’t give up on you, right?”

Lena stayed quiet.

“What happened to the Other Lena… that was a fluke. I wasn’t there to help her because I was literally enchanted never to meet her in that universe.”

“Enchanted,” Lena groaned. “I’m never getting used to those magic terms.”

Kara’s smile was paper-thin and was more of a blink or you’ll miss it kind of smile.

“It’s true though,” she said. “In any other world, in any other universe… I wouldn’t have just stood by. And I won’t just stand by now, you know that right?”

Lena looked terribly young and unsure when she looked back at Kara.

“Whatever you need, I’ll always be there for you, if you ask. If you need help with the path you’re on, or if you just need a friend to listen… you know I’ll always come to you. I hope you know that, Lena.”

Lena had started to tear up, and when Kara finished, she had tugged at her shirtsleeves so she could use them to wipe her eyes dry, letting out a short, embarrassed laugh.

“Here.”

Kara passed Lena a tissue from her bag and Lena gratefully accepted it, dabbing at her eyes with a careful hand as not to disturb her make-up.

“Thank you,” Lena said quietly. “That… that’s… I’ll try and remember that.”

“Please do.” She knew it was her fault that Lena had ever grown to think she wouldn’t. “I know I haven’t had the best way of showing it lately, but I care, Lena. I still do.”

Lena nodded, methodically folding the corners of her tissue like it would keep her from looking fragile.

“Thank you,” she whispered again, the unshed tears still in her voice. She shot Kara a little smile that seemed every bit as sad as it looked relieved, and Kara couldn’t help but shoot her an equally small smile back.

“You know,” Lena scraped her throat and shifted in her seat, “I think this is the first honest conversation we’ve had in a very long time. Or at least the first one we’ve had that I haven’t yelled at you.”

Kara chuckled, closing her eyes briefly.

“Yes,” she said, “I suppose it is.”

“Sorry for that, by the way.”

“It’s okay.”

It wasn’t, but this wasn’t the time to mention it. Not when Kara could still see the wet streaks on Lena’s cheeks.

“I like it,” Lena whispered, a shy, furtive smile on her face like she was still gauging Kara’s reaction before she felt comfortable enough to reveal her inner emotions. “I’ve missed this.”

Kara smiled back broadly.

“I’ve missed this too.”

They were both silent after that, like teenagers with red faces after sharing their first shy love admissions. Both painfully awkward and embarrassed, though they had both bared their soul in equal measure. The air felt hot around them as neither of them knew what to say. They almost stumbled over themselves to thank and tip the waitress when she came to clear their table. The woman was clearly taken aback by the abundantly overenthusiastic reactions to the – at best – mediocre drinks that had grown cold on their table. She seemed happy and confused enough though, walking away with her tray and an extra twenty-dollar bill that Lena had put on her tray like it would make up for the uncomfortable tension in their little corner of the tea house that day.

“I don’t quite know what to say now,” Lena admitted shyly after that.

“Me neither,” Kara whispered.

“Lex is going to freak out if he knows I’ve been talking to you like this.”

“Yeah,” Kara sighed, rubbing the spot between her eyebrows like it would alleviate the headache that was sure to come with Alex’s scathing reprimanding session later on. “Alex won’t like it either. But whatever,” she smiled conspiratorially at Lena. “What they don’t know yet won’t hurt us. We can at least pretend for a while that things are normal. Just for a little while?”

“Just until we have to go back to work?”

Lena’s hopeful smile wouldn’t take center over the rationality in her eyes. There was too much left unsaid between them to have a happy, joyous conversation filled with jokes and gossip like they used to. Too many secrets and too much resentment. But they could sit there, calmly, like old acquaintances on a park bench. Just enough for polite smiles and trivial little remarks.

“Just until then,” Kara agreed.

“Will you tell me a little bit about her? Not the big stuff,” she said quickly when Kara looked a little unsure. “Just… a little bit?”

“I think I could do that."

And so Lena smiled and ordered them both another drink.

I felt like it was so important for both of them to gain an understanding of the other's feelings in the matter of Other Lena, and it felt so right to have it at this point of the story. Chapter 9

Chapter Notes

See the end of the chapter for notes

For the rest of Kara’s lunch break, she and Lena talked about Other Lena. They were surprisingly successful in mentioning only the light stuff, forgoing the deep, dark, emotionally-straining information that had dominated their conversation so much in the beginning. Instead, Kara shared tidbits of information, mostly about her own place in Other Lena’s life. What books she brought in, how fast Other Lena ran through some of her books before she needed a new haul, what Kara had brought in that Other Lena had hated, and what she had distinctly appreciated.

Lena had a good laugh about Other Lena’s findings about The Secret Garden which Kara pretended to be very insulted by. She was quietly overjoyed at Lena’s laugh, though. It had been so long since she’d seen Lena laugh like that, that she’d forgotten what it sounded like. Now that she heard her again, she could compare it to Other Lena’s laugh and could observe the slight differences in both voices. Lena’s laugh was different, sweeter, more intimate, like it was something she shared with Kara as a precious gift, just for her. Almost hiding her own bubbliness as if her mother could still come in and berate her for it. Other Lena sounded smugger, more audacious, even when she was laughing. Like she was still in such control over the things she could find funny. Like she relished in the power that she had when Kara’s face lit up at the sound. It was a deeper, darker kind of laugh, but just as magical to witness as it was Lena’s.

Kara didn’t mention the chessboard. It seemed too personal to share, and she didn’t want to feel any less than at peace for gifting Other Lena something she hoped would bring her some semblance of normality.

Right after Lena had moved on to asking about Other Lena’s taste in music – and had cracked up at Kara’s reluctant admission that Other Lena had found out about her obsession with Justin Timberlake – and after her inquiry as to what other amenities Other Lena might need if she were to stay in her cell for a longer time, Kara’s phone rang.

“Oh God,” Kara moaned. “What time is it? I think I’m late for like thirteen different things. I totally lost track of time!”

Lena chuckled at Kara’s familiar bewilderedness, her frenzied ruffling through her bag to find her phone so very hopelessly in character. It seemed that Kara was always rushing from one place to another, and somehow always late, even with superspeed on her side.

“I’m sorry,” Lena said with a weak smile. “It’s my fault I’ve kept you for so long. You’re a very busy woman these days. I can’t imagine how many people would try and track you down.”

Kara looked at her phone and clicked the red phone button. Nia’s increasingly alarmed texts with an exponentially growing number of exclamation points and question marks led her to believe that a simple phone call wouldn’t be enough of an apology for having to field Andrea’s questions about her whereabouts. She would have to get a lot of powdered donuts to make it up to her. Andrea was like a hawk, and Nia was the tiny little mouse who couldn’t keep a secret to save her life, so having to endure hours of Andrea’s incessant questions would have been a terrifying experience.

“Not really,” Kara said, gathering her things as she mentally calibrated the route that would take her past the best bakeries on her way to CatCo. “I’m not that high in demand. It’s mostly just Alex and Andrea. Alex just to yell at me and Andrea… well,” she shrugged thoughtfully, “mostly to yell at me too. But that’s about it. And Cat, obviously.”

“Not many people call you, but the Queen of all Media is one of your regular callers?” Lena teased softly. “Everyone in National City is tripping over themselves trying to get a meeting planned with her within the next calendar year, but for you she schedules calls?  I’d hate to find out what your definition of high in demand really is.”

Kara blushed and cast her eyes down.

“It’s nothing,” she shook her head. “She mostly just calls to make sure I won’t let CatCo fall into financial ruin and to berate me for editorial mistakes in any articles that were published. Then she just tells me about her day. She went snorkeling this week just off the coast of Italy.”

“Oh. Fun.”

Lena’s lips quirked up and Kara broke at the sight and laughed, with Lena’s sparkling laugh following not much after, like the most delicate of instruments completing a perfect piece of music.

“Well,” Lena said after her laughter had died down, only remaining in the pretty smile still on her face, “if Andrea ever gets too big for her boots, give me a call. I’ll try and make sure she won’t be too hard on you.”

“You’re too kind,” Kara smiled, “but I’m afraid I’ve slowly become her most favorite person to yell at. It seems to really calm her down, which makes her less privy to be annoyed by other people and articles she doesn’t like, so I might have to learn to deal with it.”

“What a martyr,” Lena said with a wicked smirk.

“Please. I’ve faced much worse than Andrea Rojas.”

Lena’s smile dimmed a little. “Yes,” she murmured, “you have.”

Kara felt the awkward silence that followed in every limb, and Lena seemed to do too. They almost got caught up in it, but Kara wouldn’t let it.

“This was really nice,” Kara said, and she meant it. “I hope this isn’t the last time we do this.”

That was honest too. But neither Kara nor Lena could promise that. There was Lex and there was the D.E.O. and Other Lena just waiting in the shadow to throw another curveball their way. There was mistrust and hurt and an insanely long list of lies that neither of them was ready to unfold just yet.

“Me too,” Lena smiled, and Kara could tell that was genuine too. “I hope this isn’t the last time we talk.”

Talk like normal people. Like they could still express how much they cared for one another instead of slinging shot after shot the other’s way, just waiting for the painful hit that would shatter them both.

“It won’t be,” Kara said.

And though they both knew that to be more of a wish than a promise, they both smiled. Lena nodded, looking entirely more confident than she had in the beginning of their meeting. And that alone made all of Alex’s later angry, demanding questions about why the hell she would meet up with a woman who hated her without Alex’s supervision worth it. It felt promising in a fluttery, innocent kind of way. Like some sort of new beginning that Kara had never dared to hope for. She opened her mouth to say something else, but her phone rang again. Nia was most definitely cracking under Andrea’s watchful, narrowed eyes.

Kara groaned and Lena laughed.

“Go, Kara. I can’t save you if she decides to bite your head off!”

Kara pouted and Lena patted her hand with two quick fingers before they slipped back as if they’d never been there. The touch lingered.

“I’m going to stay here and work for a bit before I head back into LuthorCorp. I might finally get some work done in peace.”

She rolled her eyes like she was just any other employee in a big company, just clawing her way through her pile of brain-numbing work to make it to five PM before she got to go home and get wasted with her friends – just to do it all again the day after. Like she wasn’t Lena Luthor, Co-CEO of the biggest company in Northern America.

“Good luck! I’ll see you around!” Kara smiled, and when she walked out the door and passed the window that looked out on their table, Kara waved, and Lena shot her a smile, waving back. Something inside Kara’s chest fluttered and she couldn’t stop herself from smiling all the way back to work.

Not even Andrea Rojas could ruin her day after that.

 

 

Kara didn’t visit her those first few days. She couldn’t. Andrea practically kept her chained to her desk at CatCo, forcing her to write mind-numbing articles with key words that would supposedly generate more clicks and engagement than any of the interesting pieces she’d written before. While Kara started hating her job more with every passing day, she engulfed herself in it. She got completely immersed in celebrity family drama, local political scandals, and the world of clickbait. Kara worked like she actually loved it, staying glued to her computer at work as much as she could, until even her co-workers started noticing.

“Are you trying to make me look bad?”

Nia had swiveled her chair over to Kara’s desk where Kara had been dutifully typing out an article on the ethics of dating your best friend’s sister’s ex, and whether teen drama TV had made it easier for shows to demonize women and promote toxic relationships. It was an article that had required a lot of research, and Kara really wanted to send it to the editors that day so she could start with a fresh article synopsis to pitch tomorrow. Andrea had been more than satisfied with her previous article on the save-Britney campaign and her research into the discriminatory, sexist guardianship cases in the United States, but Kara doubted one article would keep her very happy for long.

Kara looked up from her laptop and looked into Nia’s expectant, big, brown eyes.

“Sorry?”

“Your work!” Nia said. “You’ve been working non-stop these last few days. I thought you hated writing Kardashian stories!”

“I do!” Kara countered. “I just thought I might be able to address some important things as I’m writing dumb articles on a controversial family.”

Nia blinked at her.

“Okay,” she said slowly, shaking her head once. “What’s gotten into you?”

Kara raised her eyebrows.

“Your work drive!” Nia insisted. “You’ve been writing so much! I see you more when we’re out protecting the city than at work! You never take breaks, I never see you around the coffee corner anymore, and you’re not even trying to sneak over to my cubicle to gossip!”

Kara chuckled at the last bit but felt a little guilty when Nia pouted in disappointment.

“I’m just keeping busy, Nia,” she reassured her. “As long as I can find an angle I like in a story I have to write, I’m happy. And it keeps Andrea off my back, which is a plus.”

They shared a knowing look, sneaking a peek in Cat’s former office where Andrea was currently fielding calls from investors demanding to know how Andrea was going to get their numbers up. Kara had been in her position before, working nights beside Cat, throwing out entire plans for the new magazine edition to start from scratch and get it exactly right, just to get the sales numbers up. It was tiring, stressful, and Kara didn’t envy her one bit.

But it was true though. Andrea had been more surprised than anyone else in the office when Kara suddenly started working like she still had something to prove. Which, admittedly, to Andrea, she still did. Andrea had barely believed her eyes when she got one email after another with Kara’s articles on subjects she’d actually requested, albeit always from a very Kara Danvers-esque’s angle. But Andrea was willing to see past that if Kara kept delivering. For the first week after Kara’s lunch with Lena, she hadn’t berated Kara once. By Wednesday on the second week, Andrea had actually walked by Kara’s desk and had muttered a stiff, quick, and uncomfortable: “good work,” before she’d rushed back to her office like she was allergic to handing out well-deserved compliments.

Nia and Kara had laughed about it all the way home.

But it was good. Keeping up with work was good. Thinking about anything other than Lena and Other Lena was good. That’s what Kara told herself.

But as the calendar days passed by, the uneasiness of the situation crept up on Kara. No matter how much she worked, no matter how many meetings she attended, or how many articles she wrote, she couldn’t forget about her. She couldn’t forget about Other Lena.

Lena hadn’t contacted her again after their unexpected conversation at the coffee house, but Kara was certain that she knew Kara hadn’t visited Other Lena yet. Whether she’d watched the camera footage or had just questioned the agents stationed near Other Lena’s cell, Lena was absolutely, one hundred percent aware that Kara hadn’t visited Other Lena in nearly two weeks.

And yet she hadn’t so much as sent Kara a single text asking her why. Kara wondered if Lena was staring at her phone just as obsessively as Kara was, either waiting on a text from Kara explaining her absence, or working up her frustration trying to write a text demanding answers. Kara couldn’t guess what Lena was thinking.

She could, however, take a guess as to how Other Lena was feeling. Because if Kara, through all the work and activities that kept her occupied until she could fall on her mattress at the end of a long day, exhausted, could feel the slew of days ticking by at an agonizingly slow pace, then she would bet her apartment that Other Lena was feeling that time pass by at least twice as slow. Kara couldn’t imagine what it was like, stuck in a cell with nothing to occupy herself with except for a mind-numbing TV and some books that Other Lena had already finished. She had enough to do, Kara knew, but she also knew that that wouldn’t cut it. Not really. Not for someone like Other Lena, whose mind ran at a pace that she could barely conceive of.

And while Kara hated it, her mind couldn’t help but trail off. When she was typing away at her computer, writing down meaningless words, Other Lena was on her mind. When she was having dinner with her friends, listening and laughing along to Nia’s wild stories, she thought of Other Lena. Her face haunted her, her words even more so. Kara relived their last conversation a hundred times a day, a nagging voice in the back of her mind while she focused on talking to the people who were actually around her.

And Kara knew what she had to do.

It was like an addiction. Like sudden, complete withdrawal that left Kara restless, almost physically aching for a new fix. Her life had become entrenched with just Other Lena, seeing her, talking to her, needing her. Not seeing her felt like a gaping emptiness in her life, no matter how much work she tried to bury herself in, or how many friends she saw during a day.
