There was this longing, a painful agitation that nestled itself in Kara’s chest like a small animal, clawing desperately to get out. Nothing felt right when there was nothing she could look forward to. When she couldn’t plan a visit anymore. If she wanted the longing and the sleeplessness to stop, she knew she had to give in. She knew she had to see her. But Kara was still angry. She wouldn’t allow herself to be insulted and made to be the victim again. She wouldn’t.

So she waited.

She made sure that if the day came where the pain and the longing became so insufferable, she couldn’t focus on anything anymore, she would be ready. She would make the visit be on her terms.

But just for now, she would hold on. She would push the urge to barge into the D.E.O. down and focus on her work. Kara would let the yearning fester and grow until her body would be screaming at her to go, and not a second sooner. She would not give in.

 

 

The next time Kara walked into the D.E.O., she wasn’t there to visit Other Lena either. She was there on a standard mission, having arrested an alien who was making a mess of the central square in the city, threatening to blow up a series of busy shops and threatening the lives of innumerable people. Capturing him had been easy enough, and Kara hadn’t even needed to call in the other Superfriends to help out. Lex had made sure the media were all too aware of her ‘heroic’ mission, curtesy of her employers at the D.E.O. (Kara got sick whenever she heard him say that) and she had had to stay for a couple of interviews and quotes before she had finally been allowed to bring the alien back to the D.E.O., where he could be locked up according to protocol.

She stayed at the building for longer than really necessary, filling out the paperwork with so little enthusiasm, that the time went by exasperatingly slowly. Kara leaned all her weight on her elbows on one of the desks, twirling the pen between her fingers as she went through a whole pile of what she deemed to be unnecessary documents, trying the best she could to document what had happened that day. And while she did find her eyes drifting to the staircase in the back corner leading to Other Lena’s cell every so often, she was proud to say that she didn’t mention her to anyone around her, and didn’t try and sneak down there, no matter how much she wanted to.

“Kara! What a nice surprise!”

Kara turned around and instantly lit up when she saw Kelly walking by struggling with a stack of overflowing files in her arms.

“Kelly! Here, let me help you with those.”

She quickly took the top of the pile from Kelly’s arms and Kelly smiled in relief.

“Thank you! Clearly one does benefit from having some super strength in the friend group,” she teased.

Kara chuckled and followed Kelly to an empty shoe closet that could almost qualify as a tiny office. Kelly dropped the files on her desk with a groan, and Kara carefully placed her files right next to them.

“Thank you so much, Kara, you’re a sweetheart.”

“Oh not at all! Anything that’ll take me away from all the paperwork.”

She rolled her eyes with enough dramatic flair to make Kelly laugh, and Kara smiled in return. It was always so easy being around Kelly. She was so genuinely kind and helpful, she felt like a breath of fresh air in the imposing, grim building that had become so associated with fear, oppression, and darkness in Kara’s head. The place she loathed being, and dreaded being called to. Kelly’s presence made her forget all about that. Even when they were standing in the objectively smallest, most suffocating little office one could find in the D.E.O., Kelly’s warm smile and her colorful, yellow blazer made all of that float away. Kara could see the fluorescent, flowery post-its sticking out from her stack of files, the labels with her cursive handwriting, and the pink planner she’d gotten from Alex last Christmas. All of that made the room seem ten times brighter than the whole of the D.E.O. put together, and it made the office seem like the prettiest in all of National City.

“I like what you’ve done with the place.”

Kara nodded at a little water glass filled with some daisies and dandelions, wilting away yet brightening the room up immeasurably. Kelly looked up from her pile with some confusion, following Kara’s eyes and beaming when she noticed the flowers.

“Aren’t they adorable?” she asked. “A girl from the group home I oversee gave them to me. She’d found them on her walk in the park that morning. Isn’t that just the cutest thing?”

Kara couldn’t help but smile too. Kelly’s happiness was infectious.

“They’re so lucky to have you, Kelly,” Kara said warmly. “I can’t imagine how wonderful it must be for those kids to have someone like you on their side.”

“Oh,” Kelly blushed, shooting Kara the sweetest, most grateful smile she had. She leaned in and Kara was taken by surprise when she pulled her in for a spontaneous one-armed hug. “You are a sweetheart, Kara Danvers. Thank you.”

Kara waved her away, blushing herself. She could see why Alex was so taken by Kelly. There was no way one could ever meet Kelly and not fall incredibly in love with how wonderfully sweet she was.

“Any time,” she whispered.

She lingered in the doorway, not quite ready to leave and go back to her paperwork, but also not quite knowing what to say. Kelly rearranged the desk and shot Kara a quick glance in between organizing the files on her desk based on urgency and importance.

“Something on your mind?” she asked casually, taking out her laptop from her bag and carefully putting it down on the desk.

“No,” Kara shuffled on her feet, leaning against the door opening, watching the D.E.O. agents pass her by, paying her no mind at all as they went about their business. “Just bored. Is Alex here?”

“No, I’m sorry,” Kelly folded some documents and put them in different-colored binders. “She’s taken a day off to get some work done around the apartment. She’ll be back tomorrow unless it’s urgent?”

“No, no, it’s nothing. Nothing to bother her for, at least,” she said quickly after Kelly shot her a look.

“So there is something on your mind,” she smiled softly. “Anything you might want to talk to me about? I mean, I know I’m no Alex,” she teased, “but I have been told I’m a good listener?”

“It’s not really about me,” Kara said. “I just wanted to ask Alex – well… Maybe it’s better I don’t ask anyway. She won’t appreciate me asking.”

“Then ask me,” Kelly said simply.

“You’re sweet, but I don’t think you’ve got answers for me here.”

Kelly shrugged. “Try me.”

Kara sighed, but Kelly folded her arms in front of her chest and tilted her head, giving Kara her undivided attention. And Kara realized it had been a while since someone had been so ready to listen to her, to just her side of the story, with no counterarguments ready, no judgment or disappointment at all. She found that she wanted to talk to Kelly. She was kind and so nonjudgmental, and Kara never felt like she could say a wrong word in front of her. She felt like Kelly wanted to listen to her, and that was more than she needed.

“It’s… it’s about the, ehm, Other Lena,” she said awkwardly. She barely dared to look up at Kelly, fiddling with her fingers instead, but when she did attempt to look at Kelly, she only found her open and supportive eyes looking back. “I, ehm… I’m worried about her.”

“In what sense?” Kelly asked lightly.

“I just… I haven’t seen her in a while. Purposefully so. She, ehm, said some awful things a while back. And… and I wasn’t – I’m not ready to just go back over there. I don’t want to be her personal punchbag just because I feel guilty.”

Kelly nodded empathetically.

“But I just… I worry she’s too lonely. I worry she’s not eating well or that she’s bored. She’s just… on my mind all the time. And every time I want to ask Alex how she’s doing, I change my mind at the very last second because I know how much she disapproves of me seeing her. It’s just…”

“Tiring?”

“Exhausting,” Kara agreed, her heart feeling just a bit lighter as Kelly found the exact right word for her abundance of feelings. “I try not to think about it, but that just makes it so much worse and I… I just… I need to know that she’s okay. And I can’t find that out anymore. The last time Alex informed me about how badly she was doing, I immediately went back to visit Other Lena, and now Alex won’t say a word about her. Like that’ll stop me from being stupid enough to keep coming over. Like that’ll stop me from caring,” she added softly.

There was a beat of silence before Kelly reached out and gently squeezed Kara’s upper arm.

“Hey,” she said softly, trying to catch Kara’s eyes. Kara looked up with some difficulty. “You’re not stupid for caring. No,” she said when Kara scoffed and tried to look away. “I mean it. You’re a kind person. You care, even after people have hurt you. That’s not a crime. And Alex, well,” she sighed. “You know your sister is the love of my life and the light of my days and I would never do anything that would jeopardize what I can call the best relationship of my entire life, right?”

Kara smiled and looked down before catching Kelly’s eyes again.

“Yes, Kelly, I know. I won’t be mad if you say something negative about her, I promise.”

“Just checking,” Kelly winked. “Alex loves you. More than anyone else in the universe. She’s the one who’s been in charge of protecting you your entire life. She’s afraid that someone would hurt you and she wouldn’t be able to prevent it.”

“I know,” Kara murmured, and felt terrible for letting herself slip again. She loved Alex. She knew Alex wanted the best for her, but it could feel so… suffocating.

“Alex isn’t always right,” Kelly said. “Especially when she’s clouded by feelings, which she often is when you’re in danger. And let’s face it, Kara. You were in danger when the Other Lena arrived. I think that she has a hard time accepting that you would revisit someone who could potentially cause you so much harm.”

“But she’s different!” Kara exclaimed. “She’s changed! I’ve seen it happen, I – ”

“Kara!” Kelly put her hands up and Kara instantly fell silent. “I believe you,” Kelly said softly, trying to get Kara to see the understanding in her eyes. “I believe you,” she repeated. “I know people have a capacity for change, I know that Other Lena is one version of a pretty amazing woman I got to know a while back, and I know that you’ve put your time and effort in to try and understand where Other Lena was coming from. You don’t know how much that can mean to someone,” she added softly. “Truly, it can make all the difference. I see it so often, people who are cast aside because no one wants to hear from them. Criminals, mentally ill people, children, people on the streets…” she sighed and took Kara’s hand. “I’ve always been a big supporter of giving people a platform to speak, and you’ve given Other Lena every opportunity to just do so.”

“She still reacted negatively to me last time,” Kara said quietly. “She acted like it was the first time she’d seen me since her accident. She wanted me dead.”

“So you believe she hasn’t changed?”

“No!” Kara said forcefully. “Absolutely not! I think it’s a defense mechanism. I think she got afraid by how close she was getting to me and she felt the need to push back! She’s not the same person who walked in here trying to kill me, I swear!” Her hand hit the steel casing of the door with a bang and the room shook just a little bit from the passionate force that had accompanied Kara’s words.

Kara quickly pulled her hands back and forced them to be still by her sides. She barely dared to look back up. She expected Kelly to be taken aback, expected her to look surprised maybe… But when she looked back at Kelly, the woman was simply smiling at her.

“You’re smiling,” Kara said warily. “Why are you smiling?”

“Because I love how passionate you are about helping people,” Kelly said gently. “I love the way you and your sister care. It’s truly a Danvers trait.”

Kara felt her cheeks heat up at one of the most wonderful compliments she’d ever gotten.

“I’ll find out what I can about Other Lena,” Kelly said. “As the D.E.O’s psychologist, I get some insight into people’s files. Not everything,” she noted with a frustrated shake of her head, “but enough to tell you a little bit more about how she’s doing. That sound okay? I – oof.”

She barely got time to finish her sentence before she was wrapped up in a tight, Kryptonian bearhug, Kara’s arms enveloping her entire frame until Kelly’s face was the only thing sticking out over Kara’s shoulder, her blonde curls tickling the side of her neck.

“Thank you, Kelly,” Kara whispered. “Thank you.”

“Oh,” Kelly tried her best to hug Kara back, her hands stroking Kara’s back with some difficulty. “You’re so welcome.” When Kara still didn’t let go after that, Kelly must’ve known she needed the hug more than she could say, and she squeezed back just as tightly. She didn't let go until Kara did.

 

 

The good thing about Kelly was that she followed up on everything with a speed and efficiency that would always crush the sluggish systems she had to work with. She never forgot a single case, following leads and making appointments like it was a naturally born skill, instead of a tiring work thing. Kelly had a heart for every single case she was involved in, and she would go to unspeakable lengths to ensure that those cases were handled with the utmost care and compassion she and her colleagues had to offer.

She acted no different when it came to Other Lena.

While her small note accompanying the file on Kara’s desk one morning apologized for not having been able to meet up with Other Lena in person, she had been able to obtain some clues as to Other Lena’s wellbeing from interviews with the guards tasked with caring for her, as well as from the D.E.O. doctor’s standard medical exam.

Kara could barely believe her eyes when she’d read the little, blue note on her desk. Even less so when she saw that there was a file – thin as the laughably sad number of sheets inside of it, but a file nonetheless – was located right under that note. Kelly’s sweet note had informed Kara that Other Lena was still alright, still resting easy in her cell. She hadn’t had any visitors since Kara, but she spent her time watching TV and reading through the books Kara had brought her before.

And while the note didn’t say, Kara could just tell that Other Lena wasn’t doing too well again. She could just imagine her sitting in her cell, a lackluster, empty expression on her face as the flickering light from the TV reflected in her eyes. How she’d pick up another book she’d already read with about as much enthusiasm as the guards watching over her as they brought her her food.

Kara swallowed and looked away from the note that suddenly seemed so taunting between her fingers. A haunting portrait of a woman she had chosen to leave behind, for good reason. But was it a good enough reason? The guilt in Kara’s gut made her think that it absolutely wasn’t. She cared. She cared about Other Lena so much more than she could understand – more than she ever hoped to comprehend. But Kara didn’t need to understand it.

And that’s when she knew. She realized that it didn’t matter what the note had said. She didn’t care whether or not Other Lena was thriving without her, she needed to see her. She wanted to see her. She was desperate to see her. The second she realized that it didn’t matter what the note had said, what the doctor could’ve claimed, or what Kelly’s advice could’ve been, there was a profound clarity in Kara’s head that made the brick on her heart evaporate, her worries blending into the air around her until she was lightheaded, CatCo swimming around her in a muted, colorful whirl.

Oh.

She cared about Other Lena. She cared. More than she ever thought possible to care for someone who so utterly disliked her; but she cared. And she was going to see her again.

 

 

Kara didn’t pause this time. She didn’t have time, she told herself. She’d purposefully planned her day up to the minute so she couldn’t afford to be seduced into spending more time with Other Lena even if she wanted to. She and Andrea were going to have a discussion on what other angles in popular media Kara could pursue in her articles, then she had a meeting with the editors, and then she would write until it was time for her to have another training session with J’onn, followed by dinner with her sister.

Kara would be so busy that day she barely had time to breathe, but it was good. It was necessary. She’d made up her mind and she knew what she needed to do. What felt right.

So Kara barely paused when she pushed open the door and walked through the D.E.O. hallway with a determined expression on her face. She didn’t even bother taking off her jacket because she wouldn’t be there long enough for it to have to be taken off.

She wouldn’t wait for the snide remarks or the tantalizing smirks, wouldn’t budge for the cruel rolling of her eyes, the way she would mock Kara for giving in yet again and going to see her. She wouldn’t let Other Lena throw her off with just one look, one raised eyebrow, one word.

And as it turned out, she didn’t even need to.

When Kara walked into the hallway, determined to get to and from the cell with an efficiency that would almost match Alex’s, she clenched her jaw and didn’t show anything. The rustling of the fabric of her clothes and the quick yet steady beat of her own heart echoed in her ears, the rush of the airflow she created whisking a few baby hairs out of her face.

The steps were loud, and the small heels gave her away pretty much immediately. She expected Other Lena to be sitting on the bed, reading a book and maybe glancing up with that frustrating half-smirk already plastered on her face. She expected Other Lena to throw her a line laughing about her inability to stay away – but none of that happened.

Instead, when Other Lena’s cell finally came into her line of vision, her heart did a little summersault at the sight.

Other Lena was lying on her back on the bed, staring up at the ceiling with her hands resting on her stomach. Her eyes drifted over to the glass window with little interest until she spotted Kara. She sat up with a start, her dull hair flying around her shoulders. She quickly stood up, stumbling a little. Kara clenched her jaw, trying to keep her face as cold and impassive as she could. Like she didn’t care.

Other Lena steadied herself as Kara walked in front of her cell, her hands tugging nervously at her shirt. Her big eyes tracked Kara’s movements almost worriedly like she wasn’t sure she was dreaming or not.

“You came back.”

Her voice was hoarse, like it had been unused for a long time. Like it had been locked up, just the same as her. As if by putting her in the cell, they’d put her into a tiny box in a drawer. Forgotten, until someone accidentally stumbled upon her when looking for a different trinket. The chapped lips and circles under her eyes only seemed to accentuate that vision in Kara’s head. Kept from daylight and human contact, she seemed to have wilted a little, her skin almost ashy in the pale light from the overhead lamps.

But what really shocked Kara, more so than her appearance, was the look in her eyes. She looked like she’d seen a ghost. She looked scared. Her hands were clutching the thin, white shirt under the blue sweater with white-knuckled fists, her eyes tracking Kara’s continuous movement forward. Her lips opened a little at the sight, but no sound came out.

“I did,” Kara said. She hoped it sounded nonchalant enough to fool even Other Lena, but she wasn’t quite sure if she’d managed until she heard Other Lena swallow, looking even more unsure than before.

“I… I didn’t think you’d come back. You were gone for a while.”

“I wasn’t sure I’d come back either,” Kara said.

That was a lie. Even if she hadn’t consciously admitted it to herself until a few days ago, Kara always knew that some part of her would feel incomplete until she’d walked down the doomed stairs to Other Lena’s cell again. Like she belonged down there in the dark hallway with her. She needed her fix, and just seeing Other Lena’s face erupted a rush in Kara’s head that made her feel more excited than she had in weeks. She could just barely keep it together and continue her walk.

Other Lena walked up to the window, stumbling on her feet as she got closer, following Kara like she was a phantom who could disappear at any given time. Like she had to make sure she was real before Kara faded away again. She waited by the glass, her fingertips leaving little prints at the height of her elbows, eyes glued to Kara’s face.

“Why… why did you come back?”

Kara sighed, digging into her bag to take out the books she’d brought with her, before continuing her walk to the hatch on the other side of Other Lena’s cell.

“Because I don’t hate you, Lena,” Kara said. “I don’t. Because despite everything you think of me, I still don’t want you to suffer here. And you can belittle me, and you threaten me,” she pulled open the hatch with a bit too much strength, and the metal protested with a rusty squeak. “It’s mean and cruel, but if that’s your way of trying to push me away, then it didn’t work, because I still care. Because I still believe in you. And I won’t let you win.”

Kara dropped the books in the hatch and pushed it back up to close it. The mechanical clang was too loud in the quiet space, and Kara watched Other Lena jump at the sound as if she was a skittish animal, stirring in their own fear, waiting for the inevitable pain to follow. Unlike other times before, Other Lena hadn’t walked over to have Kara hand her the books in person. Instead, she watched from a safe distance with big eyes as Kara angrily went about her business. Like Kara would hurt her.

When Kara actually looked up and their eyes met, she was surprised to see that Other Lena had nothing to say. No witty comment. No snide retort. She looked awfully thin and fragile, standing there behind the glass. Like it was her who needed to be protected from Kara instead of the other way around. It made Kara’s stomach do that thing again where she felt guilty, even though she knew she had every reason to be angry. But the thought of moving through the universe hurting people – hurting Other Lena… It never really gave her any sense of relief. It never made her feel better about all the hurtful things Other Lena had said to her. It never felt like it resolved anything.

Kara sighed. She shook her head and stepped away from the hatch.

“I didn’t find much,” Kara eventually said, not too unkindly. “I’ve got a feminist retelling of the Greek myth of Circe, a book called Beautiful world, where are you? by that author you liked, and Bluets by Maggie Nelson. It’s a prose poem or something,” Kara muttered. “The bookkeeper recommended it to me. I think she’s got a knack for picking out things you’d like after everything I’ve bought from her for you.”

“Thank you,” Other Lena whispered. It was clear that she didn’t know what else to say.

Kara paused. Her eyes glided over Other Lena’s delicate features, from the purple hue under her eyes to the slight scar-like indent on her chapped lower lip where her teeth must’ve bitten down too hard. Everything about her pulled Kara towards her, and it took Other Lena’s light, hesitant eyes flicking up to lock with Kara’s for Kara to realize she’d been distracted once again. She jumped at the electric shock that seemed to accompany the look in Other Lena’s eyes, and she cursed herself for letting herself get caught once again. That had not been the plan. The plan was to get in and get out before she could lose her cool. Before she could get stuck in that cellblock with Other Lena again, unable to leave until Other Lena would let her.

Kara took a step back, angry with herself. The move alarmed Other Lena, whose eyes turned wide and a little frantic at the familiar rustling that she could already tell preluded Kara leaving her.

“There should be some other magazines coming too. I’ll have them delivered to the D.E.O. so the guards can give them to you.”

Kara tightened the strap of her bag over her shoulder and Other Lena’s fists clasped together against the glass wall. Desperation grew in her eyes as Kara straightened up. She tracked her every move, looking confused, as if Kara was going too fast for her to take in, too fast to process.

“Goodbye then,” Kara whispered.

“Wait!” Other Lena finally exclaimed. “You – you only just got here.”

“I have work,” Kara said quietly. “I can’t stay.”

That was a half-truth. She did have work. She’d had work before. It had never stopped her from staying longer than she should before.

She turned, but Other Lena’s voice stopped her again.

“Will – will you come back?”

Her voice was high-pitched. There was an almost palpable fear that Kara wouldn’t return in her words. A fear she didn’t even try to cover up. It was mixed with some desperate, idle hope that made goosebumps break out on Kara’s arms. She felt her heart grow heavy, every voice in her head screaming at her to drop her bag to the floor, turn around, and sit with Other Lena again, just like she had dozens of times before. They seemed to plead with her, enticing her with the notion of how Other Lena’s face would clear up if she would only stay. If she would only shove her self-respect aside and let Other Lena regain what little power she had within the confines of the cell.

But Kara couldn’t.

She knew Other Lena’s temporary shock, probably brought about by a complete deprivation of any kindness whatsoever following Kara's departure, wouldn’t last. It would wither and die out and give way to her old self, and before Kara knew it, she’d be the one burning in no time. She couldn’t have that.

“I don’t know,” she said honestly. “Probably. I don’t know when yet.”

“Oh.”

There was silence behind Kara then, and she could hear from Other Lena’s fast-beating heart that the woman was probably lost for words, just like Kara. What was there to say, when neither of them was used to this change in power.

“Enjoy the books,” Kara said softly. “I hope you’ll like them.”

Other Lena paused, staring at the books in her hands like she’d forgotten they were even there.

“Thank you,” she said as if she were on automatic pilot. “I’m sure I will.”

With that, Kara could find no good reason to stay anymore, and forced herself to leave, never looking back.

 

 

“When were you going to tell me?”

Kara’s head whipped up when Alex stormed through her door, the oven scale with the cheese-covered pasta warm in her hands from when she’d reached out to retrieve it.

“Alex?” Kara’s eyebrows scrunched up with confusion. “What’s wrong?”

She didn’t even flinch as Alex shut the door with a loud bang, trudging forward like it was still her apartment. It would bother Kara more if she wasn’t already pretty sure what Alex would be yelling at her for now.

“What’s wrong?” Alex scoffed disbelievingly. “Are you fucking serious right now?”

“I am.”

Kara stood up straight and put the tray down on her stove. The hot cheese smelled absolutely delicious, but Kara couldn’t even take the time to relish in the successfully baked crust that she’d made. Her sister made sure of that.

“Tell me you’re not actually this stupid.”

Kara’s fingers tightened around the glass tray as she clenched her jaw, and before she could find it in herself to take a deep breath and let go of the tray, she heard a tiny crack and realized she’d fractured the rim of the tray with a long, ugly hairline fracture.

Kara let out a quiet gasp and quickly let go of the tray, pulling her fists close to her chest. Alex didn’t notice.

“You went back?” she asked incredulously, striding over to Kara with an expression of pure disbelief on her face. “After everything that happened, everything that she said, you decided to go back?”

Kara shook her head imperceptibly, trying to shake off the awful feeling of her strength overtaking her once again. She looked up and turned to Alex.

“I did,” she said. “Do you want soda or beer?”

She walked over to the fridge while Alex spluttered behind her.

“Why would you go back?” Alex asked. “And why didn’t you tell me? Did you know I had to hear from Jaxen? Jaxen?! Do you know how embarrassing it is to hear that you’ve done yet another unbelievingly stupid thing from one of my fucking agents instead of my own sister? Do you know how hurtful that is?”

Kara sighed but bit her tongue, refusing to engage. She simply made the choice for Alex and decided it was probably safer for Kara’s own sanity if they just stuck to soda. She carried the glasses and bottle to the table while Alex clung to her footsteps like a shadow.

She didn’t seem to notice – or maybe even preferred – that Kara wasn’t talking. With every new sentence flying out of her mouth, she seemed to feel more strengthened, more assured in her beliefs, more emboldened to continue.

“And I asked Lena, and she didn’t know you were going to go see the Other One either! She seemed fucking weird about it, but I’m guessing that’s also something you might know more about but just won’t tell me, right?”

Kara clenched her jaw.

“And the fact that – ”

“Alex, I get it,” Kara finally cut her off. “You’re upset. We can talk about it later. But I’ve had a pretty shitty week, so I’d really love to just have our sister’s night without all the yelling.”

“You can’t just expect me to handle a bomb like that and then drop it, Kara! What do you want me to do? I’m supposed to look out for you and keep you safe, and then you go ahead and do the dumbest fucking thing you can, leaving me to run after you to make sure you stay alive!”

“I don’t need you to save me!” Kara shot back. “I can handle myself just fine.”

“No, you can’t! And you know why?” Alex asked. Kara balled her fists at that domineering, over-confident, know-it-all tone in Alex’s voice. The one she’d used against her for so long when they were kids, and the one Kara hated encountering even more when it came to things that Alex knew absolutely nothing about. “Because you’re so fucking insane that you would run into danger head-first with zero regards for your own well-being! It’s not bravery, Kara. It’s masochism. It’s a death wish.”

Kara scoffed, dropping the glasses on the table with a loud bang. They danced precariously on the table for a few seconds before they mercifully came to a halt, remaining upright. Kara bit her lip so hard she thought she might bleed, and only stopped when she snapped her head around to glare at Alex.

“And what gives you the right to psychoanalyze me, huh? Your expired medical license?”

“Oh, very cute. It’s not expired.”

“It might as well be, seeing how little you use it.”

“No, you know what, Kara?” Alex took a big, intimidating step closer to Kara, but Kara refused to budge. She glared Alex down with a ferocity she ironically could only have learned from her. “I use that medical license – that medical degree, for that matter – every single time you turn off your brain in a fight. Because I’m the one who has to keep putting you back together. I’m the one who has to fix you. It’s my hands covered in your blood in my O.R. every single goddamn time, so I have every right to be as concerned as I damn well want to be!”

Kara rolled her eyes but had to bite the inside of her cheek so she wouldn’t give in. Because there was some truth to Alex’s words, no matter how much Kara hated to admit it. Kara could be reckless. She could be arrogant when it came to her inabilities, and it was true that she had ended up in the D.E.O.’s medical ward more times than she could count. She’d just never thought of Alex as the one having to deal with it all. Having to ward off the desperate, worried calls from Eliza, reassuring their friends on other calls, all while trying to dig the kryptonite out of Kara’s body with a scalpel at the same time.

“Why now?” Kara changed the subject. “Why couldn’t this have waited? Why couldn’t you say all of that before we planned this? All I wanted was one quiet night in with my sister, why couldn’t you let me have that?”

Alex crossed her arms over her chest, face set in stone, and Kara knew all hope for a good ending that night was ruined.

“I had meetings with her before!” Kara tried. “You didn’t say anything then!”

“Because I thought you needed it. I didn’t approve,” Alex said sharply. “But I couldn’t stop you. I figured you would get closure from realizing she was a monster, and you would be able to find at least some sense of peace in that. And you did! You stopped going! I thought it had worked. And then what do I hear today?”

Kara closed her eyes, hearing her own tired sigh echo through her head like it was bouncing against the sides of her skull.

There was a silence.

Alex took a sharp breath as if she was at least trying not to sound as angry as she was. She shook her head with a tired sigh, like the sight of Kara’s stubborn, childish refusal to talk about it broke away the overprotective anger that had led to Kara pulling away in the first place.

“Look,” she said, softer than before, controlling her anger the best she could, “I don’t want to be the bad guy here. You know I worry about you. I thought… I thought things were getting better with you. Nia says you work a lot, you’re making more time for us again… I just…” She sighed, rubbing her brow with four fingers, and Kara could almost see the painful thrumming that Alex always got behind her eyes when she was upset. “Ever since everything with Lena’s went down, I feel like I can only barely keep up with you. I know there are things you’re not telling me, and for the most part, I don’t mind.”

Her eyes softened, eyebrows knitting together in that familiar expression of worry that could make Kara’s heart melt in her chest. She had to ball her fists until they hurt just so she wouldn’t give in.

“I know you need to process things on your own. I know that Lena… Lena’s a sensitive subject. I understand that you have to… mourn that friendship, I guess. That you can’t always talk about it with me the way I’d want you to. I get that… that things haven’t been easy. But you’ve always had that reckless, self-destructive thing in you, Kara. It’s why you love being Supergirl so much. You do!” She put her hands up like she was already anticipating Kara’s protests. “I love you, but you run into danger in a way that frightens me. Frightens all of us.”

Kara hated feeling so admonished. Like she was fifteen, scolded by Eliza in the foyer because she hadn’t done what was asked for her. Because she was a child, who still had to listen to those who knew more. Knew better. But Kara rejected any notion that Alex, who wouldn’t listen to anyone who didn’t agree with her, knew better.

“So what are you saying, Alex?” Kara turned sharply. “That I have a death wish? That I'm crazy? What?”

“You know that's not what I mean,” Alex said frustratingly calmly – like she was the reasonable one. Like she was right, and Kara was the brat who refused to listen.

“Do I? You're sounding an awful lot like a therapist instead of a sister. You're not even trying to listen to me. You would rather write me off as insane than believe that I see something good in her! Do you know how messed up that is?”

“I just wish that at the very least you would let me come with you!”

“What, because I need a chaperone now?” Kara asked heatedly. “You trust me to go out and fight monsters and people who would try and make my death as slow and as painful as they could, but you don’t trust me to go and talk to a secured prisoner by myself? Do you know how hypocritical that is?”

“I trust you to go out and fight with people behind you!” Alex shot back. “I trust you to make the right calls and fall back on us – on Nia, on J’onn and Brainy and me when things go south! How do you not get that?”

“I’ve gone out on my own plenty of times and – ”

“And what, Kara?” Alex asked, shaking her head in utter disbelief. “Bad things happen when you go out on your own! You think you were fine by yourself when you were stuck in space after Myriad?”

Kara clacked her tongue in frustration and balled her fists, but Alex didn’t let up.

“You think you were fine after going out to fight Reign alone? You ended up on a table with my fucking scalpel in your body! Or do you want to wait until you end up dead on mom’s lawn again, huh?”

“You are going too far.”

“And you’re not thinking clearly! You are being reckless! If you think that she’s not smart enough to find a way to hurt you from the inside of that cell, then you’re severely underestimating her.”

“She hasn’t tried to hurt me! She’s just trying to live her life! How can you just expect me to sit by when she’s all alone in there and needs help?”

“Oh my God!” Alex’s fingers dug in her hair in frustration. “This isn't about her, this is about you!”

“And that's exactly where you're wrong!” Kara snapped. “None of you – not you or Brainy, or J’onn. None of you have tried to understand her! She needs help! She needs someone to listen to her!”

Alex scoffed and turned around and Kara thought she would explode. She felt like she was nothing, a child no one had to listen to, with no agency and no opinions worth noting, no stories worth sharing, and Kara thought she might burn up with all the frustration coursing through her body like poison.

“Yes, she can be a bitch!” Kara continued, following Alex back to the kitchen like she could still prove her point. “She can be hard and awful and mean, but she needs people! She needs me!”

“She needs you dead, Kara!” Alex spat. “That's the only way she needs you in. And I know this is probably you dealing with the fact that you have an intrinsic fucking obsession with having any form of Lena need you, or whatever, but you're going to have to learn how to deal with the fact that they don't fucking want you in their lives! One couldn't care less about your existence, and the other wants to see you dead!”

“You need to stop.”

“And you need to get a grip, Kara! You can't go on pretending this is a good idea!”

“You're not even listening to a word I'm saying.”

It was more of a realization than an accusation. Kara murmured the words and realized how true they were. How lonely she felt.

“You can't keep running to a woman who wants to hurt you just because you need that thrill to feel alive!”

“Get out.”

The words seemed to halt their conversation. Alex looked at her with insulted surprise, like she was affronted Kara would even dare say anything like that. Like Kara didn’t even have a right to kick her out of her own apartment. Kara got a dark pleasure out of watching Alex’s face contort like that. From that self-righteous bullshit into the shocked disbelief at her sister’s words.

“Seriously?” Alex said incredulously. “I'm trying to have a conversation with you about the ridiculously dangerous path you're on, but you refuse – ”

“No,” Kara said. “You're not trying to have a conversation with me. You're monologuing. You've said what you wanted. Now get out.”

“Kara.”

The look of hurt that crossed Alex's face was enough to almost make Kara falter. The fragility in just her name almost enough to get back on her words. But Kara didn't. Her jaw was set so tight she could almost feel it ache. She looked at the pitiful, lost expression in Alex's eyes – the confusion, like she couldn't recognize her own sister anymore – and she said nothing. 

“I’m just trying to help.”

“Well you’re not. Helping. You’re just making it worse,” Kara whispered.

Alex sighed and took a step closer to Kara. She inspected Kara’s face with such softness in her eyes that Kara wanted to look up, but refused to. Alex let out a tiny sound, hand going up like she wanted to reach out, but thought better off at the last possible second. Her hand lowered before it could touch Kara’s skin.

"Kara, I'm scared for you," Alex implored softly. So softly, that Kara might've actually listened to her if she'd used that tone all evening. “I thought you were getting better. I thought you were letting go.”

"Of Other Lena? Just because I stopped visiting her for a couple of weeks?” Kara said dryly.

"Of Lena.”

That hurt. Kara looked away.

“I thought you were finally done feeling guilty. I thought you were finally getting over her and everything that happened! I thought – ”

"You think that's the reason I'm visiting Other Lena? Out of guilt over what happened with Lena?" Kara asked.

"Isn't it?"

Kara looked at Alex. 

“No,” she said finally. “That’s not it at all. I'm talking to Other Lena because I like talking to her. Because I need her in my life too. Because I know that she's good for me just as I am good for her.”

“But you're not!” The confusion was dripping from Alex's words, her eyes hardening in frustration. “How can you not see how fucking toxic this whole situation is? How do you expect me to stand by and wait until she breaks free and finds a way to kill you? How do you want me – ”

“I want you to have faith in me,” Kara cut her off. “I want you to trust that I know what I'm doing and that I am doing the right thing!”

Alex shook her head and Kara's heart broke. She clenched her jaw when Alex looked away, and tears suddenly felt too close to the surface to be comfortable.

“Can you do that?” Kara was proud that despite the hurt that seemed to infect every cell inside of her, her words still came out strong. Self-assured. Even when she thought they’d come out like a childish plea for love.

Alex refused to look at her, and Kara got her answer.

“Really?” she asked, unable to repress her own bitterness. “Six years of fighting side by side, but you still don’t trust me to make the right calls?”

“I trust you to make the right calls,” Alex turned to her. “I do. Just not when it comes to Lena. Not to any version of her.”

Kara let out a breathless, humorless, little laugh.

“Okay,” she whispered. “Until you do, I don’t think we’ve got much to talk about then.”

Alex nodded curtly.

“I agree.”

She picked up her jacket from the chair.

“I’m going to Kelly’s.” She didn’t turn back around and Kara felt the room spin just a little. “Call me when you want to talk like adults.”

Kara scoffed.

“Right back at you.”

Alex shook her head and slammed the door on her way out. Kara took one look around the empty room, the take-out pizza’s cold and gross, still in their boxes, the soda’s that had gone flat, and the pile of Buffy DVD’s she had planned to go through with Alex, and Kara sank down on one of the kitchen stools. She stayed there for a long time, staring at the wall. Her phone didn’t ring once.

 

 

If Kara could blame it on anything, she’d blame it on her anger. On the emotional whirlpool of emotions raging through her that made it hard to focus on anything else. But realistically, she knew there really wasn’t anything to blame. Not really.

She got to the scene in time. She did everything that she could, doing everything exactly like Alex and the D.E.O. had trained her to do. The emergency services were there on time, and evacuation procedures had already begun before she’d even gotten there.

And yet.

Kara was sitting on CatCo’s roof, trembling from tip to toe. Her hands had cracked the stones underneath them, squeezing them so hard like they could somehow bend under her strength. They just crumbled instead.

She’d been off her game. She’d been off her game all week, and while she’d always gotten by with some quick thinking and a whole lot of luck, she’d run out today. And now…

Kara repressed a sob when she caught a whiff of smoke emanating from the building by the harbor, its embers passing through the sky on whisps of wind, long after the fire had been put out.

Seventy-three people. She’d managed to save seventy-three people. Guardian was there. Dreamer and Brainy. J’onn. Sentinel. All of them together had worked for hours trying to get everyone out of that building before it could collapse, with Kara flying around the building, breathing cold air until her airway felt like it had been frozen solid. She’d pulled people out, she’d carried them down, she’d tried her best to help the firefighters contain the fire that burst through the building’s windows and spread more rapidly than Kara could ever hope to contain it. She’d done all that, her friends just a couple of steps behind her, working just as tirelessly to help the people of National City.

And just when they all had their hands full, when they were only just, just keeping it together – holding all the tiny, fractured puzzle pieces in their hands to keep their world from crashing down around them, Kara heard it.

“Supergirl!”

She could still hear it.

So close, and yet too far for her to get to. Too distant for her to be able to drop all the pieces – the people clinging to her, the fire, just barely contained by her continuous freeze breath. Dropping one piece would mean the destruction and death of many others. Kara was stuck. She’d been stuck for hours and would be stuck for hours more. She couldn’t move without disturbing the fragile balance of things she and her friends had managed to obtain with so much hard work.

“Supergirl!”

Kara had to swallow the urge to drop everything and dash to the other side of the building to help. She begged, begged, begged the others to help. Prayed that they would find just a moment of respite in which they could cross the courtyard of the apartment building and save the anonymous voice that had called out for her. Please, her mind had whispered, please J’onn or Alex or Kelly, please. Help them.

They’d all heard it. They’d all seen or noticed the person calling for help, but they had all been unable to get there. The flames and the unsteady building and the dozens of screaming people had made sure of that. There had been no way out. No way to help. That’s what the others had tried to tell her, at least. Kara knew they were only trying to comfort her. Only trying to tell her that the person had been lost in the chaos for only seconds, that no one would have been able to do anything. That she had gotten there as fast as they could.

But it wasn’t their names that woman had screamed out. It wasn’t them she had begged to save her.

And when Kara had finally, finally been able to cross the courtyard, it was so, so very late. Kara had thought she was dead if it weren’t for the faint murmur of her heart stubbornly continuing to beat in her charred chest. But Kara hadn’t been too numbed by her outward appearance to not be shocked by her eyes. The woman’s eyes, still twinkling through the smoke-filled room she’d been choking in. They were a lively amber, glittering and so acutely aware of her surroundings. Even with her own skin melted to her furniture, her eyes had remained alert. And they’d homed in on Supergirl as soon as she had finally stepped into her room. Accusatory, delirious eyes had stared Kara down before the woman had screamed out in hoarse, terrifying agony when Kara had picked her up by the shreds of her body and had flown her to the medics.

Too late. So very, very late. She’d been able to read it in the panic of the medic’s eyes when she’d handed her over. Blackened skin and exposed flesh that made Kara want to vomit on the spot. The woman mercifully passed out, and Kara prayed that she would be out for a long, long time. She wondered if the woman would hate her for saving her at the last possible moment. If it wouldn’t have been more compassionate to let her die instead of cursing her to live a life filled with pain and hospital visits.

Kara had only recognized the light on her skin to be camera flashes when it was too late. When they’d gotten too many pictures of her already. After that, she saw her own, almost-confused-looking face reflected on every TV in the city. Her blue suit smoldering from flames that had yet to be extinguished. Her hair dark with soot and smoke. Her hands covered in other’s people’s blood. The brittle, dark, little heap of a person in her arms in high definition on every screen. Kara had only caught glimpses of the headlines, but it was enough for her to never want to put on the damn suit again.

She’d failed. She’d failed so miserably, and one woman had to pay for it. Kara’s fingers trembled, and she could feel her breaths becoming more shallow.

“Supergirl!”

She could still hear it. She could still hear her own name, so full of tears and desperation echoing through her head. She heard it over and over again, like an inescapable curse haunting her every move.

“Supergirl!”

It was still there, still so loud and scared in her ears and Kara thought she would cry, but she was too lost, too full of emotions to cry. It felt like crying was pathetic, abhorrently inadequate, lacking the horror and magnitude of everything she was feeling. It was nothing compared to the waves of pain that woman had yet to face. The endless misery that her family would have to endure with her after that damn tower.

The stone crumbled to dust in her hand, and Kara brought her trembling hands closer to herself so she wouldn’t do any more damage. Like she hadn’t done enough of that today.

How had it all gotten that bad? How had the collection of superheroes, firemen, medics, and agents failed to rescue one person? How had she messed up so bad? How could she save anyone, when she had just delivered one woman a fate worse than death?

Kara’s clammy hands wiped down her face, and a shiver ran down her spine. The city was spread out before her with all its twinkling lights getting brighter as the sky grew darker. So many people going about their evening routines, children doing their homework while parents prepared dinners and students were getting ready to go out. And Kara was on that damn balcony, while at least one person was fighting for her life in the hospital. A state Kara had put her in.

She felt so disgusted by herself.

Alex and Kelly had offered to take her in for the night. Make sure she had something to eat, somewhere to sleep. Alex’s sad, brown eyes had silently promised that the fight would be temporarily forgotten, unimportant when Kara actually needed her. They had promised a temporary refuge, food, a spot in Alex’s arms on her couch. But their pity wasn’t what Kara needed. It made her skin crawl to see someone extend so much sympathy towards her when she didn’t deserve one bit of it.

She was the monster, she wanted to scream. She deserved punishment, not love. Not a homecooked meal and some comforting words. She didn’t deserve Nia’s hug, Kelly’s promise that things would be okay, Brainy’s soft-spoken, rational explanation that “statistically, there was nothing more you could’ve done.” She deserved to be in as much pain as the woman who had called out to her. She deserved to be hated. To feel hated. She deserved pain.

And Kara knew there was only one place she could find it.

 

 

Kara had no memory of flying over to the D.E.O., scanning her badge, or getting permission to go down to the cells. She had no recollection of the people she’d spoken to or the screens she’d passed on her way down. All she knew, was that after what felt like a meaningless blip in time, she was standing in front of Other Lena yet again.

It was only when their eyes locked, and Other Lena’s lips moved, that Kara realized where she was.

“You came back.”

The worlds were a little lighter than before. The fear of Kara never visiting again had crept out of her voice, and instead, there was just a little wonder, perhaps at the notion of Kara coming by sooner rather than a lot later.

Kara didn’t say anything. She could feel she was trembling, and if she didn’t, Other Lena’s eyes drifting to her hands, a worried line appearing on her forehead, was enough to confirm it.

Kara only vaguely became aware of her surroundings. The humming of the lights above. The way Other Lena’s eyes were a little clearer than last time. Her face a little less pale. She looked… worried.

“Are you alright?” she asked.

The sincerity knocked Kara off balance and she barely registered a whispered “fine,” crossing her lips.

“Are you sure?”

Kara blinked. She didn’t understand.

Other Lena nodded hesitantly. “You’re swaying on your feet there a little, Supergirl.”

Kara had barely noticed before, but as Other Lena’s words registered, she looked down and found that she was indeed, not as steady on her feet as she thought.

“Supergirl?”

From the corner of her eye, Kara finally caught a glimpse of what had evaded her before. A testament to how blindly she had stumbled to that cell, guided by a deeper instinct that even she couldn’t explain.

The television was on. There was no sound, but it wasn’t needed either. It was CatCo’s emergency broadcast. The kind that interrupted all other programs when something so incredibly newsworthy had happened that Andrea would bet all her money people would tune in for. Kara couldn’t look at it for more than a brief second. She turned her head away.

She felt between worlds somehow. Like the entire situation wasn’t real. Like she was caught in a nightmare and knew it, but couldn’t break out before she had lived through it all. She wished she could wake up from it.

“You saw what happened.”

The words came out calm, emotionless. They didn’t linger. Other Lena just… looked at her.

“I did.”

Kara swallowed and let out a tiny gasp. As if she hadn’t expected it. As if the images of her carrying a disfigured woman to a doctor weren’t playing on the television screen behind her.

“Do you… understand what happened?”

“I did. Closed captions.” She pointed to the screen with a hesitant finger. “I asked them to turn down the sound on the television before so it wouldn’t distract me, but once I saw it was you, I…”

“You tuned in.”

Other Lena nodded.

“I’m sure you’ve got plenty to say.”

“I kind of expected you would come,” Other Lena whispered.

Kara paused. She looked up and her eyebrows knitted together in slow confusion. It was hard to wrap her brain around what was being said a lot that day.

“What?”

“Well maybe not expected,” Other Lena whispered. “But… I had a feeling you might… stop by.”

Kara’s throat felt dry. “Why’s that?”

Other Lena looked at her with almost sad eyes, and Kara felt the fire return under her skin. She didn’t want to see her own sadness mirrored in someone else’s eyes. She didn’t want the pity that made her heart ache.

Other Lena opened her mouth, before slowly closing it, thinking.

“Like I said. Just a feeling.”

Kara could feel she was lying but felt too tired to attack her over it. After all, what was a lie in the face of what she had done that day? She waited. Frustration began to grow in her chest when nothing happened. Nothing at all. Other Lena just… stared at her. She’d gone in with the idea that if she came, something would happen. She wasn’t quite sure just what she had expected, but she had imagined it would be big. Something energetic. Angry. Something unapologetically, unflinchingly raw, and honest. Something she could work with. A force of harsh truths that would break her apart piece by piece until she would go home and find a way to piece it back together. Kara guessed she was waiting on Other Lena to revert back to the woman who had first come through that portal in the D.E.O. months ago. The woman who had been able to reduce Kara to a puddle of tears just moments after meeting her.

There had to be something.

A resolution.

Something painful that would ache for days to come, that would leave Kara gasping through her tears, writhing on her bed in the guilt that would consume her.

Kara needed her to speak. To hurt her. To say the things that would break her.

But Other Lena didn’t. The wait was torture. The way Other Lena seemed to take in her features without the usual disdain and quiet amusement that could haunt Kara for days on end made Kara’s skin crawl. She didn’t like Other Lena this quiet. She didn’t like how she seemed concerned rather than relishing in Kara’s obvious discomfort. How could she be this quiet when Kara was offering up her pain on a silver platter? When she was giving Other Lena every chance to get the revenge she had come to her dimension for? How could she be this calm when Kara felt like she could burst under the tension of her own thoughts?

“Why aren’t you saying anything?” Kara asked. Her voice was rougher than before.

Other Lena rubbed the cloth of her blue pants between her fingers thoughtfully, tugging her hair slowly, carefully behind her ear. Like it could win her some time. It drove Kara mad.

“What do you want me to say?” Other Lena asked instead.

That made everything even worse. Kara’s throat felt painful, her heart seemed to shrivel in her chest like an organ she needed to expel to be able to just live.

“Anything!” Kara sounded on edge. She knew she did. Angry, but so frustrated that it made her sound petulant instead. Like a toddler who needed pity instead of the rage she wanted. The rage she deserved. 

“I don’t think you want me to say just anything,” Other Lena said quietly. She sounded much too reasonable and humane for Kara’s liking. She was almost angry that the person in front of her seemed more like the Lena Kara knew than the Other Lena Kara had met so long ago.

“What?”

“I think you came here,” she said softly, “because you want something specific. Maybe you already have the words in your head.”

Kara scoffed and turned.

“You don’t know what you’re talking about.”

“You’re confrontational. You’ve never been this confrontational with me. Even when you’re angry with me.”

Her observations were pointed, yet calm. Reasonable in a way Kara didn’t want Other Lena to be.

“I’m not being confrontational.”

“Then why are you trying to get me to yell at you?”

A shiver ran down Kara’s spine. She breathed in sharply and turned around to face Other Lena, who looked at Kara with expectant, patient eyes.

“Why are you so calm?” Kara shot back. “Weeks of you telling me you want to kill me for what I did to you, and now you’re all nice and calm? When did that happen, huh?”

Other Lena’s shoulders lowered slightly.

“I don’t know,” she said honestly. “Did you come here wanting to see that other version of me?” Kara bit down on her teeth so she wouldn’t scream. “I thought you were the one who so adamantly believed I was more than that. Was it – ”

“Did you not just see what happened?” Kara burst out, cutting Other Lena off. “Did you not just see that tower, that fire, that – that woman?”

Her words left her trembling all over. Her breaths were so shallow, Kara wasn’t actually sure how she was still breathing. Her cheeks felt red hot, her chest tight enough to strangle her. It seemed like Other Lena had been waiting for her to say exactly that.

“I did,” Other Lena said. “It seemed like a horrible situation. Too many people in one cramped-up building. It shouldn’t be legal.”

“It isn’t,” Kara said impatiently. “It’s one man taking advantage of vulnerable people and housing them in terrible conditions.”

“You seem to know your stuff.”

“I wrote an article about it last year. But that’s not what I was talking about!”

“I know it wasn’t,” Other Lena said softly. “You want to talk about that woman. The one on the news.”

Kara’s heart seemed to bulge in her chest. Her skin felt hot.

“Yes.”

The woman on the news. The woman who had called out to her. The woman she hadn’t been able to get to until the last possible moment.

“They didn’t mention her name,” Other Lena said kindly. “Do you know it?”

Kara’s throat felt like dry sandpaper.

“No. She wasn’t able to speak when I got to her.”

“Oh.”

The pity in Other Lena’s eyes was unbearable. Kara couldn’t look at it for one second.

She turned around and dug her hands into her sides like it would somehow make her feel steadier. Maybe if she looked like a powerful superhero, she would finally feel like one. Not like this useless, horrible shell of a person who could trudge around the city and break everything in her path.

“I’m sorry.”

“Don’t!” Kara raised her hands in front of her face like she was expecting fire and attacks instead of kind, soft words. “Don’t, I… I can’t – you can’t say that.”

“I can’t?” Other Lena asked softly. “Why not?”

“I don’t – I don’t deserve it. You shouldn’t… You shouldn’t say things like that.”

“How come?”

Kara let out a frustrated gasp and turned to face the cell.

“Why aren’t you yelling at me?” she demanded. “Why are you – why are you so calm? Why aren’t you furious? Isn’t this exactly what you came here accusing me of? Being a fake hero? A liar? A con artist? Didn’t you say that that’s what I did? Ruining the people I pretend to help? Letting them suffer – ”

Her voice broke and Kara had to take a second to calm her trembling hands, vague and blurry in her own eyes.

“You said… Everything you said was right. I let that woman… I let her – ”

She couldn’t finish. The woman’s honey-colored eyes filled with so much betrayal had almost been enough to bring Kara to her knees and she just… couldn’t. She couldn’t see it again; couldn’t face her again. Her stomach twisted, and it suddenly seemed like the air was getting tighter around her. The soot and the scent of burning flesh and –

“What exactly did you let happen?” Other Lena asked. She walked up to the glass, closer to Kara, who couldn’t move anymore. “From the looks of it, it seemed like you were all thoroughly overwhelmed with everything happening around you. It didn’t seem like you were letting anything happen at all. It seemed like you were trying very, very hard to ensure that no one got hurt.”

“But people did get hurt!” Kara yelled, loud enough for a shock to go through the hallway. Despite the glass trembling under the pressure, Other Lena didn’t move. “She got hurt! Did you not see – did you not… Couldn’t you – ”

“See that she was hurt beyond belief?” Other Lena asked calmly. “I could, thank you. Second to third-degree burns on about 70% of her body, if I had to guess. It will take months, if not years, for her body to recover.”

The cold, rational tone that Kara had already anticipated, did not reassure her the way she thought it would. Instead, it only added to the weight on her heart that made her chest feel too heavy for her legs to carry.

“The building was collapsing,” Other Lena said.

Kara nodded.

“And there were dozens of victims for you and your friends to save.”

Kara nodded again, like Other Lena needed to explain it to her to make it make sense.

“You didn’t know the victim.”

“No.”

“Would you have acted differently if you had known her name? Among all of the other victims?”

“What do you mean?”

Other Lena sighed.

“Supergirl,” she asked. “Did you act differently based on who she was? Did you hold some victims with one hand and ward of the fire with the other based on who they were?”

Kara shook her head.

“Of course not,” she whispered. “But that does not negate the fact that I let someone get hurt. That she’s…”

She couldn’t bring herself to go any further.

“You thought I would get angry with you for letting a woman get hurt in that mess,” Other Lena said calmly. “But I never blamed you for not being able to save everyone. I blamed Supergirl for stepping away when a Luthor was in need, as if my life mattered less than that of all those other people you saved. Like you could pick and choose who lived and died based solely on prejudices and preconceived notions of people you’d never even met!” Other Lena leaned in as if she needed to be closer to Kara to make her understand. “You had no idea who that woman was or what she was doing in that building. Her life didn’t matter any more or less than that of any other person you saved today. Pethaps you could have been able to rescue her before she got caught up in the fire, that’s true. But you’ll never know how many others you would have gotten injured instead had you made a different choice,” Other Lena implored. “From where I’m sitting, and from all the footage I’ve seen, you and your friends did what you could with the means that you have. That woman might blame you one day, yes.”

Kara flinched.

“But you did not consciously abandon her. You came back for her. You tried to help her after saving all those other people who needed you.”

Kara shook her head, unwilling or unable to listen. What Other Lena said made sense, it really did. But it was unbearable to even allow herself a minute to question the self-hatred and disgust she had carried with her for so long. She didn’t want to be forgiven. She wanted the hate and the disgust that she had hoped Other Lena would provide, but there was nothing left now. Nothing. There was just Other Lena, looking at her like she was so fragile, someone who needed to be protected and taken care of, instead of buried under all the horrible things she’d done, and all the victims she had left scattered in the wake of all her fights and all her unsuccessful missions. It made her so sick she thought she would throw up, but her body refused to do anything anymore. She was just there. Lost.

Other Lena tilted her head, her hair sliding off her shoulder in the process. Sympathy and an inordinate amount of softness that Kara had never seen before filled her eyes. She put her hands down on her lap, but her fingers spread and closed around her knees, like she was aching to take Kara’s hand in hers instead.

“Kara,” she whispered, so softly it was barely louder than all the sounds coming from the electrical appliances in the hallway. “You didn’t do anything wrong. You just couldn’t save everyone.”

“But I – ”

“You tried,” Other Lena said. “You tried really hard, and things didn’t work out the way you wanted them to. You’re grieving, and it’s hurting you so much you came here wanting me to replace that fear with rage. A different kind of pain,” she concluded softly.

“Why don’t you?” Kara asked hoarsely. “You’ve wanted to before. I’m letting you, aren’t I?”

Begging you, her mind whispered.

Other Lena smiled sadly, and Kara’s throat closed at the sight.

“I have very little rage left to give. And certainly not for a situation that you are in no way to blame for.” She leaned in, her forehead just millimeters away from the glass that separated them. “You didn’t do anything wrong, Kara. You gave it your all.”

Her knuckles rested against the glass as she looked into Kara’s eyes, a sad glint making her eyes look just a shade darker, pools of sorrow and empathy that Kara didn’t know how to look at.

“I’m sorry,” Other Lena whispered.

Kara let out a breathless, unamused laugh.

“For what? I’m not the one in the Med Bay, Lena. I’m fine! My friends are fine! That woman is still in the hospital! I don’t need your pity – she does!”

Other Lena looked incredibly sad at that, and Kara felt the guilt add to the mass already growing around her heart like a living, breathing organism. Getting heavier and heavier. Kara almost wondered what would happen once it had invaded every last square inch of space in her chest. Once she was full of it. Consumed by it. Once it started oozing from her pores until all her features were clouded by it.

“I’m sorry you came in here thinking I would hurt you. But this situation brings me no pleasure. I’m sorry you think you need to be punished for what happened in that building,” Other Lena said softly. “I’m so sorry you’re hurting. But you don’t deserve to feel this way. You did nothing wrong today.”

Kara turned her head. She could feel the burning in her eyes that she had fought so hard against all day.

“I’m sorry you felt like you deserved even more pain,” Other Lena finished softly, “and I’m sorry you thought you could find it here. I wish…”

She cut herself off, and Kara looked up. Other Lena looked at her with just as much confusion and soft longing as Kara felt herself. And if she could blame it on her grief and pain, she would. But at some point, Kara just didn’t care anymore. She stumbled blindly towards Other Lena’s cell as the other woman watched silently, fingers curling around the fabric of her pants.

Kara didn’t say anything as she sat down in front of the glass cell, shoulders drawn in like she had to protect herself from the cold. She didn’t dare look up, afraid of what she would see in Other Lena’s usually unreadable face. She didn’t have to ponder on it for long though, because Other Lena took a step away from the glass, just to sink down as well, cross-legged on the floor.

Kara raised her head and looked into Other Lena’s eyes, closer than she thought they could ever be with a wall of glass between them. She could see all the different-colored sparkles in Other Lena’s eyes, every pore on her face, and every single one of her confusing emotions mirrored in Other Lena’s soulful expression. Kara opened her mouth, but she couldn’t think of anything to say. When she did, tears shot up in her eyes and she had to bite the inside of her cheek to keep from sobbing.

Other Lena quickly raised her open hand and put it flat on the glass before her. Like she was reaching out.

“Hey,” she said kindly, a hint of worry in her voice. “Kara?”

Kara tried to blink the tears away, wiping under her eye with just the palm of her hand, staining the sleeve of her suit.

“Yeah?”

Other Lena swallowed like she was just as nervous to be this close to Kara as Kara herself was. Kara watched her throat bob, her tongue darting out to wet her lower lip, two fingers clutching at the fabric of her blue pants.

“I really am sorry you feel this way.”

Kara nodded.

“I’m sorry I yelled at you. Twice,” she murmured.

She felt emptier now. The room was quieter, though Other Lena’s heartbeat provided a warmer background sound than the humming of the lights above. It felt comforting to be this close and yet so far from someone. Like she could run away if she wanted. She just didn’t.

“Stay a while?” Other Lena whispered, forehead slowly coming to rest against the cool glass in front of her.

Kara couldn’t quite formulate a response, so she just nodded. She could see the small, hopeful smile on Other Lena’s face, the relief as she exhaled, tension draining from her shoulders. Kara felt too tired to bring it up, so she just leaned in too, resting her head against the glass before her as she closed her eyes. With just one inch of glass separating her and Other Lena, Kara felt safer than she had in months; and while nothing was right, and the hellishness of the world was still waiting on her on the outside of the D.E.O. building, she had found her refuge here with Other Lena. Kara allowed the thoughts of her sister, of the woman with the charred body, and the betrayal in brown eyes to drift away. They would still be there waiting for her when she got out of the hallway. But right then and there, her world consisted of the black tiles under her feet, the cool glass against her forehead, and the steady heartbeat and the quiet, slow breaths on the other side of the glass. The world was just her and Other Lena, and though Kara could still feel tears running down her cheeks every so often, she was at peace.

Chapter 10

Chapter Notes

See the end of the chapter for notes

“Kara?”

Kara groaned softly as she felt a gentle hand tug at her shoulder.

“Kara? It’s me, it’s… it’s Lena.”

The name sparked something in Kara’s tired head, and she opened her bleary eyes, blinking against the harsh brightness of the overhead lights. When things came back into focus, she looked right into worried, pale-green eyes, lined with dark eyeliner and a glamorous, purple smokey-eye. If she weren’t so tired and caught off guard, Kara would’ve jumped back ten feet in surprise, but as it was, she could only blink tiredly at the woman before her.

“Lena?”

Her groggy voice drew a small, sad smile from Lena.

“Hey,” Lena whispered.

“What are you – ”

Kara sat a little more upright, surprised to find that her cheek felt cool to the touch from leaning against a glass wall for too long. Lena’s hand slid from her shoulder as Kara turned her head, stretching her back from the cramped-up position she’d been sitting in for too long. She looked around and her breath hitched in her throat. Right there, leaning against the other side of the glass window, right next to a small, fogged-up spot on the glass near her lips, was Other Lena. The fading spot where Kara’s cheek had rested was only millimeters away from the edge of Other Lena’s face. Other Lena’s back was resting against the glass, her head turned to face Kara as if they were stuck in an intimate conversation that Lena had just walked in on.

Except Other Lena was still asleep.

Her eyes fluttered below her eyelids, seeing things that Kara could only hope were good. Were happy. Uncomplicated. Her cheek was flattened slightly against the glass, the other one covered in some of her dark hair that had escaped from behind her ear. Her dark lashes created intricate shadows on her cheekbone. Her lips were slightly opened, every exhale darkening the spot on the window again. She looked incredibly peaceful, even in the horribly contorted way she was propped up against the window. Kara cringed just thinking about how stiff Other Lena would be the next morning.

She forced herself to tear her eyes away from the woman on the other side of the glass to look at Lena, still bent over her, eyes sparkling with something that Kara couldn’t understand at first. Pity? Sympathy?

And then everything came rushing back and Kara could feel the heartbreak hit her like a ton of bricks. Her next breath felt impossibly hard, and Kara could both feel and hear it turn into a dry sob.

“Oh Kara, I’m so sorry.”

Lena’s hands fluttered over her shoulders and down Kara’s arms. Flickers of dust and soot rose up from her suit at the friction, and Kara felt faint at the sight. She realized with a wave of nausea that she could still smell the fire on her, and she shivered.

“It’s okay,” Lena whispered.

“That woman,” Kara said. “She’s – ”

“In the recovery wing of the Luthor Hospital,” Lena said. “I checked. She’s in the best of hands. I promise.”

Kara blinked in confusion.

“Oh.”

She tried to focus on something else. Anything else. And Lena was only, ever the logical answer.

It took her multiple tries and a lot of blinking to take it all in. Kara looked at Lena like she’d never seen her before in her life. Lena was wearing a purple gown with thin straps and sheer, smooth fabric that sparkled around her curves when she moved under the light. Her eyes were darkened with black eyeliner, accentuated by the darker shade of lipstick she wore. Kara would think the make-up would only make her look more powerful, more terrifyingly gorgeous, but all she could see was the softness of her Lena. The light-green eyes so full of tangible worry under the dark kohl lining her lashes. The way her hand was still resting on Kara’s shoulder, even though there was no real reason for it to be there anymore. It felt nice.

“Are you going to a party?” Kara asked. The confusion and sleepiness seeped through her voice, and Lena couldn’t contain a small smile from pulling at her lips.

“I just left,” she said softly.

“What kind of party was it?”

Lena frowned like she wanted to object to the quiet conversation she was making, but eventually, she let out a quiet, defeated sigh and threw Kara a small smile.

“A fundraising gala,” she said. “Nothing too special. Just some drinks and hors d'oeuvres for some generous donors.” She shrugged. “I’d been dreading it for days. Honestly, I was looking for an excuse to leave.”

“You look really beautiful,” Kara whispered.

Lena smiled despite herself. “Thank you. My secretary picked it out. I didn’t… I didn’t even leave the office. I went straight from work to the gala, I got changed in my office’s bathroom.”

Kara wanted to smile, but Lena’s face grew more serious, and the feeling that settled into the pit of her stomach seemed to realize – even before Lena had said anything – that she wouldn’t like where Lena was headed with her explanation.

“I was in meetings all day so I only saw what happened after… after a while.”

“Oh.”

Lena’s hand slid down and Kara felt a stab of fear at the thought of Lena’s hand dropping away. It didn’t. Lena turned her head to watch the Other Lena, still asleep against the glass. Her fingers mindlessly rubbed Kara’s arm, her thumb stroking up and down like it belonged there.

“How did you know to find me here?” Kara asked.

“I didn’t,” Lena said simply. “My first call was to your sister. She didn’t seem thrilled to hear from me.”

“Oh,” Kara frowned. “Yeah, I’m sorry. We, ehm, we got into a bit of a fight.”

“Oh,” Lena said. An awkward silence followed. “I’m sorry.”

“Don’t be,” Kara shook her head. “It’s stupid. We’ll be okay.”

“You sure?”

“Alex has historically been pretty bad at staying mad at me for long,” Kara whispered.

“Well,” Lena said, “that’s good then.”

There was a silence again, and Kara didn’t know where to look. She didn’t dare look at Other Lena, too scared she could wake her up just by thinking of her for too long. She couldn’t look at Lena, because her inquisitive stare was enough for Kara to feel completely out of her depths again.

“She told you I was here then?” Kara finally asked.

“No,” Lena’s eyes turned a little sadder, and her hand slid back up Kara’s arm again, like she knew Kara needed something that Kara herself didn’t even realize she did. “No, but… I figured that if you weren’t with Alex after… after what happened…”

She seemed to have trouble saying what Kara so readily knew she wanted to say.

“She expected me to come here too,” Kara whispered.

Lena’s eyes locked with hers. They slid over to her Other Self for just one second before jumping over to Kara again. Sharp and unreadable.

“Really?” she asked. “How so?”

“She didn’t say,” Kara whispered. “But it’s like she knew I would need something that my friends wouldn’t be able to give me.”

“Penance?” Lena asked softly.

Kara couldn’t look at her.

“Kara, it was an accident – ”

“I don’t really feel like talking about anymore,” Kara said softly. Lena looked like she wanted to protest, but one pleading look from Kara, and she shut her mouth.

“Okay,” she whispered. “Can I… Can I at least ask? Did she? Make you feel…”

“Guilty?” Kara asked quietly.

Lena’s mouth closed, the sadness in her eyes agreeing for her.

Kara allowed herself one quick look at the sleeping woman on the other side of the glass, resting so easily in her little place on the floor.

Kara shook her head.

“No,” she whispered. “Not once.”

“Oh,” something akin to surprise and quiet understanding passed over Lena’s face, and if Kara had any more energy, she might’ve wanted to ask Lena about it. But as it was, waking up on the cold floor under Lena’s watchful eye, Kara felt the exhaustion and emotional turmoil of the day press down on her all at once. She couldn’t suppress a yawn and covered her mouth with her hand.

Lena spotted it instantly and whatever trace of doubt and curiosity had been on her face before disappeared.

“Okay,” she said as if she needed to convince herself, “it’s time for you to go to bed.”

“But – ”

“You can’t stay here all night, Kara.”

Kara wanted to disagree, but her stiff body seemed to perk up at just the notion of getting in her own toasty warm bed and forgetting all about the day she just had. The comfort of Other Lena’s presence could only alleviate so much pain before her body started to protest and whine for actual, qualitative sleep.

Kara sighed, begrudgingly moving to stand up. A winning smile passed over Lena’s lips, but before Kara had even gotten up on her feet and Lena had extended her hand to help her up, it was gone. Like Lena didn’t care to gloat more than she wanted to help.
