Lena took another heavy breath, tears jumping in her eyes.

Right there, on the left side of her chest, where she used to only feel a coldness, metal and kryptonite strapped into her body like she was a mechanical doll, there was a budding warmth. A thrumming of human, unadulterated energy.

For the first time in three years, Lena could feel her own heartbeat.

But that wasn’t possible. She remembered the kryptonite being there. She remembered how it felt, screaming in agony, strapped to a table with her mother’s masked face hanging over her open body, blood splattered on her blue gown. She remembered…

She remembered everything. She remembered Kara’s face as she held her. How her tears spilled onto her forehead – the only warm sensation in an otherwise icy cold state. How her hand had trembled as she’d cupped Lena’s face. How Lena had ached to see her like that. How much pain she’d felt, but how utterly unable she’d been to utter a single word, despite her best efforts. She remembered Kara’s face, lit up with green traces around her eyes and mouth, floating in a hazy cloud. Those blonde curls bouncing around like a willow’s branches blowing in the wind over her face. There was nothing else. No one else. Her devastated face was the last thing she saw before…

Before she was at her desk. In another universe entirely, or so it seemed.

She had to have died. There was no other explanation for it. There was nothing that could make the situation any clearer. But if she had died, then why was she in her office? Breathing? Thinking? Why did she have a heartbeat?

Lena had never been very religious, but if this was the universe’s way of punishing her for her earthly actions than she would think she required a more in-depth reading of several religious texts because this seemed too odd for any religion to come up with.

Before Lena could process just about anything, there was a knock on the door. She jumped up in alarm, but when the door was opened, her brow furrowed.

The woman was speaking, but Lena couldn’t hear anything. That familiar face, that no-bullshit attitude, those sharp eyes that caught everything… Lena felt like she was thrown back years in just a second. She had to contain every impulse in her body not to let her mouth fall open at the sight of her. The woman looked at her expectantly, dark eyebrows so far up her hairline, Lena knew she was expected to say something back. But all she could utter was…

“Jess?”

Jess Huang, her favorite assistant. The woman who had stuck by L-Corp until Lena had come back after a year of being held in her mother’s lab. Who had stuck by Lena’s decisions and commands and who had personally kept the business up and running in her absence. The woman who had cared for Lena when she could barely walk ten steps without fainting from the pain.

She’d quit two months into the HOPE program. She was the only one who had dared to ask Lena if what she was doing would accomplish what she said it would. The only one who had voiced her misgivings about Lena’s projects. The only one who had told Lena she couldn’t work for her anymore, given the direction L-Corp was headed in.

Lena didn’t try to stop her then. Even when it had strangled the last bit of kindness out of her body, watching her only semblance of a friend walk out of her life. She didn’t know why the sight of her now made her breath hitch in her throat.

“Ma’am, are you alright?” Jess was worried. “I can cancel the interview, it’s no problem. It’ll give you some time to rest before your meeting?”

She actually looked a little too eager to send reporters away, and Lena had to bite down a teary smile at the protectiveness in her. Jess. Sweet, dedicated, incredible Jess.

She realized quickly that she was quickly raising a lot of red flags, and if she didn’t want Jess to call her private doctor and schedule some kind of spa retreat for her, she had to get some control over herself.

She cleared her throat. “No, no, it’s alright, Jess. I’m sorry, I must not have had enough to eat before. I didn’t hear you, who’s coming to interview me?”

Jess’s mouth pulled into an unamused, straight line.

“The Daily Planet. Kent,” she said, clearly fighting the urge to outright curse out his name. “He was…” her face turned sour enough to deter just about anyone with a press card attempting to get in. “Insistent.” 

“They always are,” Lena smiled, but Jess didn’t seem amused and Lena bit down a smile. “It’s alright, Jess. I’ve faced worse, haven’t I?”

That didn’t seem to make Jess feel better, but at the very least, she seemed more preoccupied with shoveling the reporters back out the door again as soon as possible, than she did worrying about Lena’s deteriorating mental state.   

Lena was still a little shaken, but she couldn’t help but think that maybe she just needed to move with everything that happened around her, that that would somehow clear things up. Whatever this world had in store for her – be it hell, purgatory, or some other, unknown reality she’d fallen into – there was no way back. Figuring out what happened could come later.

“Let him in, please, Jess.”

And Jess, sweet, loyal Jess, didn’t question her.

“As you wish ma’am.”

She walked through Lena’s office as Lena tried to compose herself, taking in shallow breaths in an effort to try and process everything that was happening as fast as she could, trying to put her questions as to whether or not she was in heaven, hell, or some infernal word in-between to rest, just in case it was something else entirely.

“Oh,” Jess said from the door opening. “I forgot to mention, there’s someone with him. Not a reporter. An… assistant, I think? She’s just here to accompany him.”

“Right,” Lena said vaguely, shuffling through the papers on her desk with meanings that had long been lost to her – financial reports from 2016? She couldn’t remember Kent ever taking assistants on his plights to grill her for whatever information she had to give him about her brother anyway. “What’s her name?”

“A certain Miss Danvers, ma’am.”

Lena’s head jerked upright as the door fell closed.

She barely had time to compose herself before the door was opened again. Her heartbeat quickened – deafening in her ears. He walked in first, as Jess held open the door, and then, after a little shuffle by the door, a quick, shy thank you to Jess, and an uncoordinated, almost clumsily shy step forward that made her bump into him as he stood before her later, Kara Danvers walked into the room. Her searching eyes scanned the office, before falling on her.

Lena could barely keep from crying as those blue eyes widened behind her glasses, her mouth falling open slightly as she took Lena in, and blushed, casting her eyes back down again, readjusting her frames.

Kara.

Lena smiled, before taking her seat and welcoming her two guests.

 

 

Their meeting had been… short. Uneventful. The same old Luthor bullshit she’d gotten to know intimately over the years. Still, it felt more venomous when it translated to mistrust and apprehension in Kara’s eyes. But it was alright. It went by in a blur.

Kara Danvers from CatCo.

Lena still couldn’t believe it. The shy little woman before her, hiding behind her annoying cousin was Kara. The last face Lena had seen before she… passed. Left. She could still see her so vividly, shouting at her in front of her cell when Lena was too cold or harsh. Extending her kindness in books and trinkets, giving away her love so freely, like Lena deserved it. She knew she didn’t. That was her Kara. And yet somehow it wasn’t.

She didn’t remember her.

Somehow, things were very different than the way Lena had imagined.

They were out of her office before she’d even comprehended what they were accusing her of. In any way, Lena had barely been able to keep her eyes off of Kara. She’d had to try with all her might not to stare at her with an open mouth and bug eyes. But Kara was just so… different. She’d seemed… quieter, tinier, in a way. Eager to prove herself, but unable to tell how. Unexperienced. Uncertain. Younger.

She didn’t seem to remember anything from what happened, so Lena had to deduce that it wasn’t her Kara. She was somewhere different altogether.

And she was all Lena could think about as she was guided through her building by Jess and her security team to another meeting on the other side of town. She barely registered going to a different section of the building, going up the stairs, until the wind hit her face – and she saw the helicopter standing on the Helipad of L-Corp.

She froze.

Years of anguish hit her square in the face, and a sharp, piercing pain shot through her heart as if to remind her of a future that awaited.

Was this it? The punishment for her misdeeds? Having to live her life over and over, ending always in the inevitable helicopter crash?

She turned her head, panic written all over her face.

“Can’t we take a car?” she asked her pilot, who shot her a disturbed look. “Can’t we drive?”

“Ah, I’m afraid that won’t be possible Miss Luthor,” he said, and she closed her eyes, already having anticipated that that would be his answer. “You’ll never get there in time.”

She felt tears push against her shut eyelids, every instinct inside of her screaming, begging her not to get in. But Lena knew she had no choice. No matter what had happened before, something was different this time. Kara was different. They’d never met before, hadn’t they? That was different. This day was different than before. Something inexplicable had led her heart to beat, and had led Kara to her office. And if Lena had learned anything from the months in that cell, it was that her face, her young, blonde head, and sparkling blue eyes, meant something new. Something exciting. It meant something good, and it was the only thing Lena needed to take a deep breath, open her eyes, and nod grimly, before strutting towards the helicopter in her heels, ready to tackle whatever future this universe held in store for her. Even if she had to die another dozen times to find out what it was.

 

 

Everything happened exactly as she remembered it.

She heard herself say that she didn’t like flying, but the words sounded hollow, far away. They went up, up, up, until they were at a dizzying height above National City, Lena’s trembling hands holding onto her headset like a safety railing. The sky so blue she could drown in it. Scattered tufts of clouds that she remembered as a white, blurry maelstrom as she fell down. But before that, they were just there, moving along with the wind, unassuming and indifferent.

Then came the drones. Lena felt cold sweat in the back of her neck, watching them hover around the helicopter before zoning in on the front glass. Aiming for her. She let out a shuddering breath and held onto her seat with white knuckles, her heart dropping to her stomach, adrenaline coursing through her veins just enough to keep her from screaming, crying, and trying to claw her way out of her own skin. She could feel her heart knocking bruisingly hard against her chest, and mourned the fact that she only got to experience it for such a short time before having to lose it all over again.

But just as the shots started firing, and Lena was about to close her eyes, waiting for all of it all to happen again – the pain, the broken bones, her mother, Kara – something changed. The sound Lena remembered so vividly in her nightmares, the sound of bullets hitting iron, and then the stomach-turning squelch of bullets piercing flesh was replaced by a different sound entirely. Bullets hit a wall far away from her, fading away before they could hit their mark. The helicopter was still desperately whirring in the sky, her pilot frozen next to her.

Lena dared to move her head, the rest of her body stuck in its seat by a combination of fear and hopelessness. But right there in front of her, blocking her view of the still-firing drones, were the two familiar red capes – the ones she knew all too well.

Hovering in front of her, preventing any bullets from coming her way, were Superman and Supergirl, arms spread protectively by their sides, a stance that indicated they were ready to do whatever it took to save them. To save Lena.

It went by in a quick blur, quicker than Lena could process. Superman left, but Kara remained, trying to shoot the drones down quicker than they could shoot at Lena. One shot managed to put her down and allowed one bullet to hit the pilot, and while Lena’s heart was racing, her fear was dissipating on the spot. Because Kara was there. And against all her rational knowledge, her understanding that this Kara didn’t know her as intimately as the one she just left behind, knowing that she distrusted her based solely on her last name and that she didn’t owe Lena anything… Lena felt, deep inside of her, that Kara wouldn’t leave her behind. Not this time. So when Kara shot back up in the sky like Lena’s personal guardian angel desperately fighting to keep her alive, she let out a shuddering, disbelieving laugh – and watched in awe as Kara destroyed the remaining drones.

She covered her mouth with her hand to stifle something between a laugh and a sob, catching her breath amidst the chaos of it all.

The door was ripped out of the helicopter, and as Lena was catching her breath, Supergirl made her way in, checking on her pilot’s state.

“He’s alright,” Supergirl said. “So are you. You’re safe now Miss Luthor.”

Lena looked at her, tears she didn’t want brimming in her eyes. It seemed to take Supergirl aback, like she hadn’t expected a Luthor to show strong emotions like that. In all truth, it wasn’t a habit for Lena to show her cards to… anyone. But the shock and surprise and disbelief over the entire situation had gotten the best of her, and she could scarcely hold in anything.

Kara was pulling the helicopter down gently, and before Lena knew it, it was on the ground. Her pilot was quickly lifted out by paramedics already on the scene, but Lena stayed put, too dazed to move.

“Miss Luthor?”

She looked over and saw Supergirl by her window, her brow creased in concern. She held out her hand, and it took Lena a few seconds to realize what she was doing. How could one blame her, though, she wondered, when none of this had happened, and Lena still wasn’t sure how or why the situation was unfolding this way. Her arm trembled as she slowly tried to find Kara’s hand, but as soon as it did, Kara’s hand folded around her own – steadily, surely… comfortingly. A spark of electricity shot down her spine and she shivered, and Kara quickly got closer.

“May I?” she asked gently.

Lena didn’t know what she was asking, but she found herself nodding. Anything, she thought, you may do anything.

Kara floated up and gently let Lena’s arm slip across her shoulders, so she could more easily lift her from her seat and float her down. From the corner of her eye, Lena caught the camera flashes, and a part of her sourly realized how helpless she would look on tomorrow’s front cover, carried out of her helicopter by her family’s archnemesis. Another part of her delighted in the idea of Lex’s face, seeing them like that.

Even once Lena’s feet unsteadily found the pavement below, she continued to clutch Kara’s arms, unconfident that her body was able to carry its own weight and manage gravity at the same time after what had just gone down. Lena let out a few shuddering breaths, the world spinning around her like she was still falling down. She wasn’t. She was on the ground. Alive. She looked down at her chest as if to check it hadn’t transformed into a cold piece of green rock while she’d been distracted – but no. A normal blouse, sticking to her body from the sweat and grim of the helicopter, dirty from the smoke of the exploding devices, but just a blouse, nonetheless. No blood. No metal. No kryptonite. Just her regular, old heart, beating anxiously against her chest.

“Are you sure you’re alright, Miss Luthor?” Kara asked gently when she’d made sure Lena had steadied herself.

“Yeah,” Lena whispered, wiping a stray tear away. “I’m fine.”

Kara’s searching eyes stayed on her face, a concerned little frown still set between those eyebrows.

“I just…” Lena shook her head. “I wasn’t sure anyone would come up to save me,” she admitted in a whisper. “I just… I wasn’t sure. I thought…”

She couldn’t finish her own thought. Too shaken to even dare think about what could’ve happened. What did happen.

Kara’s face fell, softening so much that Lena thought she could almost hear the other woman’s heart defrost, her misgivings fading with the one tear Lena had pushed away.

“Miss Luthor,” Kara said softly, her voice so young, so utterly horrified that Lena would even suggest a bias so tangible, so impossible in Kara’s eyes. “I would never – me and my cousin would never – ”

“It’s fine,” Lena said quickly. “I know, I know you would never… “

Pick who they wanted to save? Allow their judgment to define who would live and who would die?

Lena had believed all of that before.

“I have more faith in you than I do in the Luthor name and legacy is all,” she said, and that felt right. That aligned more with everything she’d thought before. Everything she knew before Kara had cried, holding her dying body. She shook the thought away. “I guess… I guess I wasn’t sure anyone would care enough to intervene.”

A crew of L-Corp’s security flooded the scene before Kara could say anything else, but Lena could tell she wanted to say more. The worry in her eyes reflected a thousand questions that Kara still needed answered, but at the same time, she looked lost. Like she felt for Lena.

As Lena was rushed into a car by a dozen people fretting over her, she couldn’t help but look back, and saw Kara staring at the ground, hands clasped in front of her, a confused little frown on her face.

 

 

Lena saw Supergirl freeze.

The press event had gone haywire – another one of her brother’s minions shooting up the place. And when Lena recognized the woman he was blocking his body with as Alex – Alex Danvers… She didn’t think twice about shooting him.

The expression on Kara’s face made her think that maybe, maybe, this time she was doing something right.

 

 

When they came by her office again, they brought the newest issue of The Daily Planet with them, where L-Corp’s shiny tower faced her, unblemished and unbroken. So unlike her memory, Lena could almost get emotional. She remembered the ruins of the tower from which she fell so long ago. How she had to rebuild such large sections of it after her return, and how the renovations had drained the little energy she had left. How the building had never looked quite right after.

But this. This was her beacon of change. Of hope. A physical embodiment of something new. Even if she still couldn’t believe it; that change was staring right back at her. A glossy future in black-and-white lettering.

Lena cleared her throat, trying to keep her emotions at bay.

“And what about you, Miss Danvers?” she asked, delighting just the slightest bit in the way Kara jumped, furtive eyes looking a little lost when they got caught in Lena’s own. “I didn’t see your name in the byline?”

Kara shuffled a little, blushing as she adjusted her glasses for what had to be the hundredth time that day.

“Oh, well, like I said, I’m not a reporter.”

Lena’s lips curled up on their own account. She remembered Kara slipping up in front of her cell, getting lost in how much she loved writing her articles. How her honesty and sense of justice had permeated her words when she spoke of it. How much of a journalist she was at heart, without even being conscious of it. How utterly unable she’d been to keep it hidden in those very early visits. How Lena had delighted in that passion of hers – and the way her eyes would widen when she realized just how bad she was at lying, begging her not to tell her sister. How utterly endearing Kara could be.

Kara Danvers. Reporter by day, Supergirl by night.

And yet, the nervous, blushing young woman in front of her didn’t look like either. She just looked at Lena.

“That’s funny,” Lena whispered. “You could’ve fooled me.”

The dusty pink that adorned Kara’s cheeks after she’d said that was the biggest win she could’ve ever gotten, Lena thought. Kara seemed to straighten her spine, a thoughtful spark lighting up her eyes. Her cousin turned to look at her, but Kara only looked at her. Lena’s eyes never left her.

“I do hope this isn’t the last time we talk,” she asked softly, meaningfully.

“It won’t be,” Kara said instinctively, blushing a little harder when she realized what she’d said. “I mean,” she corrected herself, reverting back to her blustering, blushing self. “I hope not either,” she finished, smiling at the floor.

Lena smiled back.

“I guess that’s settled then.”

Kara beamed softly from behind her glasses.

 

 

Lena figured it out at night, in her office.

She didn’t leave when her employees did, still too afraid and unfamiliar with this world to dare step out of the safety of her own four walls. Lena had nothing if it weren’t for her sanctuary, and that was the way it always had been.

There was no Lex here. He was locked in a prison Lena knew he’d one day escape from. Such was the way the other universe had shown her. There was no one else either. Her mother she’d rather keep at a distance, her friends had failed to recognize her as one of their own the moment her brother had gotten the bad press, and Jess had long gone home. Even if she rarely gave it a thought during the day, working so hard until her body would physically collapse the moment she got home, not a spare cell in her brain dedicated to her lack of social life, it often astounded her how hard it could hit in those unsuspecting, quiet moments. How lonely it could feel, looking around her empty office, knowing that there was absolutely no one waiting for her anywhere.

How much harder it hit her, now that the one person who’d always starved to see her, was nowhere to be found.

She looked up at the ceiling, the desperation she felt wrapping her up all at once. How cold it felt around her heart, with no one here.

“Kara,” she whispered, shaking her head. “Where are you?”

There was no response, and though she didn’t expect one, the pang of disappointment felt more bitter than she’d expected.

She looked back down on her calendar, the same one she’d now scanned over and over again, the same conclusions drawn each time without fail. It was September. September 2016. Four years ago. And while she had missed the next couple of months of that year, she remembered that September vividly. The last month she’d felt her own heart beat. The month she was abandoned by the city’s so-called protectors. The month everything changed.

And then it came back to her.

Piece by piece, all the information she’d ingested, sitting alone in that cell, from her doppelganger. From the documents that the woman had shoved into her hands, a peace offering. Then from Director Danvers, whose life she’d saved today, who wanted to interrogate her, but ended up sharing more than she absorbed. But mostly, she remembered every tidbit of information that Kara had shared with her over the months they’d spent together. Freely, liberally, openly. Between book reports and toxic remarks, heated discussions and games, Kara had let things escape every now and then. Frustrations she had with her Lena. Things that had happened that involved her brother. Times where she’d felt desperate enough to call on the gifts of a fifth-dimensional creature. Manifested power in the form of…

A wish.

She whispered it out loud just as it came to her. The memory of Kara, huddled in a corner of the D.E.O.’s prison hall, face red with a mixture of embarrassment and genuine hope, muttering the story in bits and pieces to her. To explain. Lena remembered. That’s how it started. That’s what Kara said. A wish to protect Lena from Kara – but one that backfired into the horror show that her life had been. A wish to heal Kara’s own heartbreak, a wish that had condemned Lena to a lifetime of agony, devoid of love or comfort. A wish that Kara had regretted as soon as she’d seen the city Lena ruled over.

A wish made in the most desperate of times, when Kara had felt so horribly undone by her fractured relationship with Lena, that she had gone to new lengths to fix it. And hadn’t Lena’s last moment in that universe not been entrenched by the desperation in Kara’s voice, in Kara’s eyes, in Kara’s presence?

Thinking back to what happened made her head pound, and Lena had to close her eyes to even try and remember, but the big pieces were there, even if all the rest was… muddled.

Trying to escape.

Almost making it out of the D.E.O., uncertain of where she would go after, but confident enough when she felt Kara’s hand in her own that the future would be better than the present.

Even if her memory was scattered, and even if she remembered it through waves of pain and a hazy vision, Lena recalled the desperation on Kara’s face, lit up by the kryptonite that had to be burning her alive. She had been crying. She’d been desperate. Lena remembered, through the pain that flooded her in waves of dizzying power, that Kara was there. Holding her. Reassuring her.

Even when the waves of pain subsided, giving way to a sudden onset of drowsiness that Lena had tried so hard not to give into, she remembered clinging to Kara. To her words. To her being. She held on, even when her body had already given up. She remembered Kara’s lips on her hairline, the touch barely registering through the cold, through the sweat, through the lack of air in her lungs. But she remembered it being there as the sole comfort in Lena’s miserable death. How Kara’s lips had whispered words into her skin that Lena had barely been able to comprehend, but had elicited something sweet and warm in the back of her head, like the honey her mother used to put in a glass of milk when Lena had had a nightmare, years ago. Comfort wrapped up in pale pink lips and tears – dripping in bursts of warm energy on her face.

A tear rolled over Lena’s cheeks, her lips open, trembling as she recounted how warm she’d felt. How… safe and sound in the safety of memories of her home long ago, things she thought she’d forgotten. All brought back to the surface by Kara’s presence, her protective arms around her, and the way Lena had felt so embraced by something larger than herself. It could have only lasted seconds, moments, but in those final seconds… it was everything. Everything. Only when the last of the pain had given away, Lena had felt like she’d been able to rest, and that someone would be waiting for her when she woke up.

Kara had made sure of that. Even if it had killed her.

Because that was clear as day too.

How hurt Kara had been. How lost, screaming for people that Lena couldn’t put a face to anymore. Swallowed up by the darkness as Kara’s face grew more and more desperate, her blouse growing darker in color right along with it. The pain in her voice that cut like a hot knife through Lena’s cold body…

She remembered. She remembered.

How ironic, she realized with bitter tears pricking her eyes, that this entire time she had been so focused, so obsessed with bringing Supergirl to her knees, that the only time she had succeeded, was when she was holding Lena so tenderly, trying to protect her from her impending death.

Death.

She’d known she was dying. Even after being shot, her brain could still put the pieces together – the blood and the kryptonite destabilizing the last functioning organs in her body, laying bare the foundations of her mother’s torturous experiments. She knew. She knew.

So how had things changed so drastically? How had she jumped dimensions? Hell – how the fuck was she alive, sitting in her own office?

The only explanation was the last memory Lena had, of Kara’s grief-stricken face. If Kara had been suffering from the exposure of Lena’s kryptonite, why had she clung on – even if Lena had so selfishly needed her to hang on. Why had she stayed with her, calling for help, disturbing Lena’s process of gliding away into a place where the pain had dimmed?

The answer was simple, and yet felt selfishly inconceivable at the same time.

She hadn’t been able to let go.

Lena’s heart wrung itself inside out remembering how shrill and cracked Kara’s pleas for help had been, how sickeningly desperate her sobs had been, holding on. It made Lena want to throw up, but the misery wouldn’t allow itself to be stopped in its tracks. Lena had to face what happened rationally. Coldly. Factiously.

But Kara’s face rendered that process utterly and completely hopeless.

The answer was simple, Lena devised. For some reason and logic-defying reason, Lena had somehow been able to earn the warm, unconditional affection of a woman she’d tried so hard to destroy, and it had saved her life in the end.

More than her life.

Lena had gotten something, a gift, a wish, a miracle – whatever she could call it. Something to reverse what Kara had wished for initially, something to give Lena the life that Kara had taken from her.

She’d been given it freely, unknowingly, alone. She couldn’t go back, she couldn’t thank Kara, couldn’t ask her why, and how she’d earned it, what she’d done to deserve the love that Kara had given her. The tangible proof of love, of friendship, of kindness… Something that Lena knew she could have never earned, spitting hatred at Kara from the safety of her cell. She couldn’t… she couldn’t have.

And yet… here she was.

Lena looked around her office and had to bring her hands up to her forearms to rub them, suddenly cold in the large space of her office.

She was alive, against all odds. All because of Kara – and Lena was convinced of that too. She didn’t know what had happened after she’d… died? Slipped away? Faded away? But there was no question in her mind or her heart that her miraculous escape was all thanks to Kara. No one else had enough willpower to command the universe to get Lena back, and Lena was sure that Kara had found a way. She just didn’t know how much time had passed. She looked down at her pale arms, speckled with freckles, broken out into goosebumps. She didn’t look like she’d been rotting, decaying, or anything.

She looked just like she had in the days leading up to her accident. She looked normal.

It all came crashing down a little all too sudden, and Lena felt a sudden wave of despair and misery wash over her. She let out a dry sob and buried her face in her hands, spiraling too much to be able to bear the confusion, anger, frustration, and hopelessness she felt, so alone in the safety that Kara had created for her. Kara was gone. Her version of her, at least. The woman who had changed so much, in tiny increments of time, in games, in conversations, in easy-going kindness… every bit of her had been stripped from Lena’s life, and now she was alone once more.

Now she had to navigate this world without her. Had Kara trusted her to be able to do so? Did she really have that much confidence in Lena that she had expected her to do better this time? To triumph instead of despair?

Lena didn’t know. Couldn’t know. But she was sure she’d spend the rest of her life driving herself crazy over the absence of answers to those questions.

She sighed, and shook her head slowly.

“Where are you?” she whispered.

Her shoulders dropped at the absence of sound that followed. Kara didn’t answer. But someone else did.

A whooshing sound on her balcony made Lena look up, and she turned around slowly, not quite sure what she was expecting. Another murder attempt to make up for the failed last one? The universe trying to right the wrong of her untortured escape from fate? Her brother, arms at the ready, waiting in his ugly prison attire to hurt her?

Whatever she had expected, it wasn’t that. Instead, Lena found herself facing a younger version of the Kara she knew. Sans glasses, clad in her blue-and-red outfit, her skirt and cape rustling in the wind.

Supergirl.

“Supergirl?”

“Miss Luthor,” Kara said, raising her chin a little as if to look more secure, stronger, Lena mused, eliciting a small smile from her. How adorable.

“Something the matter?” She crossed her arms. “Has there been another attack you wish to accuse me of?”

Kara’s eyes widened and her tough exterior immediately dropped, heat rushing to her cheeks immediately.

“Rao, no, I’m sorry, that’s not… that’s not why I stopped by at all, I just…”

She shook her head, clearly trying to regain her composure, and Lena felt a little bad for her snarky comments. She figured she could blame it on dying in one universe and popping up in another universe just to almost die again.

“I’m sorry,” Kara said carefully, “I was just flying overhead when I accidentally heard you speak and you sounded… upset.” She had the decency to look at least a little guilty about listening in, Lena thought. “I didn’t mean to overstep.”

The last words were nothing shy of a whisper, and Lena’s heart actually ached at that. She sounded so young. Like she was afraid of everything and everyone, unsure of how to help, what to do, and what to think. Lena could only imagine the things that Superman must’ve told her about being in proximity to a Luthor, but at the same time, shutting people out, no matter their background, seemed very counterintuitive to someone like Kara. Someone so warm and loving.

Lena sighed.

“I’m sorry, Supergirl,” she said, earning a surprised look from Kara. “I shouldn’t have assumed, I just…” she took a deep breath, barely able to blink some prickling tears away before Kara could see. “It’s just been a very long day,” she concluded.

Kara nodded, almost glimmering when Lena opened up, even if it was just in one short sentence.

“I understand,” she said empathetically. “I can’t imagine how scary today must have been for you.”

“You have no idea,” Lena muttered, walking back into her office.

“If I may,” Kara said quickly, tiptoeing in behind her, “I know it’s not my place but, I know someone who buries herself in her work whenever the world closes in on her, and just, from my experience, there are better ways of coping than locking yourself in your office.”

Lena turned around and Kara abruptly froze in her tracks, blue eyes widening at the close proximity of Lena’s body to her own. She took a quick couple of steps back.

“Is that so?”

Kara didn’t speak, just nodded quickly.

Lena sighed. She shifted her shoulders and felt every muscle in her back protest.

“Well,” she whispered, raising her hand to rub at the protesting top of her spine with two fingers, “I suppose it couldn’t hurt to get some sleep.”

Kara nodded.

“Do you have someone who can come pick you up?”

Lena managed to wrangle a wry smile onto her face and nodded.

“I’ll go home in a bit, Supergirl.”

She nodded, looking around nervously like there was more she wanted to say but didn’t know how to.

“Anything else?” Lena added with a tilt of her head.

Kara’s face turned red and she quickly shook her head.

“Just… get home safe, okay?”

Lena let out a short laugh.

“Don’t worry, Supergirl. I don’t usually exceed my quota of two murder attempts a week.”

“Oh.”

Kara looked a little lost at that and Lena softened. She looked so unusually misplaced in her office, a red-and-blue character, straight from a comic book, Lena mused, in those four bare, sterile white walls. And yet she was there, steadfast because Lena had sounded upset. There wasn’t anything in the world that would scream ‘Kara’ more than that.

“I’ll get my things, Supergirl,” she said gently. “I’ll be home in half an hour, tops. I promise.”

Kara’s face seemed to relax at that too, and a soft, little smile accompanied the pink hue on her cheeks that hadn’t died down yet.

“That’s good to know, thank you.”

Lena smiled. “You can be sure to check me off your mission list to ensure that every citizen in National City gets their eight hours.”

Kara laughed at that, ducking away shyly, the tension draining away so quickly, it made Lena’s heart clench just the slightest bit.

Not her Kara smiled and nodded, turning back towards the open window.

“I’m glad to see my mission fulfilled then,” she teased. “I better be on my way then.”

“Plenty of other people to warn about the negative effects of bad sleeping habits,” Lena agreed.

Kara smiled softly and made her way to the balcony. Lena followed, leaving steps between them.

“I’m glad we spoke, Miss Luthor,” Kara said, almost as an afterthought.

Lena smiled. “Me too, Supergirl.”

“Get some rest.”

“You too.”

Kara smiled, baring her teeth this time, and Lena almost fell back seeing how innocent that made her look.

“Until next time, Miss Luthor.”

Lena nodded.

“Until next time, Supergirl.”

 

 

True to her word, Lena had gathered her things up after Kara had left, and had arrived at her penthouse less than thirty minutes later. Everything seemed to pass by without her like she wasn’t all that necessary for the progression of her own life, perhaps even an annoying burden to it. She mindlessly thanked her driver, allowed her jacket to be carried in by the doorman, thanking him as well, and allowing security to guide her to the private elevator, pushing the buttons to her floor. She thanked them too, she thought, but again with no real connection to what she was saying. Her entire trip to her apartment had gone by in such a blur, that it almost puzzled Lena when she stepped out of the elevator, and into her living room.

The light went on as soon as she had taken one step into her space, and Lena had to blink against the warm light showcasing her ivory walls, French windows, and sparkling white tiles.

It looked like it had been right before she disappeared. Before she was locked up for years and months. It seemed strange, like walking back into a dream. It definitely didn’t look anything like this when she left her universe. In fact, Lena remembered the apartment better the way she had found it after. After… after she’d wrangled herself out of the car dropping her off at her building, very much like it had today. She remembered how she hadn’t recognized the porter, but had no interest in getting to know him either. How she’d been too angry and bitter at the world to even consider exchanging any words with anyone in her surroundings. She remembered they’d tried to talk to her, explain to her the state of the building – but she hadn’t listened, she hadn’t cared much at all. She just wanted to finally get back to her own space.

She didn’t really react when she saw the place for the first time again. Someone had tried their best to clean up the apartment, but there was no way to recover from so much continuous damage. It had been looted, everything that Lena had once owned that had some value, gone. The walls were decorated with obscene, hateful messages aimed at her address, and her once pristine furniture had been through worse. The legacy of Lex and Lillian Luthor. The damage they had done to National City had inspired more people to take their vengeance out on an abandoned place, on an invisible Luthor. Lena had moved to LuthorCorp fairly quickly after. She hadn’t needed much and had moved in above her office, though she spent most of her time hauled up in her lab anyway. The years had passed in that fashion, in pain and discomfort, in L-Corp.

She hadn’t been to a place she’d called home in a very, very long time.

Yet here she was. The place was as gorgeous as the day she’d moved in. A black-and-white picture of her focused, begoggled face, Erlenmeyer flask in front of her, creased brow and determination flickering in her eyes, hung on the wall, taken and gifted to her by Jack. Her certificates and degrees were stylishly arranged in the space around it, and Lena felt almost sick at the sight of such hope and aspirations captured in those frames.

She paused in front of them, watching. Behind her, the elevator doors closed with a single sigh, the thick, soundproofed walls of her apartment shutting out the last remaining sound from the outside. Lena made her way to the kitchen and found a single glass in her sink. It felt surreal, watching a glass from five years ago, just as she’d left it that last morning.

 A trembling hand reached out, and with an artificial calmness, raised it, and filled it with tap water. She carried it around with her as she walked through the apartment, inspecting the curtains, the furniture, the sights of the city, as if she was doing it all for the very first time. And in a way, she mused, it kind of was. Everything felt familiar and new at the same time. A dream, a déjà vu. Beautiful, spotless, gleaming, just the way she had left it. And yet it seemed duller, emptier, and quieter than ever.

She felt a chill around her shoulders, and realized with some suddenness, that she was completely and utterly alone now. When she would go to sleep in that king-sized bed of hers, in one of the many rooms in her apartment, she would be alone. Lena trembled, looking into her empty, dark bedroom. Bed made up in cream sheets. Window looking out on the lights of the city. No one would walk by again. No guard would check in on her in invasive and annoying visits. No bright light would stay on overhead to ensure she wouldn’t try anything. No Different Lena with her whining complaints. No blood-curdling Lex to kick out. No Alex Danvers and her scoffing, holier-than-thou attitude. And no one would come by again with sweets, babbling stories, enthusiastic gusts of energy and information, and dozens upon dozens of books. That was all gone now.

It was all gone.

 

 

Lena didn’t sleep well for two weeks. If she could even call it sleep. She tossed and turned all night, suspicious of every shadow on her walls, every sign of thrumming electricity around her. Her silk sheets felt suffocating, and Lena found herself shrugging them off at night as if they would otherwise attack her in her sleep. She counted seconds, minutes, hours, always alert, never slumbering for more than an hour, even her hitching breath in her throat enough to wake her up. Alert, panicked, on edge.

She expected an enemy at every corner, at every hour.

She couldn’t remember how many times she’d already called down to the security personnel downstairs, asking them if anything suspicious had happened in the few minutes she’d been carelessly unconscious. The answer was always the same. Sometimes Lena wondered who would get her first; her brother, or the mental ward she’d most definitely be sent to if she kept worrying her personnel with manic actions and near-constant agitation and stress.

Even Jess, who was usually stoic and professional enough not to inquire too much into Lena’s personal life had shown concern lately. Showing up at her desk with whatever files Lena might need, as well as a concealer stick – in her sleep deprivation Lena often forgot to apply make-up entirely – a paracetamol, and a recommendation for the best psychologists in town. Lena hadn’t commented on it, just shot Jess a tired smile, but she didn’t think it was enough to reassure her yet.

Truthfully, Lena didn’t know how to fix it either.

She was in her own apartment, the place she had personally, purposefully transformed into her own space, and yet she’d never felt more like an outsider before. The place felt foreign, desolate, belonging in a magazine or used as a movie set… but not as a home. It felt nothing like a home.

At night, Lena sometimes longed for that cell. It was insane, laughably disgustingly remnant of Stockholm Syndrome, if she thought too long about it, but it was true either way. She missed the quiet. The not-quite-quiet. The humming of the lamps above, and the sound of the door opening every so often to let the guards in – or, when she was in luck, Kara.

And she missed Kara immensely. Her Kara. She didn’t really know she could miss just talking to somebody so damn much, but it was killing her. Sometimes she thought she could see her right out of the corner of her eye. She’d worried an entire room of prospective investors by standing up in the middle of the meeting, her chair wobbling in place, just because she thought she’d seen Kara in the corner of the room, behind the balding man in the grey suit. Lena had even thought she’d seen the tote bag full of new books in Kara’s arms. Like she was haunted by a sad-looking version of her Kara, who seemed equally confused to see her, alive and well.

Lena had thrown up right after that meeting, and had wiped the mascara tracks off her cheeks with a tissue, before going back to her day; not a soul the wiser. 

It was bad during the day, but it was infinitely worse at night. The days had her working hard, one fight with the media, investors, and blood-thirsty board members after another, fighting till her hands were cramped up, and the bags under her eyes were a deep blue-purple. But she could only put off going home for so long. No matter how hard she stretched her workdays, they always inevitably ended in her packing her bag, dragging her feet on the carpet, already sick at the prospect of facing those white walls again. She dreaded the moment she would have to enter her car, her driver greeting her kindly, before taking her to the last place she wanted to be. One time, she’d asked him to stop, and he had. He had asked where else he was meant to be taking her. Lena hadn’t known what to say. After two minutes of no word from her, her throat choked up, and she found she had no clue, no idea where else she could go. There was no one waiting for her, no one who wanted to see her. No one who needed her. She wanted him to drive her to Kara – to her Kara, the only person who would know what to say. Something corny, filled with relentless optimism and unearned kindness that Lena would soak up like she needed it to breathe. But he couldn’t. No one could bring her back. She’d held back tears in the backseat and had just shaken her head. Lena’s driver had understood and had silently driven her to her apartment, and Lena had cried on her way up in the elevator.

The days went on like that, the nights a little longer.

Lena didn’t do much in her sleep deprivation. She could only look at the ceiling of her bedroom, letting her fingers roam over the silk fabric of her sheets. She wondered and she worried, but mostly, she thought of Kara. She tried to remember the best parts of her, the sunny smiles, the understanding growing over time, the electricity in the way her hands touched Lena’s… but they were all overshadowed by that last memory. That last glimpse Lena had gotten. Her nights – the small parts of it she spent sleeping, and the hours in which her bloodshot eyes were trying desperately to peer through the darkness – she thought of Kara’s haunted, tear-stained face. The blood spatters mixing in with the green veins on her face. She regretted immensely, that the only good thing in her life would forever be overshadowed by that last, horrible moment, no matter how hard she tried otherwise. In those weeks, she did not once sleep through the night without waking up with Kara’s pained face in her eyes.

Still, Lena at least attempted to celebrate her wins – even the small ones. She tried to store her pain away, not hiding it completely, but allowing it to simmer in a small part of her brain, allowed herself to distinguish between the old Kara and the new one. How funny, she often mused, was it, that it had been easier for her to understand and deal with her own copy, than it was reconciling the fact that she was missing her Kara, while another one was starting to waltz into her life.

And waltz she did.

Kara seemed to permeate her life incessantly, showing up on every thinkable occasion, either with her brand new notepad in hand, or simply by bumping into Lena in every possible venue. Lena was astounded by the ease in which Kara started interfering with her life, talking her way into Lena’s life with such a lack of deviance or motives, that it left Lena sort of… helpless. She was everywhere. Lena couldn’t take two steps out into the world – which was still as hostile to her as she remembered – without tripping over fucking Kara Danvers, fresh-faced reporter, superhero by night, entangled in Lena’s life as if orchestrated by an all-knowing, all-powerful designer.

If she wasn’t saving her life as Supergirl, catching her after falling from her own fucking balcony, then it was as Kara, bumping into her in a shop. And Lena had such a hard time coming to terms with her presence in her life that she wanted to yell at her to leave and take her confusingly familiar and foreign face away from her. At the same time, Lena was almost desperately trying to see Kara. Because if Kara wasn’t bumping into her, Lena herself would twist and turn to find an opportunity to see her again.

It was embarrassing.

Showing up at her job for no reason after a particularly gnarly night in which she’d dreamt of Kara’s own blood, glowing green, gushing out of her chest, Lena’s own treacherous hands around her neck, choking her. No matter how hard she’d tried, she couldn’t pull her hands away from her, and Lena had had to watch, desperately screaming, how she was choking the life out of Kara’s body. She’d woken up with a scream, after only two hours of sleep – a personal record that week – and hadn’t slept again until the sun came up, and Lena had felt at least safe enough to fall unconscious again until she had to leave for work. Lena had needed to see Kara. Had needed to see those blue eyes, happy, curious and alive just to get through the day.

She was almost worried she was purposefully putting herself in danger to attract Supergirl’s presence into her life. Though she could honestly say that that could only be partially true, as the world around her did seem extremely inclined on destroying her. Still, she couldn’t help but wonder, especially when all those around her tried to get her to change her plans, whether or not she was reckless in some of her decisions, treading the line between risk and outright danger, just to see Supergirl appear again. Red cape, determined eyes, strong shoulders… and the gleam of innocent struggle, the nervous imposter syndrome that she seemed to carry with her everywhere she went. It made Lena want to reach out and ask her a hundred more questions, all of which she didn’t know Supergirl well enough to ask. She wanted to ask Kara, and felt frustrated she hadn’t used her time better, hadn’t asked more questions, hadn’t enquired deeper into every little aspect of her life, her past, her presence, what hopes she had for own future. Did she even picture one? Or was she so focused on dying for the good of the world that she didn’t allow herself to think about it more? It killed Lena a little more.

She felt like an addict sometimes. Willfully putting herself in the proximity of someone who didn’t know her and wasn’t ready to know her – someone Lena herself knew little of. She knew one version of Kara, an older, wiser, more scarred version of Kara. She felt protective of her – of both the older and younger version. One part of her wanted nothing more than to get Kara back the way she was, and the other part wished she never had to encounter what Kara had to make her so different in the future. So much harder, so much more on edge. She longed for every part of Kara – but she would never get her back.

But any semblance of her, any shine of what Kara would one day turn into was better than nothing, even if the pain that followed later, deep at night, would be unbearable. Kara was the only thing she needed, and the one thing she would never fully get. And Lena was so addicted to getting even the faintest fix of Kara that she would do it over and over again. But she wouldn’t let her in again. She wouldn’t indulge the woman’s obsessive need to get closer on a personal level. She had to see her, but she couldn’t let her in.

But she was dealing. She was doing what Luthors did. She was surviving. Surviving this new, unfamiliar world the best she could. She was coping. She was managing. So what if she had to deal with this world in her own way? Who could blame her for surviving this world on her own terms? She was alone. She had no one to turn to. She tried to see Kara as much as she kept her at a distance. She was alone. But she was coping.

She should’ve known this balance between sleep deprivation and desperation would come back to stomp her back to reality.

It happened so quickly too.

She was in the car with her driver, scrolling through the emails on her phone to put off the thought of that horrendous, empty apartment just a little while longer, when she was suddenly thrown forward in her seat, her seatbelt digging harshly into her skin through the flimsy fabric of her dress. Her phone flew out of her hand as her head knocked against the back of the seat before her.

“What was…” Lena had to halt that train of thought as a wave of nausea and a pounding in her chest fell over her. She just barely kept herself together enough not to give in to the overwhelming urge to vomit, and instead clawed her way to the door handle, jamming it open with one eye before stumbling out of the car.

The light hit her with such force that it made her wobble. For a horrifying second, blinded by the bright sunlight, Lena faltered and lost her balance. Before she could so much as open her mouth to let out a yelp, strong arms accompanied by a gust of wind caught Lena before she could hit the ground. She was gently steadied, and as the dark spots in front of her eyes disappeared, she saw exactly who had helped her.

Who else but her. Always her.

“Miss Luthor,” Supergirl asked. “Are you okay?”

“Supergirl,” Lena said, sounding a lot steadier than she felt. “I’m starting to think I should pay you a monthly subscription for all the times you’ve had to intervene in my life.”

Supergirl laughed, blushing a little.

“Oh no,” she said. “No that’s not… no.”

Lena didn’t have the energy to laugh, too busy trying to inconspicuously stretch her muscles. Her driver was furiously inspecting the front of the car, Supergirl’s handprint indented in its hood.

“So who was it this time?” Lena asked tiredly. “International terrorist? Vengeful Luthor victim? What?”

“Nothing so cool I’m afraid,” Supergirl said, turning to look at the hood of the car with a disapproving frown on her face. “Some guy ran a red light. I overheard your car hit the brakes and came down just in time to prevent a collision. No supervillain. Just a guy in a rush to get home.”

“Shit.”

Lena had to bow over, holding her stomach, just to keep her stomach from turning. She looked at the other car, the guy sitting down on the asphalt, his head in his hands, peering into the distance with a dazed expression on his face. She couldn’t hold her position for long and felt the pressure of a headache already building behind her eyes.

“Fuck me,” Lena sighed, squeezing her eyes shut as the world turned nauseatingly around her. “Of course it is.”

“Miss Luthor, are you – ”

“Fine, fine,” Lena muttered, not looking up. “I’m fine.”

“Miss Luthor, you could have a concussion, I heard your head bump pretty hard – ”

“I said I’m fine.”

Jesus. Lena let out a low groan, eyebrows knitted together as she tried hard to fight the hazy edges clouding her vision. From her unsteady position, she could see Supergirl’s boots shuffling nervously on the asphalt before her, and sighed internally.

“Supergirl,” Lena started, moving up, “I swear I’m – ”

Whatever she’d meant to say got stuck in her throat once she’d caught sight of Supergirl’s blonde hair gleaming in the sunlight, those concerned blue eyes staring at her.

For just one split second, she wasn’t Supergirl. She was Kara, the only light in the otherwise dark and smoky room, face twisted in agony and desperation, tears falling in Lena’s own, turning her sight blurry and hazy. Those blue eyes like gleaming lights in the otherwise dark room, illuminated by the glossy tears that clouded them. For a second she was the woman holding her close, whispering for her to stay. Begging her to stay, begging her to stay in her arms, to stay with her.And how Lena had longed to stay and go all at the same time. Go, and escape the horrible pain shooting through her chest. But stay in Kara’s soft embrace, bracing the pain just to hear her whispering sweet nothings into her hair again.

“Miss Luthor?”

Supergirl’s hand reached out to touch Lena’s upper arm, but she jerked it out of her hold. Supergirl’s eyes widened in surprise, and Lena just knew she could see the hurt just shimmering in there, but she couldn’t calm herself down enough to care.

What the fuck had just happened?

Lena’s breathing was so loud in her own ears, and her racing heartbeat just seemed to add to the pounding in her head.

“I have to go,” she muttered, barely able to look up, barely able to look Supergirl back in the eye.

“But Miss Luthor, your car, it isn’t even…”

“Can it drive?” Lena demanded.

Her driver looked up from the damage and nodded, just once. That was enough for Lena. She marched towards her car like her own personal ghost was on her tail, desperate to get out.

“Miss Luthor?” Supergirl tried again, one last time. “I need to tell the police what happened. I mean the insurance – ”

“Tell them to call my office. Thank you for your help, Supergirl,” Lena said curtly, not looking back. “I sure appreciate it.”

She left Supergirl there, standing around a little helplessly on the pavement, unsure of what had just happened. Lena didn’t have any answers for her. She hadn’t dared to look out the window until after they’d turned three separate blocks. There was no one behind them but the stream of cars heading home.

 

 

Lena was drunk. She knew she was. If not for the four times she’d already bumped her hip into her marble kitchen island without feeling a thing, then because of the tragically tiny swirl of remaining amber liquid in the expensive bottle whose seal she’d torn off as soon as she’d gotten home. She’d thrown her purse somewhere she didn’t know, and had strode towards the kitchen with a singular goal in mind. She remembered drinking the first glass, her hands trembling so much she’d spilled over the rim of it without caring. She remembered the second glass, so thirsty for it that she barely felt the smooth liquid burning only slightly down her throat. But all the other glasses were just blurs of lifting them to her lips, of drinking something so bittersweet like lemonade, of spilling the drink over her dress, over the marble kitchen counter – she giggled when she remembered how furious her father would be, a hypocrite of a drunk, over spilling something so expensive, so worthy of being cherished in tiny amounts. Well, fuck him, Lena thought. She might’ve even murmured it out loud, to an empty room. Just another sign that she might finally, after all these years, all its challenges and all that pain, be losing her mind.

Lena had to laugh to herself to hide how fucking terrifying that thought was. Losing her mind. After all her work? All her determination to live? To survive? Even after she’d finally found something – someone – akin to joy? Someone who had made her forget, even just for a moment? Someone who had lifted the burden of life so easily off her shoulders, just by talking?

It took Lena a while to realize she was crying.

She blinked confusedly against the blurriness of her vision, against the cold, wet patch on her wrist after she’d rubbed it against her face. Lena looked at her fingers and saw droplets of tears falling from their tips.

“Fuck,” she whispered.

Her hand trailed down her kitchen cabinet to the hidden bar and blindly picked out another bottle. Screwtop whiskey this time. Already opened this week.

Lena grabbed the bottle and her glass in one hand and turned on her seat. She slid off her barstool and almost fell off, catching herself on the ridge of her kitchen island at the last moment. She swung unsteadily on her feet, clinging first to her island and then to the wall, just to move safely around. She almost tripped over the thick, fuzzy carpet and cursed everything and everyone she could think of. The designer who’d put the stupid carpet there, her realtor for moving her in here in the first place, and Kara, for not being there.

Not anywhere.

Not for the first time she wondered if Kara was somewhere around her, waiting, listening, hoping to see her again. That’s how it happened the first time, wasn’t it? So was she here? Somewhere?

Lena turned her head, a shiver running down her spine. It sure didn’t feel like Kara’s warmth was anywhere near her.

Lena stumbled her way into her bedroom, but as she held on to the doorframes with both hands outstretched, the mere view of her bed in the dark, lonely, cold, almost hostile in its silence, made Lena want to scream. She wanted to, at least. But the shrill, husk of a sound that clawed its way out of her throat sounded more like a swallowed plea for help than the scream of feral anger she’d felt inside of her. Lena fell to her knees in the doorway, unable to bring herself to cross the threshold. She couldn’t. She couldn’t. Not anymore. Not one more time.

Lena couldn’t go back into that room again. She’d rather sleep on the floor than move back into that room. Everything about it just seemed to taunt her, haunt her. It was so fucking cold. So fucking lonely. Lena felt herself grow smaller just looking at it – like staring into a black hole. Sinking away in a place that oozed guilt, misery and tangible anger.

She shivered and turned around. That fucking pristine apartment. Those fucking white walls, closing in on her like a prison. Worse than a prison. Her heartbeat pounded in her ears.

“Stop,” she whispered, tears in her eyes. “Just stop!”

She fisted the fabric of her scotch-stained dress, trying to get some more room to breathe because fuck – her heart was straining against her ribcage, hammering angrily against the restrictions like it wasn’t used to it. Except it was her heart that wasn’t supposed to be there, the intruder. The thought of carving it out of her own chest was a disconcerting one, but also the only one that managed to instill some sense of calm in her head. She had to move.

No, fuck that. She wasn’t going back. Blood and energy pulsed through her veins, pounding in her head, and Lena felt her heart race in her chest, encouraged by her own misery and the alcohol she’d jammed in her body. She just had to breathe. When she turned around, though, the apartment around her felt hostile, consuming, dangerous in its cleanliness. A white lab, one in which Lena would be strapped to the bed while her mother and other doctors would cut open her chest and remove organ by organ, replacing it with poisonous steel and kryptonite.

A shiver wrecked through Lena’s body, and as she remembered her mother’s cold smile as her gloved fingers picked up a scalpel – and Lena screamed.

She threw the new bottle of whiskey against the wall in such a sudden burst of uncontrollable rage, and was surprised by how calm she felt when it shattered against the wall. She was even more surprised by how relieved she felt that the perfect, unblemished white color of her wall got stained with the amber liquid splattered across its surface. A burst of something that sounded like a hysterical laugh mixed in with a dry sob escaped her lips and Lena felt a desperate pang in her heart. She had to do it again. She needed to feel that rush again. So next was her empty glass. She threw it against the wall with a victorious, beautiful splintering sound and let out a shuddering breath, balling her hands into fists.

Again.

The bottle of water behind her was next. Then the glasses. Then a decorative plate or two she hadn’t picked out. Then her entire liquor cabinet. Every single thing smashed to pieces until the floor was covered in shards of glass.

Lena was panting. She was out of breath, her arms sore and her palms covered in cuts by the small pieces of glass that had managed to ricochet. But she felt euphoric. Renewed. The energy coursing through her was almost tangible, and she could taste something akin to happiness for the first time since she’d entered this new universe alone.

She understood, then. In the midst of the chaos in her apartment, in the loudness of the crumbling glass and her own breathing, what she had been missing all this time. 

She had changed. The world had changed. But somehow, they hadn’t changed in sync. They were both strangers to one another, hostile to each other in their vulnerability. Lena didn’t belong here, and the world didn’t know how to adapt to the old world she still carried with her, even if no one else could see it.

A spark of an idea – like the glorious three AM realizations she used to have in college in the midst of an essay, or the groundbreaking formula she saw forming in her own head while she was working in her lab – struck her all at once.

Lena stumbled her way over to her phone, drunk on the insight that had wormed its way into her brain, barely missing the chards of glass that had slid all over her hardwood floors.

She found it after a full five minute search, buried under a scarf under a barstool. It was only ten thirty at night. Lena dialed Jess’s number and was both relieved and a little frustrated when she picked up on the second ring.

“What’s the biggest bookstore in National City?” Lena asked before Jess had even had the time to greet her.

“That would be Portsmouth’s over on Fieldman’s street ma’am. Followed by a Barnes and Noble over on Fourth Avenue.”

Lena let out a shuddering sigh.

“I don’t suppose either of those is still open at this hour?”

“Miss Luthor, it would take me about three phone calls to get at least one of those bookstores to open for you.”

Lena bit her lip, her alcohol-induced confidence finally wavering.

“Jess, maybe…”

“I’m reaching out to my contact as we speak, Miss Luthor.”

And forty minutes later, Lena walked into the well-lit, warm, and welcoming entrance of the Portsmouth Independent Bookstore, where two confused but happy-looking young women welcomed her into the store with gentle, helpful smiles.

“Is there anything specific you’re looking for, Miss Luthor?” a kind brunette with short hair and dark, round glasses asked her.

“Well, yes, I…” she fumbled for the folded piece of paper in her pocket, “I… well I actually have a list.”

She’d written it down by heart, every title she’d had in her hands seared into her brain. Each memory accompanied by a different outfit Kara had worn, or the different ways in which she’d styled her hair. But every book cover had always been accompanied by piercing, kind, blue eyes, and how they’d studied Lena’s face as she handed them over. It had hurt so much, writing each title down, and yet Lena felt a relief she couldn’t comprehend when she had written them down.

“Okay,” the girl said kindly, “we can work with that.”

“Oh,” she opened the list and her eyes grew big reading the seamlessly endless list of books on her list.

“It’s a lot,” Lena said, apology already on her lips, “I’m sorry.”

“No, no!” the girl said, peering back up at Lena through her glasses with a kind, genuine shine in her eyes. Perhaps she could smell the alcohol on Lena’s breath. Perfume and a quick wash-up could only do so much to conceal it. “I can work with this. Just… there’s only me and Tessa working today, so it might take us a while to get everything you need.”

“Three,” Lena said, “I can look too.”

“Perfect!” the girl said.

And so all three of them set out with a separate list of books in hand, and after less than an hour, stacks of books in all colors and sizes filled up the check-out counter. Lena only had to request one change. A different version of a children’s story she’d teased Kara about so much, but one she wanted with her so bad. After seeing two covers she didn’t like, Lena finally had The Secret Garden with its colorful, plant-covered cover in her hands, and she felt a strange sense of connection and ease, like her Kara was right beside her, ready to throw the jokes right back in her face now.

“Miss Luthor?” Lena looked up to find the shopkeeper walking over with the list in hand. “I don’t know how to tell you this but, well, there were some titles we couldn’t find.”

“Oh?”

“It’s going to sound strange but… there were some titles I couldn’t find at all. Not just in the store but… anywhere. I searched by author, by title… nothing. It’s like these books don’t even exist. I mean, Conversations with Friends? I have Normal People by Sally Rooney, but nothing else.”

“Oh well, I must’ve been mistaken then,” Lena said, smiling her brightest smile.

“But there’s a couple more – ”

“I’ll just take the ones I’ve got then,” Lena said, effortlessly but effectively cutting off the conversation.

There was no explanation that would cover the entirety of time travel and intra-universal discoveries – and Lena was fine to wait a couple of years to rediscover the titles that hadn’t been published yet. She smiled so brightly at the shopkeeper that the girl’s eyes widened in surprise. She still looked a little taken aback, but hesitantly returned Lena’s smile when she found it was still there, before nodding and walking over to the register.

As she was ringing everything up, book by book in stacks that Lena was slightly concerned would even fit in the car, the bell above the door rang. And like fate, destiny, and some overly-invested powers above were conspiring against her, in walked no one but Kara Danvers, clad in jeans, a blue sweater, and her light, tan jacket.

“Oh Jesus.”

“Miss Luthor.” Kara’s eyebrows rose to her hairline before she shook her head and smiled a small, non-convincing smile. “What a coincidence.”

“I doubt it,” Lena muttered under her breath – and of course Kara had heard it, even if she barely let it show. Lena caught a hint of hurt though, shimmering in her blue eyes, and she felt a pang of guilt shoot through her hazy mind, knowing she had caused it.

“Sorry,” the girl said, “we’re closed.”

“Oh, sorry,” Kara said. “Just… the lights were on, and I thought…”

“It was an exclusive shopping thing,” the girl said apologetically. “Once everything’s rung up, we’re closing the doors again. We’ll open again at ten tomorrow.”

If she was put off by her extravagant behavior, Kara didn’t mention it.

“I understand,” Kara smiled, “I’ll get out of your hair. Thanks anyway.”

She turned around with a weak smile in Lena’s direction, but as she headed back to the door, panic rose in Lena’s chest. She felt a rush of that familiar dread creeping back up her veins, and suddenly knew exactly how she couldn’t continue. She couldn’t continue without Kara. The Kara from before, or the new Kara she was deliberately keeping at a distance. The fear made her heart race and her skin crawl.

“Kara?”

The name was out of her mouth before Lena even knew what to ask. Kara turned around, round, questioning, blue eyes looking back at her.

Lena’s eyes quickly swept over to the stacks of books beside her.

“Would you mind helping me carry these to the car?”

“Oh.”

Kara looked a little taken aback, and Lena couldn’t exactly blame her. The last time they’d talked, Lena had been so cold… She’d been so restless, so agitated, and her desire to see Kara and her desire to push her away with everything she had in her, had clashed in the worst way possible. She’d all but kicked Kara out of her office with a distinct We have mutual professional interests, Miss Danvers. I wouldn’t want you to mistake our professional benefits for anything more than that. And yet…

“Sure,” Kara smiled tentatively.

She walked over to the counter and her eyes grew as she saw the stacks growing bigger with each scanned book. She turned to Lena.

“Are you trying to buy a gift for everyone you know?”

Lena chuckled. “No, no, these are just for me. I’m having some trouble sleeping,” she said, as if it explained everything.

“I get that.”

The tiredness in her words, and the slight slump in her walk made Lena believe her. She wanted to ask, wanted to know more, but knew she was in no position to ask any such questions.

Kara nodded and looked over the stacks of books, picking one up. A broad smile spread over her lips.

“Never Let Me Go,” she said. “The book.”

Lena felt a familiar question passing over her lips, even though she already knew the answer to it.

“You’ve read it?”

Her question was as faint as a whisper, but Kara nodded anyway, eyes mercifully still trained on the book’s cover, so she couldn’t see the ghostly expression on Lena’s face.

“No, no, I haven’t. But I’ve watched the movie.”

A friend in college made her go with her.

The memory of Kara handing over that book with her own personal anecdote hit Lena like a cold shiver, but one that wilted into a blossoming warmth when Kara looked back at her with a smile that dimmed slightly when she seemed to remember who she was talking to.

“You should read it,” Lena whispered hoarsely.

“What?”

“You should read it. You’ll love it. I loved it. It’s just… I think you’ll like it.”

“But you just bought – ”

“Do you have a second copy?” Lena asked the shopkeeper.

She nodded and quickly scurried away to retrieve another copy. Lena turned back to Kara.

“I insist,” she said before Kara could protest. “Please.”

The shopkeeper came back with the second copy and continued ringing everything up.

“Well thank you,” Kara said shyly. “I guess now I’ll have to help you load everything in your car.”

Lena laughed, and for a short moment, she felt like things would be alright. She felt a spark of lightness that uplifted her spirits just long enough for her to feel a sense of hope. For the first time since she’d come to this world, she felt like she’d made a good decision. One that would steer her life forward, and not keep her in this terrible space of limbo.

So after they’d thoroughly thanked the bookkeepers and had loaded everything in Lena’s car, she stood outside with Kara, their breaths blossoming in tiny clouds in the night sky.

“I guess I’ll be on my way then,” Kara said, seemingly more shy than before, without the shopkeepers there to protect her from being alone with Lena. “Thanks for the book again.”

“Kara, would you like to get coffee sometime after work?”

The question shook both of them, but Lena had never felt more right than when the question passed over her lips. The surprise was written all over Kara’s face, her blue eyes wide and utterly charming.

“Are you looking to do a personal piece for CatCo? Or do you have a story you need me to pursue? Because if so, I could probably make some time on Thursday to come by L-Corp and – ”

“No,” Lena said. “Not for CatCo. I just… I’d like to thank you.”

Kara’s eyes grew even bigger, her head tilting just slightly.

“For what?”

Lena’s struggled not to let her smile wobble.

She gestured to the books in her car. “For carrying my books? Or for protecting the last remaining bit of my reputation by handing over that USB drive, when we both know it could’ve done you a world of good to publish it.”

“Oh.”

Kara didn’t really seem to know how to answer that, but she blushed slightly and nodded.

“So you’ll let me take you out for coffee? As a thank you?”

A smile broke through the surprise, and Lena couldn’t stop herself from smiling back.

“Eh, sure, of course. I would love that.”

“Well great,” Lena smiled, yet again feeling the push that what she was doing was right. And what a glorious feeling that was. “I’ll be in touch then.”

“I would like that,” Kara smiled back.

 

 

Lena worked all through the night and through the next day to throw every decorative fucking thing she owned out of the white bookcase in her apartment. She had cleaners come in and clean out all the glass and broken shit she’d thrown against her walls without explaining a thing to anyone. Jess had made not a singular protesting sound when Lena had called the day off and had asked no questions about her nightly burst of inspiration that led to her bookstore visit, and Lena was grateful for it.

After everyone had left, and she had single-handedly filled the bookcase up with all the dozens of books the bookstore had been able to provide for her, only then had Lena been able to take a step back, and smile a watery smile.

There it was.

The proof that her Kara had been real. That what had happened, was real. She had suffered. She had died. And she had found someone who loved her enough to hold her in her darkest moment. Someone had cared for her. Someone had understood her. Had listened to her. She had loved someone enough to set aside her anger and hunger for blood. And someone, somehow, had loved her back. Had loved her enough to brush aside her hair, and tell her things would be okay. Had loved her enough to kiss her forehead and brave waves of hurt, just to hold her close, and remind her she wasn’t alone.

And that’s what Lena would see every day now, reflected in the colorful covers of books that Kara had given her once, and that Lena had found back in this universe. And with every book that was yet to come out in the future, she would see Kara again. She would feel her again. She would be real once more.

And when Lena cried that night, choking sobs wrecking through her shaking body as she’d covered her mouth with her hands to stifle the sounds, right in front of the dozens of books before her, there was not just sadness for what she had lost. She wasn’t just mourning the woman she’d lost, or the life that had been taken away from her. Inside, alongside the pain and loss, there was a deep sense of gratitude for the woman who had given her this chance.

A second chance. And she was determined not to fuck it up.

She only wished Kara were here to see it.

 

 

Over time, Lena was surprised by how easily and quickly this Kara became her Kara, in the best sense of the word.

It was as if that day in the bookstore had changed the course of Lena’s life dramatically. Like someone was finally on her side. To reward her for the one good decision she’d made in her life; remembering her past beautifully, artfully, without clinging to hatred and pain. And the universe’s reward was Kara.

She surprised Lena with baked goods, a dose of good news each day, rants about her boss at work through overly-emojified text messages, and hundreds of bright smiles that made Lena’s heart float. She invited Lena out on walks through the city, discussed every issue under the sun with her, without ever making Lena feel undervalued or dismissed. She was genuinely appreciative of Lena’s time, her thoughts, and her presence. Lena took her time to introduce Kara to some books, and almost cried the first time Kara gushed over a book the Other Her had given her months ago, in another universe. In another lifetime. Lena couldn’t even begin to understand how someone as sweet as Kara could find it in her to be so close to someone as dark and brooding as Lena, but to Kara, it seemed to come naturally.

She defended her when Lena was at her lowest, and held her in her arms when Lena lost Jack again.


Somehow it was worse, meeting him again, remembering how someone had come into her office, ages ago, to tell her of his passing. How dismissive she’d been, but how painful it had felt to feel the last piece of her heart dying with him.

Meeting him again, knowing he would die soon was infinitely worse.

But Kara was there. And Kara helped her through it. Every day, she was there. She became her ally, her protector, her confidante, and her very best friend, all in one. And when Kara was left heartbroken after her boyfriend was sent away, it became Lena’s turn to keep Kara from falling apart.
